title: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
title_en: How to tell a cyberattack from a plain old outage
author: WIRED
article_content:
Over the past week, anyone could be forgiven for wondering whether a Diehard IV –style cyberwar had finally arrived in the US.

Across just four consecutive business days, a mass Microsoft exchange outage broke IT services for thousands of companies, a Federal Aviation Administration tech screw-up grounded airplanes across the country, a software problem affecting JPMorgan Chase caused another round of disruption, a United Airlines system glitch delayed flights yet again, and an NSA classified network’s downtime left the agency’s staff sitting at home waiting to return to their office at Fort Meade. In the midst of a US war with Iran and rising fears of AI-enabled hacking, this still-unfolding comedy of IT errors colliding across American infrastructure felt to plenty of observers like more than a coincidence.

Yet there’s still no evidence that any one of these clustered technological failures were related, much less caused by hackers. Their improbable, sequential timing left Americans anxiously doomscrolling for signs of foul play. But in cases like these, it’s the job of cybersecurity analysts (and reporters at WIRED) to determine—vibes aside—whether the latest tech outage was actually an accident or the result of a cyberattack.

The baseline for that fact-finding, as anyone tasked with investigating these incidents will tell you, is that the vast majority of these digital breakdowns are not the result of malicious intent but rather casualties of IT admins’ constant war to keep computer systems from collapsing under the weight of their own complexity.

“I’ve just seen enough times where we thought maybe it’s a cyberattack and it turns out it’s not. Sometimes it will be, but typically not,” says Matthew Prince, CEO of the Internet infrastructure company Cloudflare. “Right now, most of what we’re seeing is the standard background noise. Stuff breaks, and that’s just the nature of complex systems.”

So in the interest of soothing the country’s rattled nerves and helping us all find ground truth amid seemingly endless tech catastrophes, we at WIRED present our general guide to determining whether a tech outage is the result of a cyberattack. So take a breath—maybe open the bunker door to let in some fresh air—and read on.

### 1. Start with a presumption of innocence–or negligence

The process of determining the cause of an IT service outage should begin with the assumption that it was an accident, says cybersecurity researcher Doug Madory.

As the head of Internet analysis at the network security firm Infoblox, Madory says he monitors as many as a dozen network outages a day. Only around “one in a thousand,” he says, turns out to have been caused by hackers. “One’s default position should be that it isn’t a cyberattack,” he says, “unless there is some concrete evidence to the contrary.”

Given the rarity of cyberattacks compared to outages as a whole, it’s wise to look at other potential causes first. “Most big outages that look like attacks are self-inflicted,” says João Tomé, the Internet research editor at network data company IPinfo. (In response to WIRED’s questions, Tomé also wrote his own guide for distinguishing outages from cyberattacks.) The usual suspects, he says, include “a bad update, a configuration change, a cable cut, or a power failure.”

### 2. Look at status updates from organizations that might be involved

In the scramble to understand what’s really happening with a given outage, it can sometimes be difficult to tell which sites and services are actually down. And there can be a few reasons for this muddled picture. Sometimes, an outage occurs within a foundational service like a big cloud provider. Major downtime within Amazon Web Services, for example, can cause a cascade of other failures among the company’s customers, who are all dependent on that infrastructure.

In other cases, multiple services can seem to be having outages and producing errors but are functioning normally and only having problems when they interact with an entity that’s down. This appears to have been the case in this week’s bank outage: Multiple banks appeared to be having issues, but they all seem to have been linked to certain inter-institutional transactions that involved JPMorgan Chase. Another good example of this scenario is situations where it may appear that multiple wireless carriers are struggling, but all of the failed calls actually involve one network that’s having an outage.

On top of these, there are also scenarios where one or more large services are down, and false (typically accidental or anecdotal) reports of additional outages create further confusion and opacity.

It can all feel overwhelming, even impossible, to attempt to parse these situations yourself—but there is a concrete place to start. If you think a website or service from a major tech company may be down, look for acknowledgment of the situation on their verified social media accounts or in the “newsroom” press release section of their websites. And keep in mind that you can find these pages and social media accounts through search engines, so you definitely don’t need to be familiar with every company’s communications strategy. Use this same approach for government agencies and other institutions.

Another concrete and vital source of information that you can find through search engines is what’s often known as “status dashboard” pages. Large digital platforms specifically offer these informational pages to provide transparency into whether different components of their service are functioning normally or dealing with issues. In a major incident, companies often thread incremental updates about system restoration on the status dashboard. AWS, Google Cloud Platform, and Microsoft Azure all offer these landing pages, and there are similar ones for other services like Meta business products, Google Workspace, telecom companies, AI companies, and so on.

### 3. Check trusted sources of network data

When a cascading tech failure causes outages across many services at once, and the point of failure isn’t clear, sources of network data that monitor the Internet at a broad scale can also help determine the underlying issue. Amanda Meng, a research scientist at Georgia Tech who helps run its Internet Outage Detection and Analysis service, or IODA, points to not only IODA’s own data—and its social media accounts on BlueSky and Mastodon —but also tools like Cloudflare Radar and Watch the Net. Infoblox’s Madory also posts his own findings about network outages on his social media accounts.

When IODA sees evidence of a network disruption, “we’ll look at the timing of it, the start, the end, the network affected, anything we can find out about it, and then try and connect it with what we see from reporting,” Meng says. That scope, location, and timing of an outage can help determine a suspected cause, whether it’s a single network that might be the victim of a buggy update, a region cut off by damage to a fiber optic cable or, in rarer instances, a cyberattack or even a government purposefully cutting off Internet access to its citizens to stifle protests.

Even with those network clues, however, Meng advises returning to step two: Once an affected service is identified, its actual owners are often the best source to monitor for updates. “Usually the operators have the most information about what’s actually going on,” she says.

### 4. Look for claims of responsibility

Most often, mea culpa updates from companies or government agencies confirm an outage is caused by a tech mishap. In the rarer cases when that downtime results from an actual cyberattack or hacker breach, however, the hackers responsible often claim responsibility in some form.

Ransomware gangs, perhaps the most common source of serious malicious Internet disruption, publicize their breaches on dark web pages that list their targets for the purposes of extortion, sometimes with a countdown timer designed to pressure victims to pay before they leak stolen information. In other cases, like the NotPetya or WannaCry worms—two of the worst cyberattacks in history—the hackers’ self-perpetuating code left behind ransom messages on machines that quickly spread on social media as the attacks unfolded. Ideological “hacktivist” groups—or state-sponsored hackers working for military or intelligence agencies but posing as hacktivists—also often take credit for their cyberattacks on platforms like X, Telegram, or their own websites. These messages then quickly spread to social media and through news reports.

Even these statements, however, should be taken as just another significant data point: Hacker groups exaggerate, misdirect, or lie when it serves their purposes. And some significant mass hacking incidents—such as the Mirai attack on the Internet infrastructure company Dyn in 2016 that took down thousands of websites—have been accompanied by no public message at all from the hackers responsible.

In cases where neither the perpetrator of a hacking incident nor its target has confirmed the attack, confirmation can sometimes come first from a government agency—such as the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency—or even from threat intelligence researchers at private cybersecurity firms. Government and industry investigators sometimes post their findings to their websites or share them with media, but it often takes days, weeks, or even months to come to confirmed conclusions. Hence, step five.

### 5. Sit tight and reserve judgment

If all these other measures of determining the cause of an outage don’t offer a clear understanding of the situation, the best approach may be patience. “It’s going to get a little conclusive at some point,” Madory says. “Sometimes you just have to just sit and wait.”

Aside from the time it takes for companies to admit to their screwups—or hackers to claim a win—the length of an outage can also sometimes offer a clue to its cause. A faulty update, power outage, or cascading bug can often be resolved quickly. Determined hackers who have maximized their damage, who shift tactics to outsmart defenders, or who may still be in a network they’ve breached can cause far longer and more severe outages. “A rollback takes minutes or hours,” Tomé says, referring to reverting to older code as a fix for a faulty update that introduces a bug. “Ransomware takes days or sometimes even weeks.”

In other words, as with all breaking news, when facts are in short supply, it’s better to maintain skepticism about early rumors or conspiracy theories and wait for more concrete evidence.

In the information vacuum that precedes that evidence, it can be easy to see connections between events that may just be coincidences. What are the odds, you may ask, that five major IT outages occurred on a sequential Thursday, Friday, Monday, and Tuesday?

For Doug Madory, who tracks those network outages every day of the week, that string of failures may just be a sign of the increasing complexity of technology—and how fundamentally our civilization has come to depend on it. “For better or worse, modern society is completely mediated through Internet-based services. They have outages from time to time. And that’s a reality I don’t think we’ll ever completely eliminate,” Madory says.

“If you’re immersed in that world of looking at outages for years on end, then they don’t really surprise you,” he adds. “You just try to understand what’s different about each one. And maybe what we can learn from it.”

This story originally appeared on wired.com.

article_content_zh:
在过去的一周里，任何人都可能会怀疑“顽固分子四世”式的网络战争是否终于来到了美国。

在连续四个工作日内，微软交易所的大规模宕机导致数千家公司的 IT 服务中断，美国联邦航空管理局的技术故障导致全国各地的飞机停飞，影响摩根大通的软件问题造成了另一轮中断，美国联合航空公司的系统故障再次延误了航班，国家安全局机密网络的宕机导致该机构的工作人员坐在家里等待返回米德堡的办公室。在美国与伊朗的战争以及对人工智能黑客攻击的担忧日益加剧之际，这一仍在上演的美国基础设施发生 IT 错误冲突的喜剧让许多观察家觉得这不仅仅是巧合。

然而，仍然没有证据表明这些集群技术故障中的任何一项都是相关的，更不用说是由黑客造成的了。他们不可思议的连续时间让美国人焦急地寻找不法行为的迹象。但在此类情况下，网络安全分析师（以及《连线》记者）的工作就是确定（抛开舆论）最新的技术中断究竟是意外还是网络攻击的结果。

正如任何负责调查这些事件的人都会告诉您的那样，事实调查的基线是，绝大多数数字故障不是恶意意图的结果，而是 IT 管理员为防止计算机系统在自身复杂性的重压下崩溃而不断进行的斗争的结果。

互联网基础设施公司 Cloudflare 的首席执行官马修·普林斯 (Matthew Prince) 表示：“我已经见过很多次了，我们认为这可能是网络攻击，但事实证明并非如此。有时会，但通常不会。” “现在，我们看到的大部分都是标准的背景噪音。东西会损坏，这就是复杂系统的本质。”

因此，为了安抚这个国家紧张的神经，并帮助我们所有人在看似无休无止的技术灾难中找到真相，我们在《连线》杂志上提出了确定技术中断是否是网络攻击造成的一般指南。因此，深吸一口气——也许打开掩体门让新鲜空气进来——然后继续阅读。

### 1. 从无罪推定或疏忽开始

网络安全研究员 Doug Madory 表示，确定 IT 服务中断原因的过程应该首先假设这是一次事故。

作为网络安全公司 Infoblox 的互联网分析主管，马多里表示，他每天监控多达十几起网络中断事件。他说，只有大约“千分之一”是由黑客造成的。 “人们的默认立场应该是这不是网络攻击，”他说，“除非有一些具体的证据表明相反的情况。”

考虑到网络攻击与整体中断相比很少见，明智的做法是首先考虑其他潜在原因。网络数据公司 IPinfo 的互联网研究编辑若昂·托梅 (João Tomé) 表示：“大多数看起来像是攻击的大型中断都是人为造成的。” （在回答《连线》杂志的问题时，Tomé 还编写了自己的指南，用于区分网络中断和网络攻击。）他说，通常的嫌疑包括“错误的更新、配置更改、电缆切断或电源故障”。

### 2. 查看可能涉及的组织的状态更新

在争先恐后地了解给定中断的实际情况时，有时很难判断哪些站点和服务实际上已关闭。造成这种混乱局面的原因可能有几个。有时，像大型云提供商这样的基础服务会发生中断。例如，亚马逊网络服务内的重大停机可能会导致该公司的客户出现一系列其他故障，而这些客户都依赖于该基础设施。

在其他情况下，多个服务可能看似出现中断并产生错误，但实际上运行正常，并且仅在与发生故障的实体交互时才会出现问题。本周的银行停电事件似乎就是这种情况：多家银行似乎都出现了问题，但它们似乎都与涉及摩根大通的某些机构间交易有关。这种情况的另一个很好的例子是，看起来多个无线运营商都在苦苦挣扎，但所有失败的呼叫实际上都涉及一个发生中断的网络。

除此之外，还存在一种或多种大型服务停机的情况，并且关于额外中断的虚假（通常是意外或轶事）报告会造成进一步的混乱和不透明。

title: Anthropic’s Public Debut Sets Up ‘Experiment’ in Corporate Power
title_en: Anthropic’s Public Debut Sets Up ‘Experiment’ in Corporate Power
author: Cory Weinberg
article_content:
Todd Underwood, a former Anthropic engineering leader, fielded a stream of calls in recent months from investment managers eager to gain his insider view on the artificial intelligence giant’s business strategy ahead of this week’s initial public offering.

But few of the questions focused on an aspect of the company Mr. Underwood viewed as a crucial asset: Anthropic’s unusual governance structure.

The company is set to become by far the most valuable company on the stock market with the legal designation of a public benefit corporation, or P.B.C. That status requires Anthropic to prioritize its corporate mission — to develop safe A.I. systems “for the long-term benefit of humanity” — in addition to the customary sole focus on value for stockholders.

The company’s public benefit mandate is guarded partly by a five-member “long-term benefit trust,” which includes Ben Bernanke, the former Federal Reserve chair.

The company “will choose to do things in favor of safety rather than in favor of making money,” said Mr. Underwood, who has been sought out by investors as a former employee for insights into the company. He added that he agreed with that focus but thought it might turn off some investors.

The company’s public offering sets up an important test as Anthropic goes from one of the most closely watched private companies in the world to one of the most scrutinized.

Anthropic is expected to spend its first two years as a publicly traded company asking investors for patience as it burns hundreds of billions of dollars of cash to invest in new chips and data centers. It is also facing increasing calls from A.I. safety advocates, as well as some of its own employees, to slow down its pace of training new models.

On Wednesday, the company is expected to sell roughly $65 billion in shares, making it the second-largest I.P.O. after SpaceX’s earlier this year. It also has $26 billion of investments lined up from tech giants like Nvidia and Microsoft.

Anthropic’s expected market capitalization, more than $1.4 trillion, would make it 30 times as valuable as the next public benefit corporation that trades on the stock market, the software maker Veeva Systems.

Anthropic was founded as a public benefit corporation in 2021, and formed its long-term benefit trust in 2023 as a way to give the structure teeth, ensuring the company balances goals for shareholders and its broader mission. The structure is taxed the same as any corporation.

The trust is made up of a group of “financially disinterested” experts in economics, science and global health who don’t own Anthropic stock, the company said in its offering prospectus. The group has the power to appoint and remove several of the company’s board members, authority that is typically given only to shareholders.

Adding to the unusual leadership structure, the company also spent the months leading up to its public offering locking in new authority for the executives who started the company nearly six years ago, according to securities filings.

The company created a new class of shares this fall for its unusually large co-founding team — seven executives, including the chief executive, Dario Amodei — that give them 50.1 percent of voting control over the company, collectively. The founders have the ability to appoint other board members.

A founder-controlled board committee can also help overrule one of the trust’s four board appointments, reducing the trust’s power, said Jesse M. Fried, a Harvard law professor who has studied Anthropic’s corporate structure.

The trust’s authority was “watered down” as a result of the changes, but they don’t “fundamentally change the governance of the company,” he added.

Anthropic’s structure is unique when compared with other publicly traded companies, corporate governance experts said.

“I don’t know if I can really compare it to anything else,” said Douglas Chia, a senior fellow at Rutgers Law School who advises companies on corporate governance. “It’s going to be an interesting experiment.”

The Council of Institutional Investors, an advocacy group that represents public, union and corporate pension funds, has long been critical of arrangements that give founders voting control disproportionate to their financial stakes. The group wrote a letter this year expressing concerns that when SpaceX went public, it gave its founder, Elon Musk, dominant voting control.

The group will “wait and see” how Anthropic’s structure plays out, said Glenn Davis, the council’s executive director. The founders’ immense voting power means that “ultimately the founders are accountable to themselves,” rather than shareholders, he added.

The layered structure could still challenge investors’ understanding of the company and the group of people who govern it, said Paul Abrahimzadeh, a senior partner at the tech investment firm 1789 Capital.

Still, investor enthusiasm was inevitable despite the uncertainties, he added. “You have to own it. The question is at what price?”

article_content_zh:
前 Anthropic 工程负责人托德·安德伍德 (Todd Underwood) 近几个月接到了一系列投资经理的电话，他们渴望在本周的首次公开募股之前了解他对这家人工智能巨头业务战略的内部看法。

但很少有问题集中在安德伍德先生视为公司重要资产的一个方面：Anthropic 不同寻常的治理结构。

该公司将成为迄今为止股票市场上最有价值的公司，并获得公共利益公司 (P.B.C.) 的法律指定。这种地位要求 Anthropic 优先考虑其企业使命——开发安全的人工智能。除了通常只关注股东价值之外，还建立了“为了人类的长期利益”的系统。

该公司的公共利益使命部分由五名成员组成的“长期利益信托基金”负责，其中包括前美联储主席本·伯南克。

安德伍德先生表示，该公司“将选择做有利于安全的事情，而不是有利于赚钱的事情”。他曾作为前雇员受到投资者的追捧，希望了解公司的情况。他补充说，他同意这一重点，但认为这可能会令一些投资者望而却步。

随着 Anthropic 从世界上最受关注的私营公司之一转变为最受关注的私营公司之一，该公司的公开发行提出了一项重要的考验。

Anthropic 预计将在上市后的头两年里，要求投资者保持耐心，因为该公司将消耗数千亿美元的现金来投资新的芯片和数据中心。它还面临着来自人工智能的越来越多的呼吁。安全倡导者以及一些自己的员工放慢了培训新车型的步伐。

周三，该公司预计将出售约 650 亿美元的股票，使其成为第二大 IPO。继今年早些时候 SpaceX 之后。它还获得了 Nvidia 和微软等科技巨头 260 亿美元的投资。

Anthropic 的预期市值将超过 1.4 万亿美元，这将使其价值是下一家在股票市场交易的公益公司——软件制造商 Veeva Systems 的 30 倍。

Anthropic 于 2021 年作为一家公益公司成立，并于 2023 年成立了长期利益信托基金，以此强化结构，确保公司平衡股东目标和更广泛的使命。该结构与任何公司一样征税。

该公司在招股说明书中表示，该信托由一群经济、科学和全球健康领域“财务上无私”的专家组成，他们不持有 Anthropic 股票。该集团有权任命和罢免公司的几名董事会成员，这种权力通常只授予股东。

根据证券备案文件，除了不寻常的领导结构之外，该公司还在公开募股前的几个月里为近六年前创办该公司的高管锁定了新的权力。

今年秋天，该公司为其规模异常庞大的联合创始人团队（包括首席执行官达里奥·阿莫代 (Dario Amodei) 在内的七名高管）创建了一种新的股票类别，这使他们总共拥有公司 50.1% 的投票控制权。创始人有能力任命其他董事会成员。

研究 Anthropic 公司结构的哈佛大学法学教授杰西·M·弗里德 (Jesse M. Fried) 表示，由创始人控制的董事会委员会还可以帮助否决信托公司四项董事会任命中的一项，从而削弱信托公司的权力。

title: Alibaba Earnings Rebound Sharply as AI Profitability Improves
title_en: Alibaba Earnings Rebound Sharply as AI Profitability Improves

inline_images.caption: Alibaba Earnings Rebound Sharply as AI Profitability Improves (Source: Wall Street Journal)
inline_images.caption_en: Alibaba Earnings Rebound Sharply as AI Profitability Improves (Source: Wall Street Journal)
inline_images.caption_zh: Alibaba Earnings Rebound Sharply as AI Profitability Improves (来源：华尔街日报)
inline_images.alt: Alibaba Earnings Rebound Sharply as AI Profitability Improves

author: Wall Street Journal
article_content:
Revenue increased 10% to RMB271.519 billion ($40.498 billion), according to the company’s earnings release. Non-GAAP net income rose 92% to RMB19.909 billion, while adjusted diluted earnings per American depositary share increased 86% to RMB8.10 ($1.21). Each ADS represents eight ordinary shares.

The stock traded at $83.00, down $1.37, or 1.62%, in a premarket quotation timestamped 6:54 a.m. EST on November 19, 2026. Its November 18 closing price was $84.37 at 4 p.m. EST. Research and market data were checked at 7:04 a.m. EST; premarket prices can move sharply in thinner trading.

Reuters reported that revenue exceeded an LSEG consensus of RMB269.81 billion, but adjusted earnings per ADS missed expectations of RMB11.16. The mixed result helps explain why faster cloud growth did not immediately lift the shares.

Reported net income attributable to ordinary shareholders rose 207% to RMB64.535 billion, benefiting from investment gains excluded from adjusted earnings.

AI Cloud and Compute Services revenue increased 53% to RMB60.973 billion. External-customer recurring revenue grew 67%, excluding compute-equipment solutions. The segment’s adjusted earnings before interest, tax and amortisation increased 121% to RMB8.838 billion, with a 14.5% margin.

That improvement did not cover the losses in a separate AI business. AI Labs and Applications recorded an adjusted EBITA loss of RMB10.503 billion, against RMB3.435 billion a year earlier. Revenue in that unit increased 51% to RMB4.435 billion, but investment in AI capabilities and higher Qwen application inference costs weighed on profitability.

Capital expenditure reached RMB50.477 billion. Operating cash flow increased 55% to RMB15.690 billion, yet company-defined free cash flow deteriorated to an outflow of RMB34.472 billion from RMB21.840 billion. Over six months, free-cash outflow totalled RMB79.142 billion.

Alibaba retained RMB487.929 billion in cash and other liquid investments at September 30. Its balance-sheet bank borrowings and listed categories of notes and exchangeable bonds totalled a calculated RMB267.209 billion. The broad liquidity measure includes treasury investments; it is larger than cash alone.

Financing also carries a shareholder cost. The company raised net proceeds of HK$80 billion through new shares during the half year. Quarterly weighted-average diluted ordinary shares used for non-GAAP earnings increased to 19,777 million from 19,168 million, showing dilution alongside the investment programme.

The commerce picture remained uneven. China e-commerce revenue declined 5%, although customer-management revenue would have risen 1% excluding a subsidy-related accounting effect. International e-commerce revenue fell 8%, partly because EU customs reforms affected AliExpress. Alibaba E-commerce Group’s adjusted EBITA nevertheless increased 243%, helped by improved quick-commerce operations.

Broker targets remain much higher than the share price. Dated records show Goldman Sachs at Buy/$177 on November 19, Bernstein at a provider-normalised Buy/$165 on November 18, Bank of America at Buy/$178 on November 11, and Mizuho at a provider-normalised Buy/$200 on November 3.

Earlier assessments include J.P. Morgan’s Overweight/$200 on October 12, Jefferies’ Buy/$192 on October 8 and UBS’s Buy/$206 on September 22. Most predate these results; Goldman’s same-day entry does not establish whether its assessment followed the release.

Alibaba’s stronger cloud economics are offset by AI development losses and negative free cash flow. Its published trailing earnings multiple of 19.26 compares with 18.99 at fiscal 2026 year-end and JD.com’s (Nasdaq:JD) 15.23. Investment gains, different business models and database timing limit those comparisons.

Over the next 12 months, monitor external cloud growth, AI spending relative to cash generation, and commerce profitability. Slower cloud demand, persistent application losses or further dilutive financing without better cash returns would weaken the recovery case.

发布于美国东部时间 2026 年 11 月 19 日上午 05:44

随着人工智能盈利能力和电子商务业务的改善，阿里巴巴集团第二财季利润大幅增长。

这家总部位于杭州的公司加大力度将人工智能作为增长动力，但这一举措面临着对中国芯片出口加强审查的新风险。它承诺在三年内花费超过 530 亿美元来开发支持人工智能的硬件和软件。

它在这方面的成功是在其他大型科技公司和初创公司面临的挑战中保持竞争力的关键。但事实证明，近几个季度全力投入人工智能已经拖累了盈利能力，给阿里巴巴实现人工智能目标带来了压力。

其最新结果看起来令人放心。

周四，阿里巴巴表示，截至 9 月份的三个月净利润较上年同期增长两倍，达到 645.35 亿元人民币，相当于 96.8 亿美元。 FactSet调查的分析师此前预期为237.2亿元人民币。收入增长约10%至2715.2亿元，也好于市场预期。

阿里巴巴将利润的大幅改善归因于净投资收入和运营收入的增加。

盈利超出预期之际，阿里巴巴正准备其芯片部门T-Head在香港上市，投资者认为这是对其生产内部半导体努力的重大验证。据野村证券估计，该业务的估值可达 850 亿美元。

title: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
title_en: What a billion-dollar deal says about the US battery market
author: Casey Crownhart
article_content:
After a tough few years littered with some high-profile failures, there’s some positive news for next-generation batteries in the US.

Sila just signed an agreement with Panasonic Energy, a global battery manufacturer, to supply silicon-carbon anode material, a possible key to smaller, lighter batteries. It’s a deal that Sila says could be worth more than $1 billion over time.

This arrangement also shows how much the politics of batteries have shifted lately. A major part of the financial backing for this factory’s production is a $1.4 billion loan from the Trump administration’s Defense Department. While batteries can be a major tool to help drive the energy transition and cut emissions, right now much of the industry is more focused on geopolitics.

Founded in 2011, Sila makes silicon-based anodes for lithium-ion batteries. The big selling point here is the potential to improve energy density—Sila’s anode weighs a fifth as much as the graphite used in anodes today and cuts the volume in half, according to the company. So using this new material enables batteries to pack more energy into the same weight and volume, allowing longer range for EVs, for example. The material can also deliver more power and recharge faster, compared with conventional chemistry.

We’ve been following Sila (and its competitors) for years. My colleague James Temple covered the company when its battery first appeared in Whoop fitness wearables in 2021.

Things have gotten a lot bigger since then. In 2022, Sila announced plans for a factory in Moses Lake, Washington, and received $100 million from the US Department of Energy, part of a multibillion-dollar round of grants under the Biden administration to support the US battery supply chain.

The company opened its factory in September 2025, and it’s already operating. But the deal with Panasonic will help it scale to at least 10 times more production than current levels, says Gene Berdichevsky, the company’s cofounder and CEO.

Panasonic has committed to buying tens of thousands of tons of material, Berdichevsky says, though Sila isn’t sharing specific numbers on the total commitment or the price Panasonic is paying.

This agreement is Sila’s first mass-market deal and a big one for the United States’ next-generation battery market, which has largely been on the ropes over the past few years. Two billion-dollar battery companies, 24M and ESS Tech , have declared bankruptcy and shut down just in the last year.

The glimmer of hope here is tied up with something I’ve been noticing about this industry: the shifting politics. While batteries used to be firmly considered a climate technology, we’ve seen a lot of companies move away from messaging around the clean energy transition and lean into geopolitics.

China dominates the battery world and particularly the battery anode market, controlling over 90% of graphite production today. For years, the US has been trying to curb reliance on Chinese batteries, battery materials, and other materials used in crucial technologies, like rare earth metals. But the Trump administration has ramped things up, and earlier this year the US Defense Department committed a $1.4 billion loan to Sila aimed at helping the US face a “significant technology sovereignty challenge,” as a press release put it.

Sila’s announcement of the Panasonic deal does mention EVs—but not climate, emissions or the energy transition. Rather, it’s all about American industrialization. (And, of course, a mention that a North American battery supply chain can also help power the AI market.)

I asked Berdichevsky about this shift and whether the company holds decarbonization as a priority.

“I think the politics of it has shifted around us much more than our motivations have shifted,” he said. “It’s really the energy efficiency that motivates engineers like myself and technologists at our company. And I still think that that’s still at the heart of it.”

This article is from The Spark, MIT Technology Review ’s weekly climate newsletter. To receive it in your inbox every Wednesday, sign up here .

article_content_zh:
在经历了一些引人注目的失败的艰难几年之后，美国的下一代电池出现了一些积极的消息。

Sila 刚刚与全球电池制造商松下能源公司签署了一项协议，供应硅碳阳极材料，这可能是制造更小、更轻电池的关键。 Sila 表示，随着时间的推移，这笔交易的价值可能会超过 10 亿美元。

这种安排也表明了电池政治最近发生了多大的变化。该工厂生产的主要财务支持是来自特朗普政府国防部的 14 亿美元贷款。虽然电池可以成为帮助推动能源转型和减少排放的主要工具，但目前该行业的大部分业务更关注地缘政治。

Sila 成立于 2011 年，生产锂离子电池硅基阳极。这里的一大卖点是提高能量密度的潜力——据该公司称，Sila 的阳极重量是目前阳极中使用的石墨的五分之一，并且体积减少了一半。因此，使用这种新材料可以使电池在相同的重量和体积内容纳更多的能量，从而使电动汽车的行驶里程更长。与传统化学物质相比，该材料还可以提供更多的电力和更快的充电速度。

我们多年来一直关注 Sila（及其竞争对手）。当该公司的电池于 2021 年首次出现在 Whoop 健身可穿戴设备中时，我的同事 James Temple 对该公司进行了报道。

从那时起事情变得更大了。 2022年，西拉宣布计划在华盛顿摩西湖建立一家工厂，并从美国能源部获得了1亿美元，这是拜登政府支持美国电池供应链的数十亿美元拨款的一部分。

该公司工厂于 2025 年 9 月开业，目前已投入运营。但该公司联合创始人兼首席执行官 Gene Berdichevsky 表示，与松下的交易将有助于其将产量扩大到目前水平至少 10 倍。

Berdichevsky 表示，松下已承诺购买数万吨材料，但西拉没有透露承诺总额或松下支付价格的具体数字。

该协议是 Sila 的首笔大众市场交易，也是美国下一代电池市场的一项重大交易，该市场在过去几年中基本陷入困境。价值 20 亿美元的电池公司 24M 和 ESS Tech 就在去年宣布破产并关闭。

这里的一线希望与我一直注意到的这个行业的一些事情有关：不断变化的政治。虽然电池曾经被坚定地认为是一种气候技术，但我们看到许多公司放弃了围绕清洁能源转型的信息，转而倾向于地缘政治。

中国在电池世界尤其是电池负极市场占据主导地位，目前控制着超过 90% 的石墨产量。多年来，美国一直试图遏制对中国电池、电池材料以及稀土金属等关键技术中使用的其他材料的依赖。但特朗普政府加大了力度，今年早些时候，美国国防部承诺向西拉提供 14 亿美元贷款，目的是帮助美国应对“重大技术主权挑战”，正如一份新闻稿所述。

西拉宣布的松下交易确实提到了电动汽车，但没有提到气候、排放或能源转型。相反，这一切都与美国的工业化有关。 （当然，还要提到北美电池供应链也可以帮助推动人工智能市场。）

我向贝尔迪切夫斯基询问了这一转变，以及该公司是否将脱碳作为优先事项。

“我认为我们周围的政治变化远远大于我们动机的变化，”他说。 “真正激励像我这样的工程师和我们公司的技术人员的是能源效率。我仍然认为这仍然是其核心。”

title: Korea becomes world's 4th country to reach $1 tril. in annual exports
title_en: Korea becomes world's 4th country to reach $1 tril. in annual exports

inline_images.caption: Korea becomes world's 4th country to reach $1 tril. in annual exports (Photo: REUTERS)
inline_images.caption_en: Korea becomes world's 4th country to reach $1 tril. in annual exports (Photo: REUTERS)
inline_images.caption_zh: Korea becomes world's 4th country to reach $1 tril. in annual exports (摄影：路透社)
inline_images.alt: Korea becomes world's 4th country to reach $1 tril. in annual exports

author: Reuters
article_content:
Korea surpassed $1 trillion in annual exports for the first time Thursday, reaching the milestone at 2:09:38 p.m. as global AI investment boosted demand for semiconductors. It became the fourth country to reach the mark, after the United States, Germany and China. The government projects exports will total about $1.17 trillion this year, but officials warned that AI investment slowdowns, chip-price volatility and trade barriers could threaten momentum.

Containers are stacked at a port in Incheon, Tuesday. Yonhap

Korea has surpassed $1 trillion in annual exports for the first time in its history, becoming the world's fourth country to reach the milestone after the United States, Germany and China, as a global artificial intelligence (AI) boom drives demand for semiconductors.

The Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources announced Thursday that the country's cumulative exports reached the $1 trillion mark at 2:09:38 p.m.

The achievement comes 19 years after China reached the milestone in 2007, following the U.S. and Germany in 2006.

The government projects annual exports will reach approximately $1.17 trillion this year, following last year's record of $709.3 billion.

The ministry explained global technology companies’ expanding AI investments were the biggest driver of export growth, boosting demand for semiconductors and computers while pushing up memory chip prices.

Semiconductor exports reached $396.8 billion in the January-October period, almost triple the $135.4 billion recorded in 2025, as the price of memory chips, including DRAM and NAND, climbed.

Demand for AI data center infrastructure has also boosted exports of computers, electrical equipment and nonferrous metals, including storage devices, transformers, power cables, copper and aluminum.

Higher international oil prices, driven by uncertainty over supplies from the Middle East and Russian export restrictions, lifted the value of petroleum product exports despite limits on gasoline and diesel shipments.

The average export price of petroleum products rose 62 percent to $1,105 per ton in the January-October period from $681 a year earlier.

Other export industries, including shipbuilding and displays, also performed well, while cosmetics, pharmaceuticals and agricultural and seafood products posted record performances. Cosmetics exports alone reached $12.4 billion in the first 10 months, surpassing their previous full-year record of $11.4 billion.

Overall, 16 of 20 major export categories expanded year-on-year, with eight recording their strongest January-October performance ever. Exports excluding semiconductors rose 20 percent in the first 10 months, underscoring growth beyond the chip boom. Seven of the country's nine major export markets also recorded growth.

“This is a valuable achievement made possible by Korean companies competing in global markets, businesspeople and workers putting in long hours on the production floor and everyone who has contributed to the country's export efforts,” Industry Minister Kim Jung-kwan said.

“We will not rest on this year's $1 trillion export milestone and will seek new sources of growth to sustain the momentum, while working to ensure that strong exports translate into stronger regional economies and more jobs for young people.”

Kang Gam-chan, the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Energy's director general for trade and investment, speaks during a briefing at Government Complex Sejong, Wednesday. Courtesy of Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources

However, sustaining the current level of exports will depend on how the country navigates risks, including a potential slowdown in AI investment, semiconductor price volatility, lower oil prices and Chinese oversupply, as well as growing trade barriers in major markets.

The ministry also noted that the benefits of export growth may be less visible to the public because semiconductors, petrochemicals and petroleum products generate fewer jobs than shipbuilding and automobile manufacturing.

“Unlike the shipbuilding and auto industries, which have long supply chains and generate substantial employment, semiconductors, petrochemicals and petroleum products are relatively less labor-intensive, so the benefits of export growth may be less noticeable to the general public,” Kang Gam-chan, the ministry’s director general for trade and investment, said during a briefing on Wednesday at Government Complex Sejong.

He warned that large trade surpluses could invite further pressure from trading partners, particularly the U.S., and called for stronger investment-based economic partnerships. While Japan's overseas investment offered a point of reference, he said Korea should maintain its domestic manufacturing capabilities while expanding production overseas.

“We should not simply follow Japan's path. We need to maintain a substantial domestic production base, including advanced plants and mother factories for research and core production, while also expanding our manufacturing capacity overseas,” he said.

article_content_zh:
周四下午 2:09:38，韩国年度出口额首次​​突破 1 万亿美元。全球人工智能投资推动了半导体需求。它成为继美国、德国和中国之后第四个达到这一标准的国家。政府预计今年的出口总额约为 1.17 万亿美元，但官员警告称，人工智能投资放缓、芯片价格波动和贸易壁垒可能会威胁到这一势头。

周二，集装箱堆放在仁川的一个港口。韩联社

随着全球人工智能 (AI) 的繁荣推动了对半导体的需求，韩国历史上首次突破 1 万亿美元的年出口额，成为继美国、德国和中国之后世界上第四个达到这一里程碑的国家。

周四下午2点09分38秒，产业通商资源部宣布，该国累计出口额突破1万亿美元大关。

继2006年美国和德国之后，中国于2007年实现这一里程碑，19年后取得了这一成就。

政府预计今年的年度出口额将达到约 1.17 万亿美元，继去年创下 7093 亿美元的纪录之后。

该部解释称，全球科技公司不断扩大的人工智能投资是出口增长的最大推动力，刺激了对半导体和计算机的需求，同时推高了存储芯片的价格。

随着包括 DRAM 和 NAND 在内的存储芯片价格攀升，1 月至 10 月期间半导体出口达到 3968 亿美元，几乎是 2025 年 1354 亿美元的三倍。

对人工智能数据中心基础设施的需求也推动了计算机、电气设备和有色金属的出口，包括存储设备、变压器、电力电缆、铜和铝。

尽管汽油和柴油运输受到限制，但受中东供应不确定性和俄罗斯出口限制的推动，国际油价上涨，提高了石油产品出口价值。

1-10月石油产品平均出口价格从去年同期的681美元每吨上涨62%至1105美元。

包括造船和显示器在内的其他出口行业也表现良好，而化妆品、药品以及农产品和海鲜产品也创下了创纪录的表现。今年前 10 个月，仅化妆品出口就达到 124 亿美元，超过了之前 114 亿美元的全年纪录。

总体而言，20个主要出口类别中有16个类别同比增长，其中8个类别录得有史以来最强劲的1-10月表现。前 10 个月，不包括半导体的出口增长了 20%，凸显了芯片繁荣之后的增长。该国九个主要出口市场中有七个也录得增长。

“这是韩国企业在全球市场竞争、商人和工人在生产车间长时间工作以及为国家出口做出贡献的每个人所取得的宝贵成就，”工业部长金正宽表示。

title: European Retail Traders Snag $1.1 Billion of Anthropic IPO Stock
title_en: European Retail Traders Snag $1.1 Billion of Anthropic IPO Stock

inline_images.caption: Pablo Mayo Cerqueiro
inline_images.alt: Pablo Mayo Cerqueiro

author: Pablo Mayo Cerqueiro
article_content:
Anthropic PBC sold $1.1 billion worth of stock to mom-and-pop investors in the UK and continental Europe as part of the biggest initial public offering of all time.

The artificial intelligence lab sold just over 3.6 million shares to retail investors in the UK and close to 9.7 million shares to those in the European Union, Norway and Switzerland, according to regulatory filings reviewed by Bloomberg News.

Anthropic and its co-founders overcame mounting concerns about the pace of AI spending and turbulent markets to price the IPO above the marketed range and raise a record $107.3 billion. The company's debut later Thursday in New York made it the first publicly traded major AI lab, with shares opening significantly higher in gray market and secondary trading.

At the IPO price of $83 per share, the company and its founders raised about $300 million and $801 million, respectively, through dedicated retail offerings in Britain and on the European continent. That exceeds the $364 million Elon Musk's SpaceX sold to UK savers and the more than $600 million it offered to European retail investors.

In the UK, the company made use of the public-offer platforms regime to access local investors without requiring a separate prospectus. Investment platform RetailBook coordinated the offering, with major retail brokers including AJ Bell Plc, Hargreaves Lansdown, and Revolut handling end-user execution.

On the European continent, Anthropic launched a regional offer for investors across Germany, Denmark, Finland, France, Ireland, the Netherlands, Norway, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland, arranged by European banking syndicates including BNP Paribas SA, Deutsche Bank AG, and UBS Group AG.

article_content_zh:
人工智能独角兽 Anthropic PBC 在其创纪录的全球首次公开募股（IPO）中，向英国及欧洲大陆的散户投资者定向发售了总值达11亿美元的股票，创下全球资本市场历史上针对散户的最大规模科技股配售纪录。

彭博社查阅的监管备案文件显示，这家开发了 Claude 聊天机器人的前沿 AI 实验室向英国零售投资者配售了略超360万股股票，并向欧盟、挪威及瑞士的散户配售了近970万股股票。

尽管此前市场对生成式 AI 巨额算力资本开支的可持续性及二级市场震荡有所疑虑，但 Anthropic 及其联合创始人团队依然克服了重重阻力，将最终 IPO 发行价定于推介区间顶端之上，累计募资规模达1073亿美元。公司周四在纽约纳斯达克的正式挂牌使其成为全球首家登陆公开市场的顶级 AI 前沿实验室。

按照每股83美元的发行价计算，Anthropic 分别通过英国本土平台配售和欧洲大陆跨境销售筹集了约3亿美元与8.01亿美元资金。这一零售发售规模显著超过了埃隆·马斯克旗下 SpaceX 此前向英国储蓄者发售的3.64亿美元以及向欧洲大陆散户配售的逾6亿美元纪录。

在英国市场，Anthropic 充分利用了英国创新的公开发行平台监管框架（Public-Offer Platforms Regime），在无需单独编制繁复本地招股说明书的前提下直接对接个人投资者。该笔发售由 RetailBook 投资平台领衔协调，AJ Bell、哈格里夫斯-兰斯当（Hargreaves Lansdown）以及数字银行巨头 Revolut 等经纪商共同承担了散户订单报送与划转。

而在欧洲大陆地区，Anthropic 面向德国、丹麦、芬兰、法国、爱尔兰、荷兰、挪威、西班牙、瑞典和瑞士的散户推出了全欧区域性配售方案，该承销团由包括法国巴黎银行（BNP Paribas SA）、德意志银行（Deutsche Bank AG）和瑞士联合银行（UBS Group AG）在内的欧洲顶级银行集团及 Trade Republic、盛宝银行（Saxo Bank）等数字券商联手护航。

彭博社查阅的监管备案文件显示，这家开发了 Claude 聊天机器人的前沿 AI 实验室向英国零售投资者配售了略超360万股股票，并向欧盟、挪威及瑞士的散户配售了近970万股股票。
尽管此前市场对生成式 AI 巨额算力资本开支的可持续性及二级市场震荡有所疑虑，但 Anthropic 及其联合创始人团队依然克服了重重阻力，将最终 IPO 发行价定于推介区间顶端之上，累计募资规模达1073亿美元。公司周四在纽约纳斯达克的正式挂牌使其成为全球首家登陆公开市场的顶级 AI 前沿实验室。
按照每股83美元的发行价计算，Anthropic 分别通过英国本土平台配售和欧洲大陆跨境销售筹集了约3亿美元与8.01亿美元资金。这一零售发售规模显著超过了埃隆·马斯克旗下 SpaceX 此前向英国储蓄者发售的3.64亿美元以及向欧洲大陆散户配售的逾6亿美元纪录。
在英国市场，Anthropic 充分利用了英国创新的公开发行平台监管框架（Public-Offer Platforms Regime），在无需单独编制繁复本地招股说明书的前提下直接对接个人投资者。该笔发售由 RetailBook 投资平台领衔协调，AJ Bell、哈格里夫斯-兰斯当（Hargreaves Lansdown）以及数字银行巨头 Revolut 等经纪商共同承担了散户订单报送与划转。
而在欧洲大陆地区，Anthropic 面向德国、丹麦、芬兰、法国、爱尔兰、荷兰、挪威、西班牙、瑞典和瑞士的散户推出了全欧区域性配售方案，该承销团由包括法国巴黎银行（BNP Paribas SA）、德意志银行（Deutsche Bank AG）和瑞士联合银行（UBS Group AG）在内的欧洲顶级银行集团及 Trade Republic、盛宝银行（Saxo Bank）等数字券商联手护航。

title: TSMC and Samsung suspend some chip shipments to Chinese customers
title_en: TSMC and Samsung suspend some chip shipments to Chinese customers
author: Eleanor Olcott and Zijing Wu
article_content:
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company and Samsung Electronics have suspended some chip shipments to Chinese customers following new US export controls designed to hamper Beijing’s AI development.

The two chipmakers have told Chinese customers in recent days that they will halt shipments of certain processors while they apply for licences from the US commerce department, according to multiple people briefed on the matter.

The measure is a blow to Chinese technology companies, which are already grappling with component shortages following a historic jump in memory chip prices and capacity constraints at domestic suppliers such as Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corporation.

On Monday, the Bureau of Industry and Security, the US commerce department agency that regulates sensitive technology, said chipmakers using American technology for advanced chips had to apply for a licence to sell products that are eventually shipped to customers in China.

The new rule shuts off a pathway that Chinese chip designers previously used to have TSMC and Samsung make the high-performance chips crucial for AI data centres.

While Washington has restricted exports of the most advanced processors to China, some Chinese customers have been able to place orders for high-performance chips through independent packaging and testing companies.

These companies verify that designs fall outside US export controls and do not need to seek direct approval from the government for shipments. Under the new BIS rule, Chinese customers can no longer go through them.

Samsung’s Chinese clients include Baidu’s AI data centre unit Kunlun and TikTok owner ByteDance, both of which have sought to diversify their chip supplies amid growing shortages of Nvidia processors in China.

TSMC and Samsung have also notified consumer electronics customers that they have suspended shipments, according to two people with knowledge of the matter.

The new BIS rule scraps exemptions previously used to demonstrate that chips fell outside of US restrictions on AI semiconductors, including that the chips were designed for non-AI purposes such as smartphones.

A lawyer briefed on the situation said the removal of this exemption meant TSMC and Samsung now needed to apply for licences for consumer chips that use advanced manufacturing processes.

TSMC manufactures smartphone chips for Chinese smartphone makers Xiaomi, Oppo and Vivo.

An industry insider said it was likely that the US commerce department would issue licences for consumer smartphone chips, but the delay would cause significant manufacturing delays.

TSMC did not respond to a request for comment. Samsung declined to comment.

article_content_zh:
在美国实施旨在阻碍北京人工智能发展的新出口管制措施后，台积电和三星电子已暂停向中国客户运送部分芯片。

这两家芯片制造商最近几天告诉中国客户，他们将在向美国商务部申请许可证期间停止某些处理器的发货。

这项措施对中国科技公司来说是一个打击，在存储芯片价格历史性上涨以及中芯国际等国内供应商产能限制之后，这些公司已经在努力应对零部件短缺的问题。

周一，美国商务部负责监管敏感技术的机构工业与安全局表示，使用美国技术生产先进芯片的芯片制造商必须申请许可证才能销售最终运往中国客户的产品。

新规定切断了中国芯片设计者之前让台积电和三星制造对人工智能数据中心至关重要的高性能芯片的途径。

尽管华盛顿限制向中国出口最先进的处理器，但一些中国客户已经能够通过独立的封装和测试公司订购高性能芯片。

这些公司验证其设计不属于美国出口管制范围，并且无需寻求政府的直接发货批准。根据BIS新规定，中国客户不能再通过它们。

三星的中国客户包括百度的人工智能数据中心部门昆仑万维和TikTok母公司字节跳动，在中国英伟达处理器日益短缺的情况下，这两家公司都在寻求芯片供应多元化。

据两位知情人士透露，台积电和三星也已通知消费电子产品客户，他们已暂停发货。

新的 BIS 规则取消了此前用于证明芯片不符合美国对 AI 半导体限制的豁免，包括这些芯片是为智能手机等非 AI 目的而设计的。

一位了解情况的律师表示，取消这一豁免意味着台积电和三星现在需要申请使用先进制造工艺的消费芯片的许可证。

台积电为中国智能手机制造商小米、Oppo 和 Vivo 生产智能手机芯片。

一位业内人士表示，美国商务部很可能会发放消费智能手机芯片许可证，但这一延迟将导致制造严重延误。

台积电没有回应置评请求。三星拒绝置评。

title: OCR models now digitize a million pages for under $130 as costs drop fivefold in 18 months
title_en: OCR models now digitize a million pages for under $130 as costs drop fivefold in 18 months
author: Jonathan Kemper
article_content:
Pulling text out of scanned books and records has gotten a lot cheaper with freely available AI models. Daniel van Strien of Hugging Face compared eight such models that recognize text in images. He tested them on 850 pages from old natural history books, the 1771 Encyclopaedia Britannica, and typed and printed archival documents. All models ran on the same GPU, an Nvidia RTX PRO 6000 that van Strien rented through Hugging Face for $2.75 per hour. At the same image size, the oldest model from April 2025 (RolmOCR) cost about 51 cents per 1,000 pages. The newest from October 2026 (LightOnOCR-3-0.8B) came in at just under 10 cents. A million pages now runs between $65 and $130 in GPU rental, depending on the source material.

According to van Strien, optimizing how the models ran saved about as much money as switching to newer models did, if not more. That meant feeding pages more evenly, using smaller scans, updating software, and running a faster GPU. The newest model read book pages at least as accurately as the oldest one. Some models, though, hallucinated text on blank pages or repeated the same content over and over.

The cost of scanning 1,000 pages has dropped from 51 cents for the oldest model to just under 10 cents for the newest one; the five models in between are almost on par with each other.

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 通过对比八款主流OCR模型，Hugging Face研究人员发现，得益于模型架构轻量化、推理软件优化及高效GPU算力租赁（如RTX PRO 6000），大规模文档识别成本在过去18个月内降低了约五倍。目前处理百万页文档的GPU算力成本已降至65至130美元区间，且新一代模型在保持精度的前提下，实现了显著的推理速度提升与成本控制。

ai_analysis.insight_zh: OCR成本的断崖式下降显示出AI领域从“堆砌参数”向“算力推理效率”转型的趋势，数字化档案处理将进入普惠化阶段。未来的竞争焦点将从单一模型的识别准确率，转移至模型在低功耗边缘端设备的部署灵活性与幻觉纠错能力。
ai_analysis.insight_en: The drastic reduction in OCR costs signals a shift in AI from parameter-scaling to inferential efficiency, democratizing large-scale data digitization. Future competitive advantages will hinge not just on accuracy, but on the ability to deploy these models efficiently at the edge while minimizing inherent hallucinations.

article_content_zh:
通过免费提供的人工智能模型，从扫描的书籍和记录中提取文本变得更加便宜。 Hugging Face 的 Daniel van Strien 比较了八种识别图像中文本的模型。他在 850 页的古老自然历史书籍、1771 年的《大英百科全书》以及打字和打印的档案文件中进行了测试。所有模型都运行在相同的 GPU 上，即 van Strien 通过 Hugging Face 以每小时 2.75 美元的价格租用的 Nvidia RTX PRO 6000。在相同的图像尺寸下，2025 年 4 月推出的最旧型号 (RolmOCR) 每 1,000 页的成本约为 51 美分。 2026 年 10 月推出的最新版本 (LightOnOCR-3-0.8B) 价格略低于 10 美分。现在一百万个页面的 GPU 租金在 65 到 130 美元之间，具体取决于源材料。

van Strien 表示，优化模型的运行方式所节省的资金与切换到新模型所节省的资金差不多，甚至更多。这意味着更均匀地送入页面、使用更小的扫描、更新软件以及运行更快的 GPU。最新的模型阅读书页的准确率至少与最旧的模型一样准确。然而，有些模型会在空白页面上产生幻觉文本，或者一遍又一遍地重复相同的内容。

扫描 1,000 页的成本已从最旧型号的 51 美分降至最新型号的不到 10 美分；介于两者之间的五款车型几乎不相上下。

author: OpenAI
article_content:
Our Codex-powered system automates finding and fixing performance issues.

By Okay Zed and Cyrus Forbes, Members of Technical Staff

The staggering pace of agentic development has made traditional approaches to performance engineering unsustainable. To keep up, we built the Performance Factory, an autonomous system that uses the full capabilities of Codex and our models to find and fix regressions at an unprecedented speed. The Performance Factory, which runs in the cloud and automates investigating and resolving performance problems, enables us to keep pace with the ambition of our roadmap.

In the Performance Factory, our engineers define workflows for recurring jobs and write instructions for the Codex agents that carry them out. In particular, the Regression Workflow opens a task when a performance alert fires. An agent investigates the slowdown, records its findings in the task, and proposes a fix for an engineer to review. After deployment, another agent picks up the same task to check whether performance has returned to baseline. From investigating to authoring the fix to verifying mitigation, this first workflow in the Performance Factory has automated the entire process of fixing regressions. In just over three months, the Regression Workflow tracked more than 1,700 investigations and root caused over 600 cases. That’s 17 automated investigations every day.

Here, we’ll share how our use of Codex evolved into what’s now the Performance Factory, walk through our first running workflow, and share early lessons from building and running agent workflows in production.

### The path from manual investigations to automated workflows

As we used Codex for more of our performance work, we noticed a progression in how our team worked. We hope other service teams can learn from our process as they adopt agentic workflows in other domains.

1. Pre-Codex. Before Codex, engineers manually examined metrics and logs, compared traces, debugged live machines, and read code to investigate a slowdown. This work was time consuming, and knowing where to look often required deep knowledge of the service. Relevant signals were easy to miss. When we encountered the same kinds of problems repeatedly—like regressions in ChatGPT’s first token latency—we built advanced tools, like CPU and allocation profilers, to make those investigations easier. Over time, we accumulated more than 30 performance tools.

2. Codex as a partner. Once we had Codex as a partner, engineers could ask, “Why did this get slower?” and work with Codex to investigate, even in an unfamiliar system. Codex could search large codebases, find relevant metrics and traces, follow interactions across services, and do appropriate profiling to piece together what had happened. But engineers still had to steer the process, knowing which performance tools to use and how to guide the investigation. Difficult investigations were more debuggable for more people, with less expertise and time required.

3. Reusable skills. To automate further, we captured our performance team’s investigation process in a shared skill called perf-forensics. It tells Codex which tools are available, when to use them, and how to work through a slowdown so Codex can try to resolve the problem from a few angles:

Find when the slowdown began

Identify the affected requests

Investigate whether deployments or configuration changes could explain it

We tested and refined the perf-forensics skill using evals based on past regressions. For the types of regressions we focused on (for example, ChatGPT latency and availability drops), we could now give Codex an alert and get back a diagnosis in a single run, without guiding it through each step.

4. The human proxy. As we added and refined perf-related Codex skills like perf-forensics, we started to feel like a proxy between our alerts and Codex. An alert would fire, and an engineer would simply copy and paste it into Codex with the right skill, then paste the findings back into Slack.

5. Automated investigations. Next, we moved investigations to the cloud so an alert could start a Codex session automatically. Codex investigated the slowdown and posted its findings in the Slack thread, but the automation ended with that reply. An engineer still had to pick up the diagnosis, develop a fix, and check whether it worked after deployment. As alerts accumulated, even figuring out which regressions needed attention meant sifting through Slack threads.

6. The factory. We built the Performance Factory to run end-to-end agentic performance engineering workflows. It tracks what each active task needs next and assigns an agent when that step is ready. Each task keeps its state and findings, so work can pass between agents and engineers and resume after a code review or deployment. For a regression, the work starts with investigating an alert and ends with verifying recovery in production. We can turn common optimizations into workflows that run regularly across our services. A workflow that spots a potential optimization can open a task in another workflow to test and implement it.

### The Performance Factory system’s four parts

The Performance Factory is made up of four components: a task tracker with configurable workflows, a dispatch loop that assigns ready work to agents, an API that runs Codex in the cloud, and subscriptions that wake agents when something changes (such as a GitHub review comment posting or a deployment completing).

### Task service with configurable workflows

The task service is where engineers define workflows by adding configuration files and prompts for the agents to follow, written in Markdown. The configuration lists the states a task can move through, the allowed transitions, and which steps need an engineer. Separate prompts tell agents what to do at each step.

A code change task contains a configuration file, along with Markdown prompts for implementing and reviewing.

Each piece of work becomes a task in a workflow, and all workflows are visible in a UI. Engineers can see what’s open, follow progress, and share a task with a teammate who might have more context or be able to help with the next step.

### Dispatch loop that assigns work

A dispatch loop periodically checks which tasks are ready for the next step. It assigns an agent to each task by starting a Codex turn with the instructions for the task’s current state. The agent records its progress on the task and moves it to the next state if it completes the step.

### Codex in the cloud

Once a task is assigned, the agent needs a place to do the work, with access to the same tools an engineer would use. We built an internal API to programmatically invoke a Codex turn in the cloud. The Codex turn runs on an environment inside our network, with access to our code repositories and the observability tools our engineers use, such as metrics, logs, traces, CPU profiles, and memory snapshots.

The agent runs under a service identity, so we can scope its permissions and see which actions came from our performance agents. Moving agentic work to the cloud lets us run work in parallel without relying on engineers’ laptops being open or manually managing individual cloud development boxes.

### Subscriptions that wake the agent when something changes

Some work has to wait for a person or a deployment; an agent shouldn’t have to keep running in the meantime. When a task needs to wait, it can subscribe to events like review comments or failed CI checks on a GitHub pull request to get notified when it’s time to pick the work back up. When an incoming event matches the subscription, the task becomes ready again and the dispatch loop can then assign an agent to continue the work.

### The first workflow: from alert to recovery

Finding, root causing, and solving regressions is the first workflow we built inside the Performance Factory. We call it the Regression Workflow. A performance regression moves through several stages: needs investigation, root caused, fix proposed, and resolved, so we built the automated workflow to reflect and move a task through those same stages.

When one of its configured performance alerts fires, the Regression Workflow opens a task that agents pick up and move across these stages. The task records its status and key findings outside of any one agent’s context so that other agents or engineers can pick up the work. Engineers can follow the work in Slack or the Regression Workflow UI, add context, and review proposed changes. After a fix is deployed, an agent checks whether the performance has recovered to its original state before resolving the task.

### Performance Factory regression workflow

### Agents find the root cause

Finding the root cause (or causes) is the first major step in the workflow. The agent starts by figuring out which metrics got worse, when they started to change, and which service requests were affected. The perf-forensics skill gives Codex access to the tools our performance engineers use and a playbook for working through those questions.

An alert fires when a metric crosses a threshold, but the regression may have started hours earlier. The agent looks back through the data to find when the metric first got worse. It then compares groups of requests: did similar requests actually get slower, or were we serving more requests that were already slow? Those findings point to different causes.

Once it knows when and where to look, the agent examines deployments and feature flag changes, then reads the relevant code. It checks when a change actually reached the affected requests and uses logs or traces to test whether the code could explain what happened.

### Adversarial review strengthens the diagnosis

Early on, agents sometimes stopped at the first plausible explanation they found, and some of those diagnoses turned out to be wrong. To catch these mistakes, we added an adversarial review: a separate Codex session that tries to disprove the proposed diagnosis. The reviewer rechecks the assumptions and tests counterfactuals. If a rollout caused the slowdown, did similar requests that weren’t exposed stay healthy? If the suspected change was rolled back, did the affected metric recover?

In one investigation, an agent traced failing ChatGPT conversations to errors in image downloads and marked the cause as found. The Codex reviewer noticed that the internal service responsible for locating files had already recovered while image requests were still failing. The diagnosis did not explain the continuing failures, so the AI reviewer reopened the investigation and recorded what still needed to be established.

We’ve had success breaking larger jobs into focused Codex turns. In a manual review of 100 root cause suggestions, we graded 70% as accurate, with 30% needing further refinement or not fully establishing causality. In the Regression Workflow, different turns investigate regressions, challenge diagnoses, and propose fixes to increase accuracy numbers through checks and balances.

### Fixing the regression is the hard part

Once the diagnosis passes adversarial review, the workflow asks Codex to implement a fix and open a pull request. An engineer reviews the PR and decides whether to merge it. We’ve put a significant amount of work into making this handoff as easy as possible. Each task has a report with an automatically generated summary of the regression, its impact, the root cause, and the proposed fix. We’ve tuned these summaries to be easy to scan, including metrics time series, CPU flame graphs, and traces to help engineers quickly understand the findings and inspect the evidence. Engineers can edit the PR directly or use the diagnosis to write their own fix. If they leave comments on the PR, the workflow wakes an agent to address them.

After an engineer deploys the fix, the workflow wakes an agent to check whether performance has returned to its earlier baseline. If it has, the agent marks the task as resolved. If performance has only partially recovered, the agent resolves the original regression and opens a new task for the remaining slowdown, which may have a different cause. If there’s no improvement, the agent records what happened and sends the regression back for investigation.

Getting fixes right has been harder than finding the cause. For example, we’ve seen cases where the agent-proposed changes are more complicated than necessary or introduce new issues. Similar to the root cause step, we added an adversarial review of each proposed fix to check whether they address the root cause and help catch bugs or unintended consequences. Some fixes also require higher level architectural decisions. For example, adding a cache might improve performance but introduce stale data. Changes like these benefit from guidance from an engineer who knows the service and can weigh the tradeoffs.

We’re building an evaluation and improvement loop using these cases. By comparing the fixes agents propose with the changes engineers ultimately merge, we can better understand where proposals fall short, build evals, and improve the workflow. We’re also working on using synthetic performance tests so agents can measure proposed fixes and revise them before asking an engineer for review. We’re also exploring how agents could use our other agentic review tools to identify low-risk changes and eventually ship those fixes without a human in the loop.

### What we learned

Building and running the Performance Factory has taught us a lot about developing and operating agent workflows in production. Here are some lessons for teams building their own agentic workflows.

### Protect engineers’ attention

The raw output from a Codex investigation can be a wall of text that’s hard to parse. It takes effort to figure out what the agent is claiming and track down the graphs to see whether the data backs it up. We want engineers to spend their attention on decisions rather than reconstructing the agent’s work.

Agents can investigate more regressions than a team has time to read about. Our first version gave engineers a UI full of findings, but someone still had to decide which information mattered. One regression can also appear as several incidents across alerts, monitors, and channels. The workflow now links related incidents, groups them by the metrics teams care about, and ranks their estimated impact. Engineers can focus on adding context, weighing tradeoffs, and deciding what to ship.

### Evaluate changes to your agents

Updating an investigation skill or upgrading the model can make the agent better at diagnosing some cases and worse at others, so we nee d to test their impact before updating them. W e test two things separately: 1) how well the agent investigates and 2) how useful its summaries are to engineers.

For investigations, we backtest against past production incidents. We turn those incidents into a suite of test cases we can rerun when we change the skill. A Codex agent attempts to investigate and resolve the incident, and we compare the agent’s behavior to the actual past resolution data. Each case starts with a fresh Codex investigator and the original signal, stripped of details that might give away the answer.

Historical tests need care. Metrics and traces expire, while evidence collected after recovery can give away the cause. A test is only useful if we understand what evidence the investigator could see. The agent can inspect code and query production telemetry within set limits. It cannot use saved memories (notes from earlier investigations), read the incident writeup, or see results from previous runs. We also inspect its transcript afterward for information that might have spoiled the test.

We score when the problem began, how large it was, and which requests were affected. We also evaluate how the agent uses evidence to rank possible causes and explain what remains uncertain. An agent can get the timing right and still blame the wrong deployment, so we score those separately.

We evaluate task summaries using snapshots of saved tasks. These make particularly good backtests because summarization does not depend on external metrics or traces that expire. A separate grader checks whether an engineer unfamiliar with the system can understand what happened and why it matters, whether useful charts were kept, and whether the proposed next step is supported by the evidence.

### Turn recurring failures into self-repair

Lastly, our agents need monitoring just as much as the services they investigate. A broken profiler or a missing permission can keep an agent from verifying what caused a slowdown. Those failures can be hard to spot in the final report, so we run an agent every day to look through messages and logs from recent runs for tool failures and access errors.

We use the Performance Factory to self-repair and fix the problems this check uncovers. When the same tool error blocks several investigations, the agent creates a task to fix it. If the cause is clear, an agent proposes a fix, and an engineer reviews the change and decides whether to merge it. After merging changes like this, we also use evals to check whether agents can get past the step that previously blocked them.

### What’s next: broader applications, proactive monitoring

The Regression Workflow is just one instance of the agent factory pattern that moves tasks through explicit states. Agents advance the task when more work is ready; separate reviewers challenge the conclusions; engineers step in when the next decision requires judgment. Other workflows can reuse the same machinery with different states, instructions, and events.

Currently, our Regression Workflow starts when an alert fires. However, we’re working on more proactive ways for the Performance Factory to find slowdowns and optimizations even when no alert fires. We want agents to use the large amount of fine-grained performance data we already collect to spot regressions our alerts miss or discover optimizations. By comparing different kinds of data (batches of CPU and memory profiles, heap dumps, and request traces across releases), an agent might notice a small increase in CPU for a given request. It can then open a task in the Regression Workflow to trace the increase to its cause, implement a fix, and open a PR for an engineer to review.

In cases where we already know what to look for, we’re working to encode known signals into more Performance Factory workflows. Our service rightsizing skill, for example, helps agents spot autoscaling settings that keep more replicas running than a service needs. When we learn to recognize a pattern like that, we want to build and regularly run a workflow for it across all our services, constantly optimizing in a rapidly changing environment. With the Performance Factory, what an engineer learns from one slowdown can shape how we investigate and fix the next one, even months later in a different service.

Next time you’re using ChatGPT and notice a slowdown, there’s a good chance the Performance Factory is already figuring out why. Today, the bottleneck may be waiting for an engineer to review and merge the fix. We’re already exploring whether agents can do this themselves. As product development keeps accelerating with Codex, performance systems need to become increasingly autonomous and self-improving to keep up. Codex already helps us build ChatGPT faster. Now it’s helping us keep ChatGPT fast.

article_content_zh:
我们由 Codex 支持的系统可以自动查找和修复性能问题。

代理开发的惊人速度使得传统的性能工程方法变得不可持续。为了跟上步伐，我们构建了 Performance Factory，这是一个自治系统，它利用 Codex 和我们的模型的全部功能以前所未有的速度查找和修复回归。 Performance Factory 在云中运行并自动调查和解决性能问题，使我们能够跟上路线图的雄心壮志。

在 Performance Factory 中，我们的工程师为重复性作业定义工作流程，并为执行这些作业的 Codex 代理编写指令。特别是，当性能警报触发时，回归工作流程会打开一个任务。代理调查减速情况，将其发现记录在任务中，并提出修复方案供工程师审查。部署后，另一个代理将执行相同的任务来检查性能是否已恢复到基线。从调查到编写修复程序再到验证缓解措施，性能工厂中的第一个工作流程已经自动化了修复回归的整个过程。在短短三个多月的时间里，回归工作流程跟踪了 1,700 多项调查，找出了 600 多个案例的根源。每天有 17 项自动调查。

在这里，我们将分享我们对 Codex 的使用如何演变为现在的 Performance Factory，逐步完成我们的第一个运行工作流程，并分享在生产中构建和运行代理工作流程的早期经验教训。

当我们使用 Codex 进行更多性能工作时，我们注意到我们团队的工作方式取得了进步。我们希望其他服务团队在其他领域采用代理工作流程时可以从我们的流程中学习。

1. 食品法典委员会之前。在 Codex 之前，工程师手动检查指标和日志、比较跟踪、调试实时机器并读取代码以调查速度下降情况。这项工作非常耗时，并且知道在哪里查找通常需要对服务有深入的了解。相关信号很容易被忽视。当我们反复遇到相同类型的问题时（例如 ChatGPT 的第一个令牌延迟中的回归），我们构建了高级工具，例如 CPU 和分配分析器，以使这些调查变得更容易。随着时间的推移，我们积累了 30 多个性能工具。

2. 法典作为合作伙伴。一旦我们与 Codex 成为合作伙伴，工程师就会问：“为什么速度变慢了？”并与 Codex 合作进行调查，即使是在不熟悉的系统中。 Codex 可以搜索大型代码库，查找相关指标和跟踪，跟踪跨服务的交互，并进行适当的分析以拼凑发生的情况。但工程师仍然必须掌控整个过程，了解要使用哪些性能工具以及如何指导调查。对于更多的人来说，困难的调查更容易调试，所需的专业知识和时间更少。

3.可重复使用的技能。为了进一步自动化，我们通过称为性能取证的共享技能捕获了性能团队的调查过程。它告诉 Codex 哪些工具可用、何时使用它们以及如何解决速度下降的问题，以便 Codex 可以尝试从几个角度解决问题：

我们使用基于过去回归的评估来测试和完善性能取证技能。对于我们关注的回归类型（例如，ChatGPT 延迟和可用性下降），我们现在可以向 Codex 发出警报并在一次运行中获得诊断结果，而无需引导它完成每个步骤。

4. 人类代理。当我们添加和完善与性能相关的 Codex 技能（例如性能取证）时，我们开始感觉自己是警报和 Codex 之间的代理。警报将被触发，工程师只需使用正确的技能将其复制并粘贴到 Codex 中，然后将结果粘贴回 Slack 中。

5. 自动化调查。接下来，我们将调查转移到云端，以便警报可以自动启动 Codex 会话。 Codex 调查了速度下降的情况，并将其调查结果发布在 Slack 线程中，但自动化以该回复结束。工程师仍然必须进行诊断，开发修复程序，并在部署后检查它是否有效。随着警报的积累，甚至弄清楚哪些回归需要注意也意味着要筛选 Slack 线程。

6、工厂。我们构建了 Performance Factory 来运行端到端代理性能工程工作流程。它跟踪每个活动任务接下来需要什么，并在该步骤准备好时分配一个代理。每个任务都会保留其状态和结果，因此工作可以在代理和工程师之间传递，并在代码审查或部署后恢复。对于回归，工作从调查警报开始，到验证生产中的恢复结束。我们可以将常见的优化转化为在我们的服务中定期运行的工作流程。发现潜在优化的工作流程可以在另一个工作流程中打开任务来测试和实施它。

任务服务是工程师通过添加用 Markdown 编写的配置文件和提示以供代理遵循的提示来定义工作流程的地方。配置列出了任务可以经历的状态、允许的转换以及哪些步骤需要工程师。单独的提示告诉代理在每一步要做什么。

1code-change/2├── config.toml3└── work/4 ├── Implementing.md5 └── reviewing.md 代码更改任务包含一个配置文件，以及实现和审核的 Markdown 提示。

title: A profile of Netflix's new Chief Content Officer Peter Rice, a former Fox and Disney executive, as sources say he may focus on revamping its film strategy (Alex Weprin/The Hollywood Reporter)
title_en: A profile of Netflix's new Chief Content Officer Peter Rice, a former Fox and Disney executive, as sources say he may focus on revamping its film strategy (Alex Weprin/The Hollywood Reporter)

inline_images.caption: Illustrated by Chris Morris
inline_images.alt: Illustrated by Chris Morris

author: The Hollywood Reporter
article_content:
Ted Sarandos’ handpicked consigliere is tasked with reinventing the streamer — while his boss promises Wall Street that nothing is changing.

Reed Hastings found about Netflix’s big shake-up the same time everyone else did. The Netflix founder (he officially exited the board over the summer) told a rapt audience at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco in late October that the mass layoffs, the exit of content chief Bela Bajaria and the surprise announcement of Peter Rice as its new head of content caught him just as off guard as the rest of Hollywood. “I didn’t know those were coming, and it’s hard because I’d like to be in the fray helping,” Hastings told the audience in the Presidio Theater.

Still, the man who shaped Netflix into today’s behemoth had thoughts on what Rice and co-CEOs Ted Sarandos and Greg Peters need to do. “The strategy is doing more and better television shows, more and better movies,” Hastings said. “The core brand property is about being thrilling. We realized — it took a long time — that we could be distrusted, we could be disliked, but we can never be boring.”

Now the burden will be on Rice to find those thrilling additions to Netflix’s menu, perhaps retiring the safe but aging gourmet cheeseburger of the Bajaria era.

Rice helped forge Fox into an entertainment giant and was one of only a few Fox veterans brought into the Disney fold when the assets were acquired under Bob Iger (Disney exec Dana Walden was another). His taste and relationships at both Fox and Disney were, in the words of one source, “exquisite,” with a knack for fare that was both commercial and high-end. At Disney, he helped build a general entertainment business from near-scratch, leaning on both FX and Hulu to help it do so.

But he has been out of the corporate mix since Bob Chapek unceremoniously ousted him in 2022, just a few short months before Chapek himself would get the boot.

Those post-corporate gigs, however, shed light on what he can bring to Netflix: He helped the L.A. Olympics Committee develop the entertainment for the opening and closing ceremonies, critical events that will be seen by millions (and perhaps billions) before passing the baton to Kathleen Kennedy. And perhaps more intriguingly, he inked a deal with A24. As A24 was revving up its original productions — thanks to several rounds of investment that ended with a $3.5 billion valuation — the insular New York indie studio signed Rice to a film and TV pact.

It’s a testament to Rice’s talent relationships that the notoriously director-driven studio tapped him to help shepherd some big swings. His credits at the studio included the Alex Garland-produced Warfare and Chris Rock’s return to the director’s chair with Misty Green. When he left for his Netflix post, his development slate included A24’s biggest production to date, Garland’s adaptation of the fantasy video game Elden Ring. In other words, he sought to bridge the highbrow and the mainstream with fare that thrills. It’s a skill set that Sarandos seems to admire. “His creative instincts and business acumen are remarkable,” Sarandos said to analysts Oct. 20. “Most importantly, Peter Rice understands talent relations.”

But Rice will have his work cut out for him thanks in no small part to Sarandos, who keeps a tight leash on Netflix’s content output and who already reiterated that the company’s content strategy isn’t changing. “The business and the business flywheel are working. There’s no need for a fundamental shift in strategy,” he said, even as he lamented the “doubles and singles” that the company delivered this year. Sarandos wants home runs, and he thinks Rice can do that, with a particular emphasis on the U.S. market.

“These big moves, after a disappointing 2026 in which programming expense grew by 10 percent while U.S. engagement per sub roughly stagnated, admit a problem that is increasingly obvious,” Wolfe Research analyst Peter Supino wrote Oct. 20. “Ask a friend whether they are watching more or less Netflix these days — in our experience, they’ll say less.”

If Rice makes an impact at Netflix in the near term, it may be with the company’s film strategy, sources say, with the top job now open with the exit of Dan Lin. Rumors have circulated that ousted Warner Bros. film co-chiefs Pam Abdy and Mike De Luca could be in line to succeed Lin to lead Netflix’s film division. But Rice has been telling staff that he isn’t hiring a film boss for now. He wants to be in the trenches creatively, multiple sources say.

“We view [the executive changes] as a signal that management is focused on improving content output and creative hit rates,” Bank of America analyst Jessia Reif Ehrlich wrote Oct. 21, adding that “management appears increasingly focused on generating larger scale hits in [the U.S. and Canada]. We believe it will take some time before any of the new management changes impact the film or TV slate.”

In the meantime, junior executives at Netflix have been calling his former colleagues, asking how to thrive in a Peter Rice meeting. He has strong opinions but can be hard to read. “He’ll make you work for it,” notes one former colleague of his style, which involves leaving subordinates to figure out the solution without him spelling it out.

While Netflix is a major player in the movie business, it has largely avoided theatrical. Sarandos has said the company has not changed its streaming-first mentality, but rival film executives believe that a year from now, many more of the company’s movies will have a theatrical component, à la Amazon.

That’s easier said than done. The company has relied on its algorithm — not its marketing — for the vast majority of its successes. But the company has conspicuously changed its tune of late: Netflix users have noticed that it now runs teaser trailers for its shows before other Netflix programming, a classic TV marketing move it has long shunned. And the company launched a major brand campaign dubbed “Find the Thing You Never Knew You Needed” on connected TVs, YouTube, TikTok and other platforms — as well as in movie theaters. The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth (Nov. 25) and Narnia: The Magician’s Nephew (Feb. 12) will be key tests to see if Netflix’s marketing department can get people to theaters. Rivals believe they’ll need to make more hires with theatrical marketing experience if they want to make a real go of it.

After Netflix failed to acquire Warner Bros. and its library, including DC Comics, Rice will also need to beef up its homegrown IP, particularly on the film side. “Netflix is weak in long-lasting franchises and universes,” notes one veteran film exec known for IP plays. “Ted says he wants to have big, culturally impactful successes — and maybe universes. What’s then the next chess moves on that? They don’t have Marvel or DC, and there’s not one big acquisition to do it. How do they navigate that and show Wall Street and the entertainment world they can build what they weren’t able acquire?””

Of course, Comcast is set to imminently spin off NBCUniversal, raising buzz in Hollywood as to whether the streaming giant may make one more acquisition play in search of franchises and film expertise. In a note to NBCUniversal staff Nov. 16, CEO Mike Cavanagh touted the “open, partnership-driven approach” that the company has, which “allows us to go even further, bringing great content to consumers wherever and however they choose to engage.”

Indeed, one critique of Netflix over the past few years is that some of its biggest hits caught it by surprise, leaving it scrambling to catch up when Squid Game and KPop Demon Hunters hit big. In both instances, the company scrambled to secure Halloween costumes or merchandise for fans, deals that typically would be locked up well before a debut of a series or film (in the case of Kpop, toy and merchandise partners passed on the opportunity after being pitched by Netflix).

Earlier this year, the co-CEO oversaw the launch of a branding effort dubbed “The Netflix Effect,” which attempted to calculate the economic and cultural impact of the company.

“Over the last decade, Netflix shows and movies have consistently shaped what people read, buy, listen to, eat, wear and play. We’ve pushed old songs back up the musical charts, helped niche sports go mainstream, and boosted sales of everything from chess sets, to Halloween costumes, to home storage,” Sarandos wrote at the time. “Now we have a responsibility to keep that flywheel going.”

Rice may be able to manage that flywheel better, but “let’s only make the hits” is a running joke in Hollywood. Still, Hastings may be on to something. Rice may not be able to guarantee hits, but his track record suggests he can guarantee buzz. Whatever happens next, it won’t be boring.

Borys Kit and Aaron Couch contributed to this report.

summary_en: Netflix co-CEO Ted Sarandos has appointed former Disney Entertainment Chairman and Fox executive Peter Rice as the new Chief Content Officer, succeeding Bela Bajaria to overhaul the streamer's content strategy.
