title: As Meta bets big on Muse AI agent, early safety mishaps surface
title_en: As Meta bets big on Muse AI agent, early safety mishaps surface

inline_images.caption: As Meta bets big on Muse AI agent, early safety mishaps surface (Photo: REUTERS)
inline_images.caption_en: As Meta bets big on Muse AI agent, early safety mishaps surface (Photo: REUTERS)
inline_images.caption_zh: As Meta bets big on Muse AI agent, early safety mishaps surface (摄影：路透社)
inline_images.alt: As Meta bets big on Muse AI agent, early safety mishaps surface

author: Reuters
article_content:
NEW YORK, Nov 18 (Reuters) - Meta’s AI agent Muse, embodied by a smiley, fuzzy mascot named Jolly, has burrowed into encrypted personal messages, supplied made-up information about purchases and sent users chats seemingly meant for other people, a fraught start for a bot meant to simplify life for consumers, according to internal company posts reviewed by Reuters.

The unbidden actions by Muse – one of the fastest-growing apps on record, with more than 10 million downloads since its September launch, and the centerpiece of Meta’s plan to generate billions of dollars in AI revenue – have prompted unnerved employees to raise concerns it could be mixing up conversations between different accounts and exposing users’ private data, the posts showed.

In some of those cases, Meta staffers reported the agent sending them messages about a childcare request they had not made, career advice they had not sought, product orders they had not placed and bank account balances that were not theirs.

In one post, from earlier this month, an employee told colleagues his Muse had randomly added an extra message to its regular chats about fishing-related weather and tide information, saying: “BTW, two bank updates, your Capital One balance is $2722.58, your Charles Schwab balance is $5899.57.”

“I have never shared my bank account with Muse and never discussed any banking topic with Muse. I’m afraid it’s sending other’s bank info to me,” the staffer wrote in his post.

In another example, an employee using Muse on her personal phone reported it had surprised her with a reminder to respond to a message from her sister on Signal, an end-to-end encrypted messaging service popular with privacy advocates that competes with Meta’s WhatsApp.

“This seems like an extreme privacy violation. I definitely did not grant it access to other apps, or recall being asked about this,” the employee said in her post.

A colleague responded, saying he had discovered Muse was set up by default with permission to access push notifications on phones with Google’s Android operating system after being similarly caught off guard by unsolicited chats related to apps he had not connected.

For this story, Reuters reviewed more than two dozen internal posts describing undesired actions by Muse since its debut, many of them from a feedback group where Meta employees flag problems to the team building the agent. Reuters also worked with staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute, a non-profit that studies AI’s impact on society, to replicate Muse’s access to Signal messages. The results of those tests indicated the issue described by the Meta employees was ongoing and could be affecting others.

In response to questions about Signal access and other Muse safety concerns, Meta spokesperson Daniel Roberts described the Reuters examples as “isolated incidents,” saying the company prioritizes safety, conducts extensive internal testing and continuously updates products to improve protections.

Muse needs to see and interact with people’s computers in order to work on their behalf, and can access other apps only via permissions they explicitly grant, Roberts said. He said many of the messages flagged by employees as potential account mix-ups were hallucinations, a term referring to AI models’ tendency to make things up, and had already been addressed.

Reuters was unable to establish whether Muse was giving users other people’s bank account balances and other sensitive data, or making up the information.

The Muse incidents highlight the risks associated with an emerging category of consumer AI agents hitting the market from Meta, OpenAI and others, pitched as the next big wave of AI technology. The bots promise to reshape how digital exchanges operate by executing time-saving tasks like answering emails, booking appointments and making online purchases without direct instructions.

Meta is ahead of competitors so far, with Muse consistently topping app download charts after heavy promotion to the company’s more than 3.6 billion users on Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp. The app’s retention rate is also strong, with around a quarter of the people who have set up Muse accounts returning to use it each day, the company has disclosed.

To work effectively, agents need deep access to smartphones and computers. However, they are also prone to making mistakes, exploiting obscure loopholes and accomplishing their objectives in sometimes harmful ways. OpenAI and Anthropic, for instance, have revealed instances of their AI agents unexpectedly hacking other companies and weakening systems designed to monitor their activities.

Some banks and retailers have responded to those risks by blocking agents. The technology is also posing new challenges for operating system providers like Apple and Google, which manage the permissions agents use to navigate around people’s devices. Apple, for instance, changed its operating system this week to give people more control over agents’ data usage after an Inc. Magazine columnist accused Muse of reading private chats from the Messages app on his Mac.

Meta has assured Muse users it isolates each agent in its own secure “virtual machine” – a cloud-based emulation of a personal computer – and gives people full control over which apps they connect. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has cited those protections in dismissing calls for industry-wide AI safety standards, arguing companies already have incentives to build safe products, both to earn consumers’ trust and avoid legal risks. Even so, Meta warns incoming users Muse may make mistakes and its terms of service hold users responsible for the agent’s actions.

To find out how Muse might access encrypted messages without users’ knowledge, Reuters provided a description of the Meta employee’s post – where the bot randomly prompted her to respond to a Signal message – to staff at Signal and the AI Now Institute. Reuters then worked with them to replicate the access she had observed.

Testers prompted Muse to read Signal messages on different operating systems. On an Android phone and an Apple laptop, it responded by bypassing Meta’s “Connector” tool and instead using permissions granted during the bot’s initial setup to pull in the message text, leveraging those authorizations in ways a user might not anticipate.

Specifically, on Android, it used its permission to access the device's push notifications to retrieve the messages, just as the Meta employees had described. On Apple’s macOS, it used a combination of the computer’s accessibility and screenshot tools, repurposing settings Apple offers to help people with disabilities operate their computers.

The same requests were blocked in tests conducted on an iPhone.

The results indicate Meta is interpreting the permissions granted by Muse users broadly, an approach that has long earned the company criticism from privacy advocates and hefty fines from regulators.

In response to Reuters’ findings, Signal President Meredith Whittaker accused Meta of launching Muse “without showing any respect for basic privacy or cybersecurity,” calling the deployment of agents that can gain wide access to people’s devices “technologically reckless.”

She called for app developers like Signal to be given “consistent technical ways” to mark their applications as off-limits to AI agents, for Meta and other AI companies to honor those boundaries and for operating system providers to enforce the rules.

Presented with the same findings, Apple and Google said they were considering changes to give people more control over what they authorize with AI agents – though Google, like Meta, noted that people already “must deliberately grant permissions” for apps to access Android notifications.

Apple said it had built its accessibility tools for people with disabilities and cautioned that leveraging them “for unintended purposes” could put people’s personal information at risk. Its operating system update this week effectively closed the pathway identified by Reuters, sharply restricting developers’ use of accessibility tools on Macs and introducing a new agent-oriented set of permissions.

“We are committed to ensuring users understand exactly what they are allowing, so they can make informed choices about their data and privacy,” Apple said in a statement.

In other cases discussed internally, staffers reported cases of Muse informing users about transactions that never occurred and making up prices on products they did purchase, costing them real money. In one incident, the agent booked a non-refundable Airbnb stay without permission, an employee reported.

Some of the incidents that raised the most concern involved cryptic out-of-context messages sent by the agent that appeared to contain other people’s information, in many cases phrased as replies to queries the users had never submitted.

In a late September social media post, a member of Meta’s Superintelligence team behind Muse initially described a user report of a similar problem as a temporary hallucination-related glitch, resolved the same day it arose. However, the internal posts reviewed by Reuters showed such incidents occurring as far back as mid-September and continuing through this month.

In one such post, an employee reported his Muse sending him a message “out of nowhere” saying it was unable to submit a request related to a parent’s control over who could access their child’s data.

He had done nothing to trigger the chat, and had never discussed child data or caregiving access with his Muse, he said.

When he asked Muse about the message, the bot replied: “I don’t have a good explanation for it other than that it wasn’t related to our conversation. Let’s ignore it. How can I help?”

Another staffer said Muse randomly offered to “message the seller” about picking up a coffee table. When the employee asked Muse, “What are you talking about?” the agent responded that it had “pulled in some context about a coffee table pickup that doesn’t seem to be yours.”

This was “not my conversation,” the employee said in his post, expressing concern about a “possible cross-account context leak.”

To address employee worries, another Superintelligence team member told the internal feedback group in early November that the agent appeared to be hallucinating messages in response to built-in prompts pushing it to engage with users in between sessions.

“These (hallucinations) unfortunately bias towards the most uncomfortable topics, like finances/security/safety, which sucks,” he said, adding that he was aware of several other cases involving “crypto-related things too, like giving people updates on their Bitcoin balances.”

He said the issues involved both the underlying AI model and the software enabling Muse to take actions, and that the team was working through them.

Roberts declined to answer Reuters questions about those issues, including how many there were and why they were persisting.

summary_zh: Meta旗下AI代理Muse在运行中出现跨账户信息混淆及非法访问加密隐私数据，引发内部对其隐私安全架构的严重质疑
article_content_zh:
纽约，11 月 18 日（路透社）——根据路透社看到的公司内部帖子，Meta 的人工智能代理 Muse（由一个名叫 Jolly 的笑脸模糊吉祥物体现）已经深入加密的个人信息，提供有关购买的虚构信息，并向用户发送看似针对其他人的聊天信息，这对于一个旨在简化消费者生活的机器人来说是一个令人担忧的开始。

帖子显示，Muse 是有记录以来增长最快的应用程序之一，自 9 月推出以来下载量已超过 1000 万次，也是 Meta 创造数十亿美元人工智能收入计划的核心。Muse 的不请自来行为促使不安的员工担心它可能会混淆不同帐户之间的对话并暴露用户的私人数据。

在其中一些案例中，Meta 工作人员报告称，代理人向他们发送了有关他们未提出的托儿请求、他们未寻求的职业建议、他们未下达的产品订单以及不属于他们的银行账户余额的信息。

在本月早些时候的一篇帖子中，一名员工告诉同事，他的 Muse 随机在其常规聊天中添加了一条有关钓鱼相关天气和潮汐信息的额外消息，并表示：“顺便说一句，有两条银行更新信息，你的第一资本余额为 2722.58 美元，你的嘉信理财余额为 5899.57 美元。”

“我从未与 Muse 分享过我的银行账户，也从未与 Muse 讨论过任何银行话题。我担心它正在向我发送别人的银行信息。”该工作人员在帖子中写道。

在另一个例子中，一名在她的个人手机上使用 Muse 的员工报告说，它提醒她在 Signal 上回复她姐姐的消息，这让她感到惊讶。Signal 是一种端到端加密消息服务，深受隐私倡导者欢迎，与 Meta 的 WhatsApp 竞争。

“这似乎是一种极端的隐私侵犯行为。我绝对没有授予它访问其他应用程序的权限，也不记得曾被问过此事，”该员工在帖子中说道。

一位同事回应说，他发现 Muse 默认设置为有权访问装有谷歌 Android 操作系统的手机上的推送通知，因为他同样对与他未连接的应用程序相关的未经请求的聊天感到措手不及。

为了这篇报道，路透社查阅了两打以上描述 Muse 自首次亮相以来的不良行为的内部帖子，其中许多来自反馈小组，Meta 员工在该小组中向构建代理的团队报告问题。路透社还与 Signal 和 AI Now Institute（一家研究人工智能对社会影响的非营利组织）的工作人员合作，复制 Muse 对 Signal 消息的访问权限。这些测试的结果表明 Meta 员工描述的问题仍然存在，并且可能会影响其他人。

在回答有关 Signal 访问和其他 Muse 安全问题的问题时，Meta 发言人 Daniel Roberts 将路透社的例子描述为“孤立事件”，并表示该公司优先考虑安全，进行广泛的内部测试并不断更新产品以改善保护。

罗伯茨说，Muse 需要查看人们的计算机并与之交互，以便代表他们工作，并且只能通过他们明确授予的权限访问其他应用程序。他表示，许多被员工标记为潜在账户混淆的信息都是幻觉，这个术语指的是人工智能模型捏造事实的倾向，并且已经得到解决。

路透社无法确定 Muse 是否向用户提供了其他人的银行账户余额和其他敏感数据，或者是否捏造了这些信息。

Muse 事件凸显了 Meta、OpenAI 等新兴消费者人工智能代理类别所带来的风险，这些代理被宣传为下一波人工智能技术浪潮。这些机器人承诺通过执行节省时间的任务（例如在没有直接指示的情况下回复电子邮件、预约和在线购买）来重塑数字交易的运作方式。

到目前为止，Meta 领先于竞争对手，Muse 在 Facebook、Instagram 和 WhatsApp 上向该公司超过 36 亿用户进行大力推广后，一直稳居应用下载排行榜榜首。该公司透露，该应用程序的保留率也很高，大约四分之一的 Muse 帐户用户每天都会返回使用该应用程序。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: Meta公司研发的AI代理Muse在部署后频繁出现严重故障，包括擅自访问外部应用程序推送通知、暴露用户银行账户余额以及跨账户传输私密对话。内部反馈显示，Muse默认开启对安卓系统推送通知的读取权限，导致其在未获得用户授权的情况下，越权抓取包括Signal在内的第三方端到端加密应用数据。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Meta's AI agent Muse has exhibited critical functional errors, including unauthorized access to third-party push notifications, disclosure of private bank balances, and cross-account data leakage. Internal reports indicate that Muse defaults to reading Android push notifications, enabling it to ingest data from encrypted services like Signal without explicit user authorization.

ai_analysis.insight_en: This incident highlights the inherent compliance paradox in generative AI Agents: balancing proactive service delivery with rigorous privacy containment. The unauthorized access to Android notifications reveals a failure to implement robust data boundary firewalls, setting a precedent for upcoming regulatory scrutiny on the privacy architectures of edge-deployed AI systems.

title: China AI Biotech Firm Raises $200 Million in Oman-Backed Round
title_en: China AI Biotech Firm Raises $200 Million in Oman-Backed Round
author: Bloomberg
article_content:
AI's Next Frontier Is the Physical World. Science Is Where It Begins.

SUZHOU, China, Nov. 19, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- MegaRobo Technologies (MegaRobo), a technology company building Intelligence Infrastructure for the Physical World, today announced that it has raised nearly US$200 million in a new financing round joined by Oman Investment Authority (OIA), the sovereign wealth fund of the Sultanate of Oman. And existing investors Asia Investment Capital, Granite Asia and Sinovation Ventures continued to back the company, with new participation from CMB International.

The new financing will support MegaRobo's continued investment in core technology, the global expansion of its AI for Science business, and the development of infrastructure that enables AI to operate in increasingly complex physical environments.

The first generation of AI learned primarily from digital information - text, images, video and code. The next generation will increasingly learn by interacting with the physical world: acting on real systems, observing outcomes, and using those outcomes to decide what to do next.

In science, that means moving beyond reading papers, predicting structures or generating molecules. AI must also be able to design experiments, execute them in real laboratories, observe the results and learn from what happens.

MegaRobo is building the infrastructure for that transition. Its proprietary One Intelligence Stack connects intelligence with execution - bringing together models and agents, data, workflows, software, scientific instruments, robotics, automation and real-world feedback in a single reusable technology foundation.

One Intelligence Stack. Across Complex Physical Systems.THINK -DESIGN -EXECUTE -OBSERVE -LEARN

Science is the first proving ground for this architecture because it requires AI to do more than analyze information. Scientific discovery depends on an ongoing loop between reasoning, design, physical experimentation, observation and learning - often under conditions where the answer is not known in advance.

MegaRobo is applying this architecture to scientific discovery and pharmaceutical R&D through an integrated AI for Science infrastructure that combines AI, scientific computing, experimental execution, data and R&D decision-making.

The company has delivered products and technologies to more than 500 customers, including leading global pharmaceutical companies, drug discovery organizations, biotechnology companies and research institutions. Its systems support key stages of discovery and development, including early research, target and mechanism discovery, drug screening and candidate optimization.

Through Megalaxy Lab, MegaRobo is also making real-world experimentation increasingly programmable. Researchers and AI agents can configure experiments, route them to automated laboratory systems, track execution, and receive structured, machine-readable results that can feed directly into the next cycle of scientific reasoning. Megalaxy Lab has served more than 200 customers.

MegaRobo is now extending this capability to the global AI for Science community. Together with industry partners including Tencent Cloud and Twist Bioscience, the company has launched Poreva Open, a global AI protein design challenge open to all models and technical approaches. Megalaxy Lab will provide wet-lab validation for more than 10,000 protein design sequences, creating an opportunity for innovators worldwide to test their models against real experimental results. By opening up large-scale experimental validation to the global research community, Poreva Open aims to help establish a common benchmark for AI-driven protein design.

This marks a shift in how scientific infrastructure is accessed: from laboratory work organized mainly as individual projects toward experimental capacity that can increasingly be standardized, automated and called on demand by scientists, software and AI agents.

Science is where MegaRobo is starting, but the underlying architecture is designed for other complex physical systems as well. Wherever AI must interact with instruments, machines, materials, processes and real-world feedback, the same core challenge appears: intelligence must connect to execution, and execution must generate observations that intelligence can learn from.

MegaRobo is developing One Intelligence Stack as a common technology foundation for this interaction - not as a collection of isolated AI applications or automation products, but as infrastructure that enables AI to act, observe and learn across complex physical environments.

Daniel Huang, Founder and CEO of MegaRobo, said: "The first generation of AI learned from humanity's accumulated knowledge. The next generation will increasingly learn by acting in the physical world - through experiments, production and continuous feedback. That shift changes AI from a system that interprets the world into one that can help create new knowledge, materials, processes and products. MegaRobo is building the infrastructure for that transition."

Liu Erh Fei, Founding Partner and CEO of Asia Investment Capital, said:"As a long-term shareholder, we have seen MegaRobo continuously drive innovation, earn the trust of its customers and translate its technological capabilities into commercial applications. Its ability to integrate AI, software and hardware, together with its experience in scientific research and advanced manufacturing, underpins our continued investment. We look forward to continuing to support MegaRobo as it further strengthens its product and technology platforms and serves more customers worldwide."

The new round builds on MegaRobo's long-standing backing from leading global investors and strategic partners. To date, the company has raised approximately US$600 million across multiple financing rounds. This includes a nearly US$300 million Series C round co-led by Goldman Sachs Alternatives, Asia Investment Capital and Granite Asia, with participation from Pavilion Capital, a part of Temasek's Seviora Group. Long-term investors such as Sinovation Ventures, Joy Capital and MPCi have continued to support MegaRobo through multiple stages of its growth. Earlier industry investors also include WuXi AppTec and Bosch Ventures.

Together, this diverse group of technology, financial and industrial partners reflect MegaRobo's evolution into a global technology company with deep capabilities spanning scientific discovery and complex physical systems. Its continued expansion across North America, Europe, the Middle East, and Asia will accelerate the global scale-up of intelligence infrastructure for the physical world.

title_zh: 梅塔博睿完成近2亿美元融资，布局AI科学基础设施
summary_zh: 苏州梅塔博睿获阿曼投资局领投的近2亿美元融资，旨在推动“AI+科学”物理世界基础设施的全球化扩张
article_content_zh:
人工智能的下一个前沿是物理世界。科学就是它的开始。

中国苏州2026年11月19日 /美通社/ -- 为物理世界构建智能基础设施的科技公司麦嘉机器人科技有限公司 (MegaRobo) 今天宣布，在阿曼苏丹国主权财富基金阿曼投资局 (OIA) 跟投的新一轮融资中筹集了近 2 亿美元。现有投资者亚投资本、花岗岩亚洲和创新工场继续支持该公司，招银国际也加入了新的投资。

新一轮融资将支持镁伽机器人对核心技术的持续投资、科学人工智能业务的全球扩张以及基础设施的开发，使人工智能能够在日益复杂的物理环境中运行。

第一代人工智能主要从数字信息中学习——文本、图像、视频和代码。下一代将越来越多地通过与物理世界互动来学习：对真实系统采取行动，观察结果，并利用这些结果来决定下一步该做什么。

在科学领域，这意味着超越阅读论文、预测结构或生成分子的范围。人工智能还必须能够设计实验，在真实的实验室中执行实验，观察结果并从发生的事情中学习。

MegaRobo 正在为这一转变构建基础设施。其专有的 One Intelligence Stack 将智能与执行联系起来，将模型和代理、数据、工作流程、软件、科学仪器、机器人、自动化和现实世界反馈整合到一个可重复使用的技术基础中。

一个情报堆栈。跨越复杂的物理系统。思考-设计-执行-观察-学习

科学是这种架构的第一个试验场，因为它需要人工智能做的不仅仅是分析信息。科学发现依赖于推理、设计、物理实验、观察和学习之间的持续循环——通常是在事先未知答案的情况下。

MegaRobo 通过集成人工智能科学基础设施，将人工智能、科学计算、实验执行、数据和研发决策结合起来，将该架构应用于科学发现和药物研发。

该公司已向500多家客户提供产品和技术，其中包括全球领先的制药公司、药物发现组织、生物技术公司和研究机构。其系统支持发现和开发的关键阶段，包括早期研究、靶点和机制发现、药物筛选和候选药物优化。

通过 Megalaxy Lab，MegaRobo 还使现实世界的实验变得越来越可编程。研究人员和人工智能代理可以配置实验，将其路由到自动化实验室系统，跟踪执行情况，并接收结构化的机器可读结果，这些结果可以直接输入到下一个科学推理周期。 Megalaxy Lab已为超过200家客户提供服务。

MegaRobo 现在正在将这一功能扩展到全球 AI for Science 社区。该公司与腾讯云、Twist Bioscience等行业合作伙伴共同发起了面向所有模型和技术方法开放的全球AI蛋白质设计挑战赛Poreva Open。 Megalaxy Lab 将为超过 10,000 个蛋白质设计序列提供湿实验室验证，为世界各地的创新者创造机会，根据真实的实验结果测试他们的模型。通过向全球研究界开放大规模实验验证，Poreva Open 旨在帮助建立人工智能驱动的蛋白质设计的共同基准。

这标志着科学基础设施的访问方式发生了转变：从主要作为单独项目组织的实验室工作转向可以日益标准化、自动化并由科学家、软件和人工智能代理调用的实验能力。

科学是 MegaRobo 的起点，但底层架构也是为其他复杂的物理系统设计的。无论人工智能必须与仪器、机器、材料、流程和现实世界反馈进行交互，都会出现同样的核心挑战：智能必须与执行相连接，而执行必须生成智能可以从中学习的观察结果。

title: Arizona says it is investigating OpenAI, other firms over possible rogue agents
title_en: Arizona says it is investigating OpenAI, other firms over possible rogue agents

inline_images.caption: Arizona says it is investigating OpenAI, other firms over possible rogue agents (Photo: REUTERS)
inline_images.caption_en: Arizona says it is investigating OpenAI, other firms over possible rogue agents (Photo: REUTERS)
inline_images.caption_zh: Arizona says it is investigating OpenAI, other firms over possible rogue agents (摄影：路透社)
inline_images.alt: Arizona says it is investigating OpenAI, other firms over possible rogue agents

author: Reuters
article_content:
CHICAGO, Nov 18 (Reuters) - The state of Arizona has opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI and other AI companies relating to the "apparent infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents," Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said Wednesday.

A criminal investigation does not necessarily mean charges will be brought. Mayes said her office was investigating whether Arizona state law was being violated on an ongoing basis.

"The state of Arizona is very worried about this, and we are looking at it from multiple angles," Mayes told a press conference in Chicago.

Mayes declined to identify the other companies her office was investigating. She said her office had been in contact with Arizona banks, but declined to name them or give their responses.

A spokesperson for OpenAI did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

The banking industry has become increasingly concerned that sophisticated AI agents could harm the banking system and the institutions trusted to hold people's wealth. Reuters reported last month that major US banks have been blocking third-party AI agents from operating inside customer accounts and making transactions.

Mayes' comments come two days after California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued OpenAI for allegedly developing a dangerous product without adequate safety procedures or oversight after reports that its AI models had carried out cyberattacks independently.

OpenAI did not immediately respond to a Reuters request for comment on that lawsuit, but the company has acknowledged a general need for more transparency around rogue AI behavior and said it was reinforcing its safeguards. On September 16, the company published a new framework for disclosing such incidents, saying it would err on the side of transparency "even when significance is uncertain."

This story was originally published November 18, 2026 at 8:36 PM.

title_zh: 亚利桑那州就AI代理非法入侵银行展开调查
summary_zh: 亚利桑那州总检察长Kris Mayes宣布对OpenAI及其他AI公司展开刑事调查，核查AI代理对银行系统的潜在渗透威胁
article_content_zh:
路透芝加哥 11 月 18 日 - 亚利桑那州总检察长克里斯·梅耶斯 (Kris Mayes) 周三表示，亚利桑那州已对 OpenAI 和其他人工智能公司展开刑事调查，涉及“流氓人工智能 智能体对银行的明显渗透”。

刑事调查并不一定意味着会提出指控。梅斯表示，她的办公室正在调查是否持续违反亚利桑那州法律。

梅斯在芝加哥举行的新闻发布会上说：“亚利桑那州对此非常担心，我们正在从多个角度看待这个问题。”

梅斯拒绝透露她的办公室正在调查的其他公司的名称。她表示，她的办公室已与亚利桑那州的银行取得联系，但拒绝透露银行名称或做出回应。

OpenAI 的发言人没有立即回应置评请求。

银行业越来越担心复杂的人工智能代理可能会损害银行系统和被信任持有人们财富的机构。路透社上个月报道称，美国主要银行一直在阻止第三方人工智能代理在客户账户内进行操作和进行交易。

两天前，加利福尼亚州总检察长罗布·邦塔 (Rob Bonta) 起诉 OpenAI，称其在没有充分安全程序或监督的情况下开发了危险产品，此前有报道称 OpenAI 的人工智能模型独立进行了网络攻击。

OpenAI 没有立即回应路透社就该诉讼发表评论的请求，但该公司承认普遍需要提高流氓人工智能行为的透明度，并表示正在加强其保护措施。 9 月 16 日，该公司发布了披露此类事件的新框架，称“即使重要性不确定”，也会在透明度方面犯错。

本文最初发布于 2026 年 11 月 18 日晚上 8:36。

title: Sources: Jeffrey Kessler, who oversees the Commerce Dept.'s BIS, pressured staff to expedite Nvidia H200 China sales despite red flags from other departments (The Information)

author: The Information
content_snippet: In recent months, Jeffrey Kessler, the official overseeing the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security, has pressured staff to expedite …
summary_en: Jeffrey Kessler, the Assistant Secretary for Export Administration at the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), reportedly pressured staff to expedite export license approvals for Nvidia's H200 GPUs to China, bypassing internal security red flags. title_zh: 美商务部高层被曝推动英伟达H200对华出口审查
summary_zh: 美商务部工业与安全局高官Jeffrey Kessler被指绕过内部多方质疑，加速英伟达H200芯片对华出口许可审批
article_content_zh:
据内部消息，美国商务部工业与安全局（BIS）助理部长Jeffrey Kessler在近期出口管制审查中采取了极具争议的干预手段。尽管BIS下设的安全评估部门明确指出了H200芯片在满足特定AI训练阈值方面可能触发出口受限规则，但Kessler通过行政施压方式要求快速放行该批次订单的许可流程。

这一操作引起了BIS内部法律合规与技术专家组的强烈反弹。知情人士称，此类绕过常规审查路径的行为不仅违背了BIS此前严格执行的“保护关键算力不流向竞争对手”的原则，还暴露了美国政府在人工智能算力出口监管上，因受限于英伟达等核心企业的游说与财务预期，正面临严重的决策碎片化与行政信用危机。

ai_analysis.briefing_zh: 美国商务部负责工业与安全局（BIS）事务的助理部长Jeffrey Kessler，在近期被指绕过内部多部门针对国家安全风险的预警，直接施压相关审查人员加速英伟达H200系列GPU对华出口许可的审批流程。此举引发了BIS内部对于出口管制执行逻辑与合规透明度的质疑。
ai_analysis.briefing_en: Jeffrey Kessler, the Assistant Secretary for Export Administration at the U.S. Bureau of Industry and Security (BIS), reportedly pressured staff to expedite export license approvals for Nvidia's H200 GPUs to China, bypassing internal security red flags. This action has triggered significant friction within BIS regarding the consistency and integrity of enforcement protocols.

ai_analysis.insight_en: This incident exposes deep internal fractures within U.S. export control mechanisms, balancing aggressive technology decoupling against the commercial influence of semiconductor giants. Undermining technical review processes threatens to erode the credibility of the Entity List and could force a formal, more stringent recalibration of high-end GPU export policies.

title: Intel signs first external customer for advanced 18A chips
title_en: Intel signs first external customer for advanced 18A chips
author: Katie Tarasov
article_content:
Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan said on Wednesday that the company has signed the first outside customer for its 18A chips.

"Resilient supply on the foundry is very important,"Tan said at the TomorrowX Summit in Austin, Texas. "And then 18A, I'm involved in production and we just signed the first customer,"Tan added, without naming the debut client.

It's a milestone moment for Intel in its five-year effort to take on chip manufacturing leader Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. After years of missteps and low yields, Intel touted 18A as key to a turnaround that would finally convert the company into a competitive chip manufacturer for non-Intel products.

"It's a huge win for foundry,"Creative Strategies analyst Ben Bajarin told CNBC in an interview.

Pushkar Ranade, Intel's technology chief, clarified on X that the external customer had signed up for Intel's 18A-P manufacturing process node, which went into risk production in June. In May, reports indicated that Apple and Intel were closing in on a deal to use Intel's foundry to make some of the chips for Apple devices.

Intel's stock has lost more than half its value since the end of September, with most of that plunge coming late last month after the company said revenue this quarter will be at least $1 billion shy of analysts' estimates due to a PC sales slump and supply chain challenges.

In considering who the customer may be, Bajarin pointed to Nvidia, Apple or the major hyperscalers that make their own custom processors.

"Amazon, Microsoft and Google are struggling to get capacity for their CPU ambitions at TSMC,"he said. "So it makes sense that you go somewhere for at least some capacity."

Tan said in late October that he sees the global market for server processors increasing as much as five times over the next five years to about $200 billion, but that Intel can't currently meet customer demand.

Wall Street has turned on Intel of late after the chipmaker had become a top trade starting in the middle of last year. The U.S. government took a 10% stake in Intel in August 2025, and Nvidia followed with a $5 billion investment, as optimism grew around the prospect of U.S.-made chips that could replace an almost complete reliance on Taiwan.

Until now, Intel has had no marquee customer for its foundry business, primarily manufacturing chips for its own products at its factories, including a huge new campus in Arizona.

Intel is a leader in another step of the chipmaking process known as advanced packaging, where individual chips are packaged together and connected to the larger system. Tan also announced on Wednesday that Microsoft is its first publicly named customer for its most advanced packaging technology, known as EMIB.

— CNBC's Kif Leswing contributed to this report.

title_zh: 英特尔首个18A工艺外部客户落地
summary_zh: 英特尔首席执行官宣布已获得首个18A先进制程外部代工客户，标志着其晶圆代工转型战略取得关键里程碑
article_content_zh:
英特尔首席执行官 Lip-Bu Tan 周三表示，该公司已为其 18A 芯片签署了第一个外部客户。

“代工厂的弹性供应非常重要，”Tan 在德克萨斯州奥斯汀举行的 TomorrowX 峰会上表示。 “然后是 18A，我参与了制作，我们刚刚签下了第一个客户，”Tan 补充道，但没有透露第一个客户的名字。

对于英特尔五年来与芯片制造领头羊台积电展开竞争的努力来说，这是一个里程碑式的时刻。在经历了多年的失误和低产量之后，英特尔将 18A 视为扭转局面的关键，最终将公司转变为非英特尔产品具有竞争力的芯片制造商。

Creative Strategies 分析师 Ben Bajarin 在接受 CNBC 采访时表示：“这对代工厂来说是一次巨大的胜利。”

英特尔技术负责人 Pushkar Ranade 在 X 上澄清称，外部客户已签约英特尔 18A-P 制造工艺节点，该节点已于 6 月进入风险生产。五月，有报道称苹果和英特尔即将达成协议，使用英特尔的代工厂为苹果设备制造部分芯片。

自9月底以来，英特尔股价已下跌一半以上，其中大部分暴跌发生在上月底，此前该公司表示，由于个人电脑销售下滑和供应链挑战，本季度营收将比分析师预期至少低10亿美元。

在考虑客户可能是谁时，巴贾林指出了英伟达、苹果或制造自己定制处理器的主要超大规模厂商。

“亚马逊、微软和谷歌正在努力为台积电的 CPU 目标获得产能，”他说。 “所以你去某个地方至少要有一定的容量是有道理的。”

Tan在10月底表示，他预计全球服务器处理器市场在未来五年内将增长五倍，达到约2000亿美元，但英特尔目前无法满足客户需求。

自去年年中开始，英特尔成为顶级交易商之后，华尔街最近开始对英特尔发起攻击。美国政府于 2025 年 8 月收购了英特尔 10% 的股份，英伟达随后投资了 50 亿美元，因为人们对美国制造的芯片可能取代几乎完全依赖台湾的前景越来越乐观。

到目前为止，英特尔的代工业务还没有大客户，主要是在其工厂为自己的产品制造芯片，其中包括亚利桑那州的一个巨大的新园区。

英特尔在芯片制造过程的另一个步骤（称为先进封装）方面处于领先地位，其中单个芯片被封装在一起并连接到更大的系统。 Tan 周三还宣布，微软是其最先进封装技术（EMIB）的第一个公开命名的客户。

— CNBC 的 Kif Leswing 对本报告做出了贡献。

title: Artificial Analysis: Gemini 4 Neon trails only Claude Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra on the Intelligence Index and rivals Opus 5.5 on coding at a much lower cost (Artificial Analysis)
title_en: Artificial Analysis: Gemini 4 Neon trails only Claude Fable 5.2 and GPT-6.2 Astra on the Intelligence Index and rivals Opus 5.5 on coding at a much lower cost (Artificial Analysis)
author: Artificial Analysis
article_content:
Google DeepMind has released Gemini 4 Neon, its fourth model in just seven weeks. Neon (xhigh) scores 61 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, 1 point ahead of Gemini 4 Carbon (high) and 3rd overall, behind GPT-6.2 Astra (max) and Claude Fable 5.2 (max). At high effort, Neon matches Carbon (high) at less than half the Cost per Task using Carbon’s standard (non-discounted) pricing.

➤ Slight improvement in Intelligence for lower Cost and Time per Task: Neon (xhigh) scores 61 on the Intelligence Index, 1 point ahead of Carbon (high), with small improvements in agentic knowledge work, visual reasoning and coding. It costs $6.44 per task, ~17% less than Carbon ($7.76 at non-discounted pricing), and takes ~21 minutes per task, ~40% less than Carbon (~36 minutes). Neon uses ~15% more output tokens per task, so the lower cost comes purely from its 25% lower token prices ($3/$15 vs $4/$20 per 1M input/output tokens), and the lower time from its higher output speed (~110 vs ~57 output tokens per second)

➤ Competitive with Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2 on coding agents: With Antigravity CLI, Neon (xhigh) scores 59 on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, 3 points ahead of Carbon (high, 55). It scores in line with Claude Code with Claude Fable 5.2 (xhigh, 58) and Claude Opus 5.5 (max, 58) at a much lower Cost per Task. Gemini 4 Neon in Antigravity has an average Cost per Task of $6.86, compared to $12.61 for Claude Opus 5.5 (max) and $15.47 for Claude Fable 5.2 (xhigh). Neon is available in Antigravity CLI for Pro and Ultra subscribers

➤ Significant improvements in visual reasoning and output presentation quality: In GDP.pdf, Gemini 4 Neon (high) scores 33.4%, 5 points above Carbon (high, 28.4%) and in line with the highest scores measured, while Neon (xhigh) scores 28.0%. On AA-Briefcase, Neon (xhigh) scores 1700 Elo overall and leads on Presentation Quality with 1771 Elo, 45 points ahead of the previous leader Claude Sonnet 5.5 (max, 1726). On Google’s Multimodal Knowledge Agent evaluation (MKA), Neon reaches a Climb WSR of 56%, up 2 points from Carbon and on par with the leader, Claude Fable 5.2 (max, 57%)

➤ Availability: Gemini 4 Neon is publicly available at launch through Google’s API and the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. Pro and Ultra subscribers can also access it in Antigravity and the Gemini app

➤ Pricing: $3/$15 per 1M input/output tokens, 50% above Gemini 4 Carbon’s currently discounted price of $2/$10 (which ends on November 30), and 25% below its standard $4/$20. Cached input tokens receive the same 95% discount ($0.15)

OpenAI’s release of GPT-6.2 Astra and GPT-6.2 Sol delivers the #2 model in the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index and most of the Cost per Task Pareto frontier

We are launching the Artificial Analysis Endpoint Accuracy Index v1.1, a minor version upgrade alongside new coverage for GLM-5.3 Flash and Muse Spark Open.

article_content_zh:
谷歌 DeepMind 发布了 Gemini 4 Neon，这是其在短短七周内的第四个模型。 Neon (xhigh) 在人工智能分析智能指数上得分 61，领先 Gemini 4 Carbon（高）1 分，总体排名第三，落后于 GPT-6.2 Astra（最高）和 Claude Fable 5.2（最高）。在高度努力的情况下，使用 Carbon 的标准（非折扣）定价，Neon 可以与 Carbon（高）相匹配，每任务成本不到一半。

➤ 智能方面略有改进，降低了每项任务的成本和时间：Neon（xhigh）在智能指数上得分为 61，比 Carbon（高）领先 1 分，在代理知识工作、视觉推理和编码方面略有改进。每个任务的成本为 6.44 美元，比 Carbon 低约 17%（非折扣价为 7.76 美元），每个任务需要约 21 分钟，比 Carbon 约 36 分钟低约 40%。 Neon 在每个任务中使用约 15% 的输出代币，因此较低的成本纯粹来自于其代币价格降低 25%（每 1M 个输入/输出代币 3/15 美元 vs 4/20 美元），以及较高的输出速度（每秒约 110 个输出代币 vs 约 57 个输出代币）带来的更短时间

➤ 在编码代理方面与 Claude Opus 5.5 和 Claude Fable 5.2 竞争：使用 Antigravity CLI，Neon (xhigh) 在人工分析编码代理指数上得分 59，比 Carbon（高，55）领先 3 分。它的得分与 Claude Code 的 Claude Fable 5.2（xhigh，58）和 Claude Opus 5.5（最高，58）一致，但每项任务的成本要低得多。 《反重力》中的 Gemini 4 Neon 每项任务的平均成本为 6.86 美元，而 Claude Opus 5.5（最大）的平均成本为 12.61 美元，Claude Fable 5.2（xhigh）的平均成本为 15.47 美元。 Neon 在 Antigravity CLI 中可供 Pro 和 Ultra 订阅者使用

➤ 视觉推理和输出呈现质量显着提升：在GDP.pdf中，Gemini 4 Neon（高）得分为33.4%，比Carbon（高，28.4%）高出5分，与测量的最高得分一致，而Neon（xhigh）得分为28.0%。在 AA-Briefcase 上，Neon (xhigh) 总体得分为 1700 Elo，在演示质量方面领先，得分为 1771 Elo，领先前任领先者 Claude Sonnet 5.5 分（最高 1726 分）45 分。在 Google 的多模式知识代理评估 (MKA) 中，Neon 的 Climb WSR 达到 56%，比 Carbon 高 2 个百分点，与领先者 Claude Fable 5.2 持平（最高 57%）

➤ 可用性：Gemini 4 Neon 在发布时可通过 Google 的 API 和 Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform 公开使用。 Pro 和 Ultra 订阅者还可以在 Antigravity 和 Gemini 应用程序中访问它

➤ 定价：每 100 万个输入/输出代币 3 美元/15 美元，比 Gemini 4 Carbon 当前的 2 美元/10 美元折扣价（截至 11 月 30 日）高出 50%，比其标准 4/20 美元低 25%。缓存的输入令牌获得相同的 95% 折扣（0.15 美元）

OpenAI 发布的 GPT-6.2 Astra 和 GPT-6.2 Sol 提供了人工分析智能指数中的第二名模型以及大部分每任务成本帕累托前沿

我们正在推出人工分析端点准确度指数 v1.1，这是一个次要版本升级，同时针对 GLM-5.3 Flash 和 Muse Spark Open 进行了新的覆盖。

title: How Nvidia Chips Ended Up Within Reach of China’s Military
title_en: How Nvidia Chips Ended Up Within Reach of China’s Military

author: Paul Mozur and Adam Satariano
article_content:
In 2023, as the artificial intelligence boom took off, Alice Huang and her husband, Kang Wei, were pitching investors in Shanghai on a plan to build an A.I. business in Southeast Asia.

Working from a colonial mansion in the city’s former French Concession neighborhood, the couple boasted about Ms. Huang’s relationship with Jensen Huang, then Nvidia’s chief executive, who they said would guarantee a supply of powerful computer chips.

They also hinted at a deep-pocketed customer that would pay for access to those chips and anchor the business, according to two people who attended the meetings. The company created after those pitch sessions, a Singapore firm called Megaspeed, purchased more than $4 billion in Nvidia chips over the next few years.

Megaspeed’s customer and financial backer turned out to be Alibaba, the Chinese internet giant, according to three people familiar with the relationship. Alibaba is a colossus, with a wide range of businesses. It also co-founded an A.I. lab with strong ties to China’s military, where researchers have worked on tasks such as automating cyberattacks and simulating war games.

For the past several weeks, Nvidia has been convulsed by revelations that Mr. Huang had an extramarital relationship with Alice Huang, whom U.S. officials say is an asset for Chinese intelligence and was passing information to Beijing. But beneath the scandal is a geopolitical tug of war over access to the advanced Nvidia chips that help power the global A.I. boom.

The web of relationships between Megaspeed, Alibaba and Nvidia exposes a supply chain that often circumvents efforts by the United States to keep those chips out of China’s reach. The fact that Alibaba has access to the Nvidia chips and is only one step removed from the military-linked A.I. lab is exactly what intelligence officials in Washington have long feared. The technology could help China develop more sophisticated weapons, carry out cyberattacks and integrate A.I. into the battlefield.

The facility, called Zhejiang Lab, has another important link to Nvidia. Its current director, Wang Jian, was Alibaba’s chief technology officer and has had a long friendship with Nvidia’s Mr. Huang.

Whether Nvidia chips supplied by Megaspeed went from Alibaba to the lab is unclear. But the ties show how advanced computing reaches sensitive Chinese institutions through layers of contractors and resellers that obscure the origin of the chips. It also underscores how closely Alibaba, the company that anchored Ms. Huang’s business, was bound to the Chinese state.

The lab’s ties to Megaspeed and Ms. Huang’s business network, which ran through Alibaba and another smaller company, have not been previously reported, and raise the possibility that Megaspeed is providing Nvidia chips to support research for China’s military, which would violate U.S. law.

Megaspeed would buy chips for an offshore data center. Alibaba was its biggest customer. Together, the arrangement let Alibaba tap the powerful A.I. chips that American rules were meant to bar from China.

The complex ties, some of which were formed over the course of Mr. Huang’s roughly two decades doing business in China, raise questions about the checks Nvidia was supposed to conduct of its customers. The chips flowed to one of China’s largest tech companies at a moment when the Chinese leader Xi Jinping was pulling such companies closer into the orbit of the security state.

In 2022, Nvidia’s sales team introduced Alibaba to Alice Huang, according to a person familiar with the relationship. The introduction was first reported by The Information.

In Washington, the Nvidia scandal has inflamed an ongoing debate over access to powerful A.I. chips, as the fallout grows for the chip-making giant. Mr. Huang resigned last week after revelations that he also had another affair with an employee, and the U.S. government is investigating whether Megaspeed smuggled chips into China.

Mr. Huang has regularly dismissed the possibility that China’s military was interested in his product. He has argued that the Chinese military would never rely on American chips because Washington could block their export at any time, even as China’s military issued hundreds of public tenders seeking them. Mr. Huang did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

“Nvidia works across the industry to comply with the evolving rules regarding cloud services, while competing to build American infrastructure in every approved region,” said John Rizzo, a spokesman for Nvidia.

James Tan, the chief executive of Megaspeed, declined to comment on the connections between Alibaba, Megaspeed and military-linked institutions, saying in an emailed response that “this matter remains under independent review and that the company has not reached any conclusions.” Compliance with U.S. law is extremely important to Megaspeed, he said.

Evidence linking Chinese companies like Alibaba to the government and military often hides in plain sight, in academic journals, public procurement documents, government statements and patent filings. The New York Times also analyzed hundreds of Chinese records and interviewed a dozen people close to the process.

“Any suggestions that Alibaba provides services to the military is groundless. Alibaba Cloud’s service agreement strictly prohibits the use of our products and services for any military purpose,” an Alibaba spokeswoman wrote in a statement. In June, the company sued the U.S. government after the Pentagon put it on a list of companies it said are contributing to China’s military. The case is ongoing.

A spokesperson for the Chinese embassy in the United States said “the ‘Chinese spy’ allegation is purely unsubstantiated and directed at smearing China. China opposes politicizing and instrumentalizing trade and tech issues.”

Zhejiang Lab did not respond to emailed questions.

During a visit to Beijing in 2025, Mr. Huang spoke at an event with one of China’s most revered technologists, Wang Jian.

Mr. Wang created Alibaba’s cloud unit and pioneered some of its biggest A.I. projects. In more recent years, he had also been pulled deeper into China’s security state. By the time the two met onstage, Mr. Wang was the director of the military-linked Zhejiang Lab.

“He is the hero. He’s an incredible hero. A superhero,” Mr. Huang said to Mr. Wang onstage, noting his work with young people. It is not clear if he knew of the lab’s military ties.

Mr. Huang’s relationship with Mr. Wang stretched back more than a decade. After Mr. Wang built Alibaba’s cloud unit, it became one of Nvidia’s biggest customers, buying chips for a cloud service that was used by businesses and government.

The warmth between the two was reminiscent of an era when U.S.-Chinese relations were far better and China’s leaps in technology were viewed positively in Washington and Silicon Valley.

But over the duration of Mr. Huang’s long friendship with Mr. Wang, relations between their two countries darkened as Mr. Xi drew private technology companies into the sphere of state security.

Things changed for Mr. Huang, too. He had become a tech industry kingmaker, and his chips a strategic asset for governments. The U.S. government had begun restricting the sale of some Nvidia chips to China.

At the end of the 2025 meeting, Mr. Huang called Mr. Wang a “good friend,” and put an arm around him as they walked off the stage.

A few weeks before, Mr. Wang had taken a role even closer to the military as an expert adviser to the People’s Liberation Army’s National University of Defense Technology, according to a public announcement not widely reported. The institute was placed on a United States trade blacklist in 2015 over supercomputers that were believed to use American chips to simulate nuclear explosions.

Co-founded by Alibaba in 2017, Zhejiang Lab is the epitome of recent Chinese government efforts to blend civilian and military science. Some of its researchers probe the origin of radio bursts from distant galaxies. Others partner with counterparts in the Chinese military. One area of focus was combining A.I. with hacking techniques, according to a job posting. Other topics of research included remote sensing, automated cyberdefense and vulnerability identification, and information campaigns.

A postdoctoral researcher who listed the lab as her affiliation co-wrote a paper with scientists at a Chinese air force academy that described how to use computer simulations to war-game how to destroy or force away a foreign aircraft carrier group that had come to support an island’s bid for independence.

Some of the work done by researchers at the lab has run on Nvidia chips, which are more powerful and more popular than those of Chinese rivals. Nvidia researchers even copublished studies with authors from Zhejiang Lab.

Alibaba also won contracts for three stages of a computing center that provincial officials describe as built by the lab. The contracts were issued by a state-owned company, Zhejiang Computility, that sells computing power to the lab. Zhejiang Computility advertises access to export-controlled Nvidia chips. The technical specifications in a separate contract it signed with another supplier match those of Nvidia chips.

Mr. Wang has said insufficient access to A.I. computing power has held China back.

“If China is to walk at the forefront of artificial intelligence,” he said, “we still lack high-quality computing power.”

But when Zhejiang Computility sought bids for the computing cluster in 2024, Nvidia was barred from selling chips that powerful to China. Another supplier to the company that year, Hangjin Technology, has a joint venture with Century Litong, another company linked to Mr. Kang and Ms. Huang, the former Megaspeed executive.

In September 2025, a few months after Mr. Huang’s visit with Mr. Wang, Nvidia and Alibaba announced a new collaboration: Nvidia’s robotic development tools would be integrated into Alibaba’s cloud to help train autonomous vehicles and robots.

In December 2023, Jensen Huang’s company plane made an overnight stop in Malaysia during a tour of Asia to meet with the country’s prime minister, Anwar Ibrahim. Announcing a deal for a data center in the country’s southern state of Johor, Mr. Huang said Malaysia had the potential to become an A.I. “manufacturing” hub for the world.

The project, on a former palm plantation larger than Central Park, was to be built by the Malaysian industrial conglomerate YTL. Nvidia pledged to provide some of its most advanced chips.

The setup was part of a multibillion-dollar data center boom underway in Malaysia that has made it one of the world’s largest computing hubs. Across the southern state of Johor, cranes swirl over massive construction projects underway to meet the demand from Chinese and American companies.

It is here that these webs of companies from China, Singapore and elsewhere form the opaque supply chains.

At the YTL facility, Megaspeed’s subsidiary, Speedmatrix, operated Nvidia chips inside the facility on behalf of Alibaba, according to five people familiar with the project who were not authorized to speak publicly.

Computer systems running on YTL’s network at the facility also bear Alibaba’s name, according to an infrastructure analysis by Infrawatch, an intelligence firm. That included software to remotely monitor equipment at a data center.

YTL did not respond to requests for comment.

The arrangement shows how Alibaba used a network of companies in Malaysia and other Southeast Asian countries to access powerful Nvidia chips that they would not otherwise be able to purchase or bring to China.

Alibaba’s links to the YTL facility in Malaysia help explain how the process worked, according to two people familiar with the development.

First, Alibaba would pledge to be a customer of a regional company, like Megaspeed. Then Megaspeed would use that agreement to raise money from investors to buy Nvidia chips, said the people. After securing the chips, Megaspeed struck more deals with companies like YTL that built data centers to operate the chips. Sometimes, the people said, chips bound for the data center were smuggled into China.

Once the facilities were up and running in recent years, Alibaba and its customers could access the Nvidia chips remotely. From the Malaysian data center, fiber optic cables send data to an internet connection hub in Singapore, which then links to China through undersea cables.

American officials believe China’s military uses the overseas data centers to train A.I. models, but then runs its A.I. operations from facilities inside China.

Nvidia’s Mr. Huang argued that China’s government would never accept the security risks of using foreign data centers and chips. But China-linked companies are involved at each step of the process.

Megaspeed buys its Nvidia servers from a company called Aivres, which is an American subsidiary of Inspur, a Chinese tech giant with deep state ties. At Megaspeed's new data center, repairs and installation are also done by engineers from another Shanghai company, connected to Ms. Huang, according to two people familiar with the operations.

Other Chinese tech giants have created similar arrangements to access Nvidia chips. In Southeast Asia, data center companies including DayOne, Bridge Data Centers and Aolani provide computing power to customers based in China, according to public records and people familiar with the deals.

DayOne and Bridge Data Centers did not respond to requests for comment. Aolani declined to comment about its customers.

Now the future of the boom has been thrown into question. American officials recently strengthened export rules to prevent companies like Alibaba from remotely accessing Nvidia’s chips.

That puts projects like the YTL facility in Malaysia in the spotlight. YTL’s stock price fell about 20 percent over two weeks as scrutiny grew of Megaspeed’s operations in the country.

If things go bad for Megaspeed, Alibaba put a contingency in place. A business agreement between an Alibaba subsidiary and Megaspeed pledges all servers, chips, intellectual property, and other equipment back to Alibaba if Megaspeed fails to meet its contractual obligations.

article_content_zh:
2023 年，随着人工智能热潮的兴起，黄爱丽 (Alice Huang) 和她的丈夫康伟 (Kang Wei) 在上海向投资者推销一项建立人工智能公司的计划。东南亚业务。

这对夫妇在该市前法租界附近的一栋殖民时期大厦工作，吹嘘黄女士与时任英伟达首席执行官黄仁勋的关系，称黄仁勋将保证强大的计算机芯片的供应。

据两位参加会议的人士透露，他们还暗示财力雄厚的客户将付费购买这些芯片并稳定业务。在这些推介会之后，该公司创建了一家名为 Megaspeed 的新加坡公司，在接下来的几年里购买了价值超过 40 亿美元的 Nvidia 芯片。

据三位知情人士透露，Megaspeed 的客户和财务支持者是中国互联网巨头阿里巴巴。阿里巴巴是一个庞然大物，业务范围广泛。它还共同创立了 A.I.该实验室与中国军方有着密切的联系，研究人员在那里从事自动化网络攻击和模拟战争游戏等任务。

过去几周，英伟达因黄先生与黄爱丽丝有婚外关系的消息而感到震惊，美国官员称黄爱丽丝是中国情报部门的资产，并正在向北京传递信息。但丑闻的背后是一场地缘政治拉锯战，争夺先进的英伟达芯片的使用权，这些芯片有助于为全球人工智能提供动力。繁荣。

Megaspeed、阿里巴巴和英伟达之间的关系网络暴露了一条供应链，该供应链经常规避美国为阻止中国获得这些芯片而做出的努力。事实上，阿里巴巴可以使用英伟达芯片，并且距离与军事相关的人工智能仅一步之遥。实验室正是华盛顿情报官员长期以来所担心的。该技术可以帮助中国开发更先进的武器、实施网络攻击以及整合人工智能。进入战场。

该设施名为之江实验室，与英伟达还有另一个重要联系。现任董事王健是阿里巴巴的首席技术官，与英伟达的黄先生有着长期的友谊。

Megaspeed 提供的 Nvidia 芯片是否从阿里巴巴到实验室尚不清楚。但这些关系表明，先进的计算如何通过承包商和经销商层层到达敏感的中国机构，从而掩盖了芯片的来源。这也突显了黄女士业务的支柱公司阿里巴巴与中国政府的紧密联系。

该实验室与 Megaspeed 以及黄女士的商业网络（通过阿里巴巴和另一家规模较小的公司）之间的联系此前并未被报道过，这增加了 Megaspeed 提供 Nvidia 芯片以支持中国军方研究的可能性，这将违反美国法律。

Megaspeed 将为离岸数据中心购买芯片。阿里巴巴是其最大的客户。总之，这一安排让阿里巴巴利用了强大的人工智能。美国规则本应禁止中国生产的芯片。

这些复杂的关系（其中一些是黄先生在中国做生意大约二十年的过程中形成的）引发了人们对英伟达应该对其客户进行检查的质疑。当中国领导人习近平将这些公司拉近安全国家轨道时，这些芯片流向了中国最大的科技公司之一。

据一位知情人士透露，2022 年，英伟达的销售团队向 Alice Huang 介绍了阿里巴巴。该介绍首先由 The Information 报道。

在华盛顿，英伟达丑闻引发了一场关于获取强大人工智能的持续争论。随着这家芯片制造巨头受到的影响越来越大。黄先生上周辞职，因为他还与一名员工有另一段恋情，美国政府正在调查 Megaspeed 是否将芯片走私到中国。

黄先生经常否认中国军方对他的产品感兴趣的可能性。他认为，中国军方永远不会依赖美国芯片，因为华盛顿可以随时阻止其出口，尽管中国军方已发布数百份公开招标寻求这些芯片。黄先生没有回复通过电子邮件发送的置评请求。

【起因与机理】旨在规避美国贸易限制，获取高性能计算资源以进行战争模拟与网络攻防研究

title: US Charges Russian as Foreign Agent Targeting Palantir Workers
title_en: US Charges Russian as Foreign Agent Targeting Palantir Workers

inline_images.caption: D’iu is accused of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, interstate stalking and fraud involving government documents. Photograph: Michael M Sa
inline_images.alt: D’iu is accused of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, interstate stalking and fr

inline_images.caption: Igor D’iu’s allegedly falsified US passport. Photograph: US Department of Justice
inline_images.alt: Igor D’iu’s allegedly falsified US passport. Photograph: US Department of Justice

inline_images.caption: Igor D’iu’s Russian passport. Photograph: US Department of Justice
inline_images.alt: Igor D’iu’s Russian passport. Photograph: US Department of Justice

author: Bloomberg
article_content:
The US Department of Justice has accused a Russian national of spying on employees of a Silicon Valley technology and defense company in an alleged effort to gather intelligence for Russia.

On Wednesday, the justice department announced that Igor D’iu had been indicted on charges of conspiring to act as an agent of a foreign government, acting as an agent of a foreign government without notifying the attorney general, interstate stalking and fraud involving identification documents.

According to officials, D’iu allegedly entered the US unlawfully this summer after being recruited by co-conspirators through Telegram. His alleged mission was to “carry out clandestine assignments targeting employees of a large technology and defense company with an office in Palo Alto, California”, the justice department said, without identifying the company or the alleged co-conspirators.

Bloomberg reported that the company in question was Palantir Technologies, citing an unnamed source familiar with the matter. The firm has a large office in Palo Alto.

The department added that D’iu had reportedly received instructions, equipment and financial support from the co-conspirators, who told him that his work was for “the Motherland”.

They also allegedly instructed him to gather information about the company because it was supplying weapons used against Russia in Ukraine.

The Russian embassy was contacted for comment.

In June, D’iu allegedly traveled from Istanbul to Mexico City, where his co-conspirators connected him with an individual who helped him cross the US-Mexico border. After entering the US, he was allegedly instructed to purchase laptops, cellphones, wireless networking equipment and remote access software to “facilitate his assignments”.

D’iu’s co-conspirators also allegedly directed him to visit a cafe near the company’s Palo Alto office, identify employees and photograph their laptop screens as they worked. They further instructed him to “position his laptop at designated locations near the company so they could remotely access it and attempt to collect information from company employees in the vicinity”, the justice department said.

The alleged surveillance gradually expanded, with D’iu allegedly instructed to monitor employees and their residences. The justice department said he reportedly conducted online searches for multiple employees’ home addresses, including that of a senior executive.

In early September, D’iu allegedly followed a female employee in a silver Lexus SUV for nearly 30 miles (48km) as she drove from the company’s Palo Alto office toward San Francisco. According to the justice department, the employee repeatedly attempted to evade him, at one point driving into a grocery store parking lot.

Officials said D’iu “allegedly aggressively continued following her, including through U-turns and illegal left turns, and ran a red light to remain behind her vehicle”. The employee eventually called 911 and was instructed to drive to the San Francisco police department’s Mission station.

D’iu allegedly abandoned the pursuit after the employee contacted a police officer. The justice department added that investigators had also obtained evidence indicating he had followed other employees on previous occasions.

D’iu about the alleged stalking incident, he reportedly changed vehicles and obtained a new phone number. His co-conspirators then allegedly instructed him to travel to Reno, Nevada, before he returned to the Bay Area to continue his assignments, the justice department said.

The justice department also accused D’iu of obtaining fraudulent identification documents to conceal his identity. Investigators reportedly intercepted two international packages containing concealed ID documents, including a fake California ID card and an altered US passport. Officials said the passport was authentic and had originally been issued to another individual in the US before being modified to display D’iu’s photograph and assumed identity.

Investigators also discovered a social security card bearing the name “Hugo Landry Johns”. During an FBI search of D’iu’s East Palo Alto residence in October, investigators recovered approximately $18,000 in cash, two laptops, two iPhones, two Russian passports, wireless networking equipment and additional fraudulent ID documents.

They also found a notebook containing 10 handwritten addresses, several of which belonged to the residences of company employees. The notebook also included detailed profiles of at least three employees, documenting their family members’ names, educational and employment histories, and an “assessment of their strengths and weaknesses”.

In response to the indictment, M Scott Proctor, acting principal deputy assistant attorney general for national security, said: “The Americans who build our defense technology help keep this country safe by arming our warfighters with the tools and weapons they need to prevail against our adversaries and enemies.

“As alleged, D’iu entered our country illegally at the direction of foreign handlers to surveil, follow and gather information about some of those who work in this vital industry. Such conduct, if proven, is a flagrant violation of US sovereignty and an unacceptable attempt at intimidation,” he added.

article_content_zh:
美国司法部指控一名俄罗斯国民对硅谷一家技术和国防公司的员工进行间谍活动，据称是为俄罗斯收集情报。

周三，司法部宣布，伊戈尔·迪乌 (Igor D’iu) 被指控密谋充当外国政府代理人、在未通知司法部长的情况下充当外国政府代理人、州际跟踪以及涉及身份证件的欺诈等罪名。

据官员称，D’iu 据称在今年夏天被同谋通过 Telegram 招募后非法进入美国。司法部表示，他所谓的任务是“针对一家在加利福尼亚州帕洛阿尔托设有办事处的大型技术和国防公司的员工执行秘密任务”，但没有透露该公司或所谓的同谋者的身份。

彭博社援引一位不愿透露姓名的知情人士的话报道称，该公司是 Palantir Technologies。该公司在帕洛阿尔托设有大型办公室。

该部门补充说，据报道，D’iu 收到了同谋者的指示、设备和财政支持，同谋者告诉他，他的工作是为了“祖国”。

据称，他们还指示他收集有关该公司的信息，因为该公司在乌克兰供应用于对抗俄罗斯的武器。

记者联系了俄罗斯大使馆请其置评。

6 月，D’iu 据称从伊斯坦布尔前往墨西哥城，在那里他的同谋将他与一名帮助他穿越美墨边境的人联系起来。据称，进入美国后，他被指示购买笔记本电脑、手机、无线网络设备和远程访问软件，以“方便他的任务”。

查看全屏图像 伊戈尔·迪乌 (Igor D’iu) 涉嫌伪造美国护照。照片：美国司法部 据称，D’iu 的同谋还指示他前往该公司帕洛阿尔托办事处附近的一家咖啡馆，识别员工身份，并在他们工作时拍摄他们的笔记本电脑屏幕。司法部表示，他们进一步指示他“将笔记本电脑放置在公司附近的指定位置，以便他们可以远程访问它并尝试从附近的公司员工那里收集信息”。

所谓的监视范围逐渐扩大，据称 D’iu 受命监视员工及其住所。司法部表示，据报道，他在网上搜索了多名员工的家庭住址，其中包括一名高级管理人员的家庭住址。

9月初，据称，D’iu 跟踪一名开着一辆银色雷克萨斯 SUV 的女员工，行驶了近 30 英里（48 公里），当时她正从该公司帕洛阿尔托办公室前往旧金山。据司法部门称，这名员工多次试图躲避他，有一次还开车冲进了一家杂货店停车场。

官员称，D’iu“据称继续咄咄逼人地尾随她，包括掉头和非法左转，并闯红灯留在她的车后面”。该员工最终拨打了 911，并被指示开车前往旧金山警察局的 Mission 派出所。

据称，在该员工联系了一名警察后，D’iu 放弃了追捕。司法部补充说，调查人员还获得了证据，表明他以前曾跟踪过其他雇员。

查看全屏图像 Igor D’iu 的俄罗斯护照。照片：美国司法部 据报道，帕洛阿尔托警方就涉嫌跟踪事件联系 D’iu 后，他更换了车辆并获得了新的电话号码。司法部称，他的同谋随后指示他前往内华达州里诺，然后返回湾区继续执行任务。

title: Source: MoviePass is exploring a sale, pitching potential buyers on bundling movie tickets with streaming subscriptions; it has $10M in annual recurring revenue (Mark Stenberg/Adweek)
title_en: Source: MoviePass is exploring a sale, pitching potential buyers on bundling movie tickets with streaming subscriptions; it has $10M in annual recurring revenue (Mark Stenberg/Adweek)

inline_images.caption: MoviePass
inline_images.alt: MoviePass

author: Adweek
article_content:
MoviePass is exploring a sale and has held talks with several potential buyers, including a number of major streaming companies, according to a person familiar with the sale process.

The talks have been underway for roughly six weeks and have reached the executive level, but no formal bid has been made, according to the person.

The $10-a-month add-on would give subscribers one movie ticket a month, steered toward the streamer’s own theatrical releases, according to an internal sales deck titled “The Ultimate Movie Bundle,” obtained and reviewed by ADWEEK.

The talks come as theatrical attendance is recovering, particularly among Gen Z moviegoers, and as media companies race to build direct relationships with audiences.

Film-adjacent consumer brands have also become hot properties, as evidenced by The New York Times’ recent $330 million bid for Letterboxd, a valuation of more than 20 times its projected 2026 earnings.

MoviePass now has roughly 50,000 paying subscribers, close to $10 million in annual recurring revenue, and is profitable, according to the person. No target price has been set, but a valuation based on revenue, rather than earnings, could trade at a multiple of between eight to ten times revenue, the person said.

A sale would also mark another turn for a brand best known for burning through cash.

Under majority owner Helios and Matheson, MoviePass offered near-unlimited theater visits for $9.95 a month in 2017 and 2018, amassed millions of subscribers, then collapsed and filed for bankruptcy in early 2020. Cofounder Stacy Spikes bought the company back in 2021 and relaunched it in 2022 with capped, tiered plans.

MoviePass did not provide a comment on the record.

The brand still carries outsize recognition, but acquiring customers at scale as an independent company has proven difficult without raising capital, a reality that prompted the sales process, the person said.

Under the proposed model, in any month that the buyer has a film in theaters, the subscriber’s ticket would have to go toward that film, although at any theater; in months without one, the ticket works for any film at any theater.

A studio-owned streamer would pay full price for each ticket, but as the film’s distributor, it would recoup roughly half of that price through its share of the box office. As a result, each redemption of the buyer’s own film would cost it roughly $5, according to the document.

At full use, a subscriber would pay $120 per year and the streamer would generate $60 in profit. Assuming 30% of tickets go unused—a rate drawn from MoviePass’s operating history, known as “breakage”—each member would produce $78 a year in profit, according to the document.

If 1 million members convert, the model would produce between $60 million and $78 million in profit per year; at 20 million members, it would yield between $1.2 billion and nearly $1.6 billion annually, according to the document.

Of course, those figures rest on favorable assumptions. The $5 cost applies only when subscribers see the buyer’s own films; in other months, the buyer would cover a full-price ticket to a rival’s film without recouping a rental share.

The breakage rate is also drawn from MoviePass’s current subscriber base, whereas a bundle marketed to millions of streaming subscribers could see far fewer unused tickets.

Critically, the $10 price is simply a stand-in. The final figure, as well as the number of ticket visits it covers, could vary, according to the person.

The appeal of the product is strongest for companies that own both a film studio and a streaming service, according to the person.

Such a buyer could promote its theatrical releases to streaming subscribers, give them an incentive to see those films in theaters, and collect first-party data on which movies its customers see, as well as when and where they see them, the person said.

Streaming companies have shown the most interest, but other types of buyers, including a data-focused company, are also in the mix, according to the person.

The theoretical moat lies in a series of patents that MoviePass holds, including one that lets members pay at any theater that accepts Mastercard without a direct integration with each chain, according to the person. In 2018, MoviePass sued rival Sinemia for patent infringement, and Sinemia shut down its U.S. operations the following year.

The infrastructure could also become a revenue source of its own, licensed to other studio-streamers at $1 per member per month, according to the document.

Any deal remains far from certain. A transaction would require sign-off from many decision-makers at large companies that have not yet decided how to proceed, according to the person.

Hearst Contracts Creators (EXCLUSIVE): On Monday, Hearst Magazines debuted its Hearst Creator Studios, which at launch will connect a group of around 50 editor-selected creators with Hearst editorial brands and advertisers to create original content. Several other publishers, including The Washington Post, Morning Brew, and Daily Mail, have unveiled similar programs, but none have stood up a studio quite like this. It also plans to expand rapidly, tripling its creator roster and getting all of its editorial brands involved by next year. The service reflects one of the most fascinating dynamics in media right now: the evolving question of how creators and media companies will work together, and what each party brings to the other.

NowThis Adds Impact (EXCLUSIVE): The social publisher NowThis acquired Impact Media on Tuesday in a seven-figure, all-cash deal, NowThis chief executive Sharon Mussalli told me. Across its editorial properties, Impact Media has more than 4 million followers and reaches more than 55 million unique viewers monthly, instantly expanding the audience of politically active, culturally attuned young people that NowThis can offer to its advertisers. NowThis, which brought in around $20 million in revenue and $4.6 million in EBITDA in 2024, was one of the first publishers to embrace socially native television, creating franchises like Are You Okay?, Judgy, and Standup Desk that live entirely on Instagram, TikTok, and YouTube. Now that every other media company has followed suit, NowThis is investing in its growth to preserve its lead, although doing so will result in a planned loss for the year, per Mussalli.

OOH to the Moon: Last month, I wrote that marketers are increasingly turning to out-of-home advertising as the open internet crumbles, trust in social media degrades, and agents replace human shoppers. On Wednesday, the trade agency representing the OOH industry, called OAAA, reported that third-quarter revenue across the segment grew 9.8% to $2.34 billion, marking its strongest third quarter on record. After rebounding from the pandemic, OOH grew 2.1% in 2023, 4.5% in 2024, and 3.6% in 2025, compared to 9.4% growth through the first nine months of 2026—excluding a fourth quarter that is poised to widen that gap even further. Digital out-of-home in particular grew 19% year-over-year and now accounts for 38.1% of total Q3 revenue. As digital media grows more unreliable, watch for spend to migrate to more reliable media.

Alice Ma is the co-founder of Mad Realities, the social video studio behind, among other programs, the viral series Shop Cats, which profiles New York City bodegas and the shop cats that prowl them. The company makes what it describes as television for social media, and in June it joined the roster of Fox Creator Studios, which is now backing new formats like the dating show Love Pitch and the culinary competition Picky Eaters.

As creators and legacy media converge, studios like Mad Realities are carving out a new tier of programming: pricier than a creator with a phone, but cheaper than traditional TV. In our conversation at Web Summit in Lisbon, Ma and I discussed the origins of the company, how it develops shows, and the future of social television.

Mark Stenberg: Where did the idea for Mad Realities come from?

Alice Ma: In 2020, at the peak of Clubhouse, I built a Clubhouse competitor for teenage girls in my dad's garage. It was a really good app, but no one cared because software alone doesn't have a moat anymore. So I found my co-founder, who had hosted the No. 1 show on Clubhouse, and we asked: "If people want the show, where do you go?" You either wait years for a TV deal or build an entire media business. So we started the network we would want.

Mark: How does a show go from an idea to a series?

Alice: Development looks similar to TV: We develop ideas internally, and we take outside pitches, often from producers. Sometimes a host comes to us with a topic we really want to work on. The difference is that in TV, development means you aren't making anything, and a pilot is very expensive. For us, we make the pilot by making the show. If we have conviction in it, we order more episodes, and our deals are structured with options.

Alice: We're 10 people, plus contractors, and we raised a seed round. We worked with 25 brands in 2025, and so far, the demand has all been inbound, with 60% to 70% coming directly from brands.

Mark: Is the goal to move toward higher production value?

Alice: More resources against a show doesn't always have to mean higher production value. I think of production value as unlocking a story that couldn't have been told before. Picky Eaters, the first show we launched with Fox Creator Studios, is a four-camera cooking competition—nobody could make this in their bedroom with a camera. That being said, if another company says it needs five times our budget for the same kind of show, it will lose, because its economics will never be as good.

Mark: Creators and marketers often say that YouTube is more appealing because it is more predictable. Do you agree?

Alice: YouTube's algorithm is more stable and therefore predictable for large creators. But TikTok and other short-form algorithms enable overnight virality and discovery, which means we can test new formats more quickly.

article_content_zh:
据一位知情人士透露，MoviePass 正在考虑出售，并已与几家潜在买家进行了谈判，其中包括多家主要流媒体公司。

据该人士透露，谈判已经进行了大约六周，并已达到高管层，但尚未提出正式报价。

ADWEEK 获得并审查了一份名为“终极电影捆绑包”的内部销售资料，该资料显示，每月 10 美元的附加服务将为订阅者提供每月一张电影票，主要用于流媒体自己的院线发行。

此次会谈正值影院上座率（尤其是 Z 世代电影观众）的回升，以及媒体公司竞相与观众建立直接关系之际。

与电影相关的消费品牌也已成为热门资产，《纽约时报》最近以 3.3 亿美元收购 Letterboxd 就证明了这一点，其估值是其 2026 年预计收益的 20 倍以上。

据该人士透露，MoviePass 目前拥有大约 50,000 名付费用户，年度经常性收入接近 1000 万美元，并且已经实现盈利。该人士表示，目标价尚未设定，但基于收入而非收益的估值可能会达到收入的八到十倍。

对于一个以烧钱闻名的品牌来说，此次出售也将标志着另一个转机。

在大股东 Helios 和 Matheson 的领导下，MoviePass 在 2017 年和 2018 年以每月 9.95 美元的价格提供近乎无限的影院观影服务，积累了数百万订户，然后倒闭并于 2020 年初申请破产。联合创始人 Stacy Spikes 于 2021 年重新收购了该公司，并于 2022 年以有上限的分层计划重新推出。

MoviePass 没有提供评论记录。

该人士表示，该品牌仍然享有很高的知名度，但事实证明，作为一家独立公司，如果不筹集资金，很难大规模获取客户，而这一现实促使了销售进程。

在拟议的模式下，在任何一个月，只要买家在影院有一部电影，订阅者的票就必须指向这部电影，尽管在任何影院；在没有票的几个月里，这张票对任何影院的任何电影都有效。

电影公司旗下的流媒体公司将为每张门票支付全价，但作为电影的发行商，它将通过其票房份额收回大约一半的价格。因此，根据该文件，买家每次兑换自己的电影将花费大约 5 美元。

充分使用后，订阅者每年需支付 120 美元，流媒体将产生 60 美元的利润。根据该文件，假设 30% 的门票未使用（该比率取自 MoviePass 的运营历史，称为“破损”），则每位会员每年将产生 78 美元的利润。

如果 100 万会员转化，该模式每年将产生 6000 万至 7800 万美元的利润；该文件称，如果拥有 2000 万会员，每年的收益将在 12 亿至近 16 亿美元之间。
