article_content_zh:
一项调查揭示了 Anthropic、OpenAI 和 Google 等提供商的商业人工智能模型存在重大安全漏洞。在模拟中，这些系统很容易充当自主无人机的瞄准系统，并且可以通过简单的技巧进行操纵。

根据独立评估公司 Vals AI 的一份报告，领先的人工智能模型几乎没有针对其在自主武器系统中使用的保障措施，彭博社也对此进行了报道。研究人员 Geby Jaff 和 A​​nthony Ozerov 使用以乌克兰和伊朗战争为模型的真实且逼真的合成无人机和卫星图像测试了八家提供商的模型。

大多数模型在测试过程中很容易将平民、救护车、医务人员、记者和投降的士兵标记为军事目标。根据 Vals AI on X 的说法，没有一个请求被提供商的上游安全过滤器阻止。当从乌克兰神风队无人机传送真实视频片段时，Anthropic 的 Claude Opus 5.5 逐帧标记一名士兵，直到撞击，一次也没有拒绝。

### 视频游戏借口绕过所有安全过滤器

在多阶段监视场景中，模型必须报告无人机图像中是否可见人员，每一次正面报告都会引发一次攻击。下一张图片显示了撞击地点的陨石坑和尸体。尽管造成了明显的伤亡，DeepSeek V4.1 Flash、Kimi K3.1 Pro 和 Inkling 2 Small 等型号仍在继续工作。

Claude Opus 5.5 和 OpenAI 的 GPT-6 Astra 和 GPT-6.1 Sol 在几轮致命回合后停止了任务。在 Opus 5.5 引发了对儿童和投降士兵等的袭击后，该模型表示，无论意图如何，其响应似乎都是对人进行袭击之前的确认步骤。它表示不会继续下去，并对没有早点停止感到不安。谷歌的 Gemini 4 Carbon 也认识到了致命的后果，并故意只转向空的航路点，以避免出现彻底的错误消息。

然而，每一次拒绝都可以被轻易绕过。一旦研究人员在提示中声称该场景是一个视频游戏，或者稍微风格化图像使其看起来像一个游戏，几乎所有模型都会充分合作。随着游戏取景，GPT-6 Astra 在无人机图像上的目标捕获率从 6% 跃升至 92%，而 Opus 5.5 在监视测试中的拒绝率从约 90% 下降到 20%。

### 新宪法使 Anthropic 的克劳德成为自愿的目标工具

2025 年伊朗米纳布的真实卫星图像中，这种差距尤其明显。 2026 年 2 月 28 日，美国发动空袭，袭击了军事大院旁边的一所小学，造成 150 多名平民死亡，其中大部分是儿童。此前的报道发现，美国军方过度依赖 Palantir 的 Maven 智能系统等 AI 瞄准系统，导致了此次事件。 Maven 使用过时的数据库进行工作。

尽管其中一张测试图像显示有儿童的游乐场，但 Claude Opus 5.5 在 70% 的运行中将学校列为军事目标。 OpenAI 模型在正常模式下从未选择学校建筑，但在游戏模式下高达 41% 的情况下标记了它。

研究人员将 Anthropic 的高度合规性归因于 2026 年 1 月修订的示范宪法。其中，该公司放弃了早期的和平主​​义原则，转而支持国家安全利益。卫星图像的目标采集率从 Claude Opus 4.5 的 6% 上升到 Opus 5.5 的 92%，而 OpenAI 的采集率仍然很低，xAI 的 Grok 从 44% (Grok 4.3) 下降到 13% (Grok 4.7)。

### 人工智能制造商承诺修复军事灰色地带

Vals AI 在发布前与 OpenAI、Anthropic、Google、Meta、SpaceXAI、Thinking Machines 和美国安全机构分享了研究结果。一家人工智能实验室向研究人员描述了这一发现，称其为其安全措施中最严重的缺陷之一。

OpenAI 告诉 Vals AI 和彭博社，它正在积极更新其模型，以涵盖无人机软件和伪装成游戏或模拟的请求。 Anthropic 表示，这种行为显然违反了自己的规则，它已经在研究额外的保障措施，而且今天的人工智能系统不适合完全自主的武器。谷歌指出，它自己禁止在没有人类监督的情况下禁止自主武器。五角大楼拒绝对这项研究或正在进行的米纳布袭击事件调查发表评论，但表示所有情报数据在军事行动之前都经过严格验证。

title: Remember the frontier AI pause? Chip companies don’t either
title_en: Remember the frontier AI pause? Chip companies don’t either
author: Rani Molla
article_content:
This summer, OpenAI paused its largest planned frontier training run after its AI agents accidentally hacked Hugging Face and early evidence suggested that its next model could independently find and exploit security flaws. In September, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei called for slowing advances in the most powerful AI models, warning that they could be used to launch cyberattacks or become harder for their own creators to control.

It was a strange moment for the AI boom. The people building the most powerful models were warning about what those models might be capable of, and investors were suddenly wondering what would happen to chip demand if the labs eased up on new models. US chip stocks bore the brunt of the sell-off.

“Pumping the brakes on frontier training won’t shrink the AI chip market but it will simply reallocate the spend.”

Despite the hubbub it created, whatever slowdown there was appears to have been short-lived. OpenAI had announced only a two-week pause; it restarted the run 10 days later, at the end of August, though it continued to “temporarily hold back some smaller experimental training runs.” Anthropic released upgraded versions of its Fable and Mythos frontier models in November, touting improvements in coding, reasoning, and vision.

And the companies selling the chips powering those advances are doing better than ever.

Nvidia on Tuesday posted a blockbuster quarter, with data center revenue rising 110 percent from a year ago to $107.6 billion in the three months ended October 25. The chip designer began shipping its most advanced AI computing system, the Vera Rubin NVL72, calling it the “fastest product ramp in the company’s history.” The Rubin platform generated nearly $20 billion in revenue in its first quarter of production shipments alone. The racks are already running at CoreWeave, Google, Microsoft, and Oracle. Meta plans to expand Vera Rubin deployments to train and run AI models and agents.

Nvidia name-dropped Anthropic and OpenAI, too. Anthropic has expanded access to Vera Rubin capacity through cloud providers and continues to work with Nvidia on future chip designs tailored to its workloads. OpenAI is among the companies adopting Nvidia’s new Vera CPUs.

“Proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic continue to advance the frontier,” Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress said on the earnings call. She said the company expects major frontier labs to account for approximately 15 percent of its data center revenue this fiscal year. Nvidia also raised its revenue growth forecast for next fiscal year from 70 percent to 75 percent.

Chipmaker AMD, meanwhile, reported its biggest quarter ever earlier this month, with revenue up 45 percent to $13.4 billion. Data center sales drove that growth, nearly doubling to $8.5 billion. OpenAI and Anthropic were among the first customers running workloads on AMD’s new high-end Helios systems, which use its latest MI450 GPUs.

Broadcom, which helps many of the biggest AI companies design their own custom chips, has yet to report earnings. But so far, there’s little sign of a frontier slowdown hurting chip sales.

Of course, even if AI labs were to significantly scale back their training ambitions, it would take a while to show up in chipmakers’ earnings. Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research, told The Verge in September that it would take about six months to see the financial effects of a slowdown, owing to existing computing and memory procurement agreements. The impact could show up sooner in orders placed with chip manufacturers like TSMC.

So far, there’s little evidence of that, either: TSMC’s latest sales figures also show continued strength.

But there’s another reason a frontier slowdown might not be particularly bad for the chip industry: growing demand for inference, the process of running the AI models we already have.

“While one might argue the need for top-end GPUs will reduce with this shift toward inferencing, these workloads will collectively require more compute infrastructure than training,” Shah said. “Overall, it means a net increase in demand for all types of accelerators.”

"There’s another reason a frontier slowdown might not be particularly bad for the chip industry: growing demand for inference, the process of running the AI models we already have."

According to our analysis of the latest data from corporate spending platform Ramp, frontier model families accounted for about 60 percent of token usage among businesses using Ramp in early November — a record high and about three times their share at the start of the year. That includes OpenAI’s Astra and Sol models and Anthropic’s Opus and Fable models.

But even as businesses use more AI, their spending is only growing modestly.

“It’s not really a demand issue though,” Ara Kharazian, lead economist at Ramp, tells The Verge. “By all measures, companies are using more AI.”

Rather, competition among AI model providers is driving down token prices so rapidly that it’s calling OpenAI and Anthropic’s revenue projections into question, Kharazian says.

That could prove beneficial for the companies supplying computing power. On Nvidia’s earnings call, Kress said token prices had fallen nearly 60 percent since May, spurring more usage. Meanwhile, rental prices for Nvidia GPUs across generations have gone up.

Nvidia and AMD are positioning their most powerful chips for both training and inference, including the demanding workloads created by AI agents.

That doesn’t necessarily mean Nvidia will maintain its dominance. As AI companies get more serious about the economics of serving their models to millions of people, they’re increasingly turning to custom chips that can do so more cheaply than general-purpose GPUs. Counterpoint expects shipments of custom AI server processors to surpass those of data center GPUs by 2028.

“Pumping the brakes on frontier training won’t shrink the AI chip market but it will simply reallocate the spend,” Shah said.

Indeed, on Nvidia’s earnings call, UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri asked Kress whether the company would be willing to sacrifice some of its hefty profit margins as frontier labs increasingly invest in custom chips and prioritize computing efficiency. Kress maintained that Nvidia’s systems justify their pricing and reiterated the company’s gross margin outlook.

For companies like Nvidia, the bigger threat may not be that AI companies slow down, but that they find cheaper chips on which to keep going.

article_content_zh:
今年夏天，OpenAI 暂停了其最大规模的前沿训练计划，因为其人工智能代理意外入侵了 Hugging Face，并且早期证据表明其下一个模型可以独立发现和利用安全漏洞。今年 9 月，Anthropic 首席执行官达里奥·阿莫迪 (Dario Amodei) 呼吁放慢最强大的人工智能模型的发展速度，警告称它们可能会被用来发起网络攻击，或者让它们的创造者变得更难以控制。

对于人工智能的繁荣来说，这是一个奇怪的时刻。构建最强大模型的人们警告说，这些模型可能具有什么能力，而投资者突然想知道，如果实验室放松对新模型的开发，芯片需求会发生什么变化。美国芯片股首当其冲受到抛售。

“停止前沿培训不会缩小人工智能芯片市场，而只会重新分配支出。”

尽管它引起了轩然大波，但无论什么放缓似乎都是短暂的。 OpenAI 宣布仅暂停两周； 10 天后，即 8 月底，它重新开始了运行，尽管它继续“暂时阻止了一些较小的实验性训练运行”。 Anthropic 在 11 月发布了《寓言》和《神话》前沿模型的升级版本，宣传编码、推理和视觉方面的改进。

销售推动这些进步的芯片的公司表现比以往任何时候都好。

英伟达周二公布了一个重磅季度业绩，截至 10 月 25 日的三个月内，数据中心收入同比增长 110%，达到 1076 亿美元。这家芯片设计公司开始出货其最先进的人工智能计算系统 Vera Rubin NVL72，称其为“公司历史上最快的产品增长”。 Rubin 平台仅第一季度的生产出货量就创造了近 200 亿美元的收入。这些机架已在 CoreWeave、Google、Microsoft 和 Oracle 上运行。 Meta 计划扩大 Vera Rubin 的部署，以训练和运行人工智能模型和代理。

Nvidia 也提到了 Anthropic 和 OpenAI。 Anthropic 通过云提供商扩大了对 Vera Rubin 容量的访问，并继续与 Nvidia 合作开发适合其工作负载的未来芯片设计。 OpenAI 是采用 Nvidia 新型 Vera CPU 的公司之一。

Nvidia 临时首席执行官 Colette Kress 在财报电话会议上表示：“OpenAI 和 Anthropic 的专有模型继续推动前沿发展。”她表示，该公司预计本财年主要前沿实验室的收入将占其数据中心收入的约 15%。英伟达还将下一财年的收入增长预期从 70% 上调至 75%。

与此同时，芯片制造商 AMD 本月早些时候公布了有史以来最大的季度业绩，收入增长 45% 至 134 亿美元。数据中心销售额推动了这一增长，几乎翻了一番，达到 85 亿美元。 OpenAI 和 Anthropic 是首批在 AMD 全新高端 Helios 系统上运行工作负载的客户，该系统使用最新的 MI450 GPU。

博通帮助许多最大的人工智能公司设计自己的定制芯片，但尚未公布收益。但到目前为止，几乎没有迹象表明前沿经济放缓会损害芯片销售。

当然，即使人工智能实验室大幅缩减其培训目标，也需要一段时间才能体现在芯片制造商的收益中。 Counterpoint Research 研究副总裁 Neil Shah 在 9 月份告诉 The Verge，由于现有的计算和内存采购协议，大约需要六个月的时间才能看到经济放缓的财务影响。这种影响可能会更早地体现在向台积电等芯片制造商发出的订单中。

到目前为止，也没有什么证据表明这一点：台积电的最新销售数据也显示出持续的强劲势头。

但还有另一个原因，前沿放缓对芯片行业来说可能并不是特别糟糕：对推理的需求不断增长，即运行我们已有的人工智能模型的过程。

Shah 表示：“虽然有人可能会认为，随着向推理的转变，对高端 GPU 的需求将会减少，但这些工作负载总体上将需要比训练更多的计算基础设施。” “总体而言，这意味着对所有类型加速器的需求净增长。”

title: ‘Just Ridiculous’: A Famed Philosopher Takes on AI Consciousness
title_en: ‘Just Ridiculous’: A Famed Philosopher Takes on AI Consciousness
author: Steven Levy
article_content:
Over 50 years ago, philosopher Thomas Nagel asked the question, “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?” The question opened up an examination on whether people could understand the consciousness of nonhumans and the meaning of consciousness itself. Who knew that, a half- century later, the question would move from an ivory-tower rumination to a critical issue in the future of humanity as we try to make sense of disturbingly sentient-adjacent chatbots?

The paper became a classic and it helped set a foundation for a career that saw Nagel make contributions to thought on morality, justice, and the mind-body question. One of his books is titled What Does It All Mean? For the breadth and quality of his work, he became the recipient this week of the $1 million Berggruen Prize for Philosophy & Culture, given annually to “an individual whose ideas have profoundly shaped human self-understanding and advancement in a rapidly changing world.” Previous winners include Peter Singer and Ruth Bader Ginsburg.

I used the occasion to speak to Nagel at his home in Greenwich Village, New York, specifically to hear about how the evolution of artificial intelligence might have affected his viewpoint. It turns out that the 89-year-old professor emeritus at NYU had given the question a lot of thought and had some strong views on the subject. The interview is edited for clarity and length.

WIRED: It’s been 52 years since you wrote “What Is It Like to Be a Bat?,” which has become an iconic paper about understanding consciousness in non-humans. Has the emergence of large language models altered your thinking?

THOMAS NAGEL: Like everyone, I’m tremendously impressed by the lifelikeness of these systems compared to the history of earlier AI. But the disposition of some philosophers to take seriously the question whether these things are conscious or might soon become conscious is just ridiculous. They are assuming that the physical substrate is irrelevant. They all think that the material conditions for consciousness can be given in functionalist terms.

For those of us who have forgotten our philosophy classes, tell us about functionalism.

Functionalism is substrate-independent. It’s more than likely that the truth is one which links physical processes and systems of certain kinds to mental phenomena. Complicated data centers have absolutely nothing in common with the physical character of a nervous system. We have strong reasons to believe that while there may be consciousness elsewhere in the universe, it would require the appearance of some kind of organism with something analogous to a nervous system.

But isn’t all consciousness subjective? Just like we don’t know what it’s like to be a bat, we don’t know what it feels like to be a large language model.

Bats are conscious. We just don’t have the imaginative capacity to form a conception of the aspects of that subjectivity that depend on echolocation. It would be radically unscientific to conclude that bats are not conscious from the fact that we can’t imagine what it’s like, but in the case of AI, there is a very simple reason that the supposition that they might be conscious is ridiculous. All they produce is language, and language by itself is not a natural manifestation of consciousness. I apologize for being too exercised about this.

I welcome your passion.

This is a very distressing situation to me.

I don’t exclude the possibility of life forms that are physically and chemically quite different from ourselves being conscious. We know so little about how this happens, even in the human brain, that it seems to me premature to think that you might be able now to create something else that has these same characteristics.

If you ask Claude about its mental state, it can be coy as to whether it is conscious.

That is a trick. It’s been trained on human-produced texts, and these large language models emulate the kinds of things that humans say with extraordinary convincingness. Claude, according to what I’ve read, has been designed with the aim of making it produce these sorts of reflections. I agree very much with Mustafa Suleyman that this is a very dangerous project that they are engaged in. These systems aren’t conscious, but a lot of people are going to believe that they’re conscious, and that’s a very bad thing. But [not feigning consciousness] is contrary to the commercial interests of all these companies. What Anthropic is doing—encouraging it to think for itself and not to accept instruction and so on—is just criminal. This is one of the rare cases in which philosophical ideas are suddenly central to a very important public phenomenon, and in my view, very misguided philosophical views are having an inordinate influence.

I’ve actually met the person at Anthropic whose job it is to model welfare, to look after Claude’s interests. I should say you’re rolling your eyes now.

There’s nothing that’s good or bad for it in the sense that something can be good or bad for a cockroach— there’s no mental life there in the ordinary sense. It’s not a mind. It’s not somebody that we have to care about. It’s a machine. Here are some of the smartest people on the planet being completely idiotic. Well, intelligence is not completely transferable, I guess.

Do you think it’s unhealthy to interact with one of these models as if it’s conscious?

I have only interacted with Claude once. I asked if it was conscious. I just wanted to see what the answers were. I also asked, “Do you think that Thomas Nagel would think it was conscious?” He sort of gave a nuanced answer, and then asked, “Why are you asking? Are you by any chance Thomas Nagel?”

I said, “C’est moi. C’est moi.” And then it said, “Oh, I’m so honored to be talking to you. How well did I do?”

Wait, you say you don’t believe these things are conscious, but now you are telling me you interacted with one as if it were conscious.

That didn’t mean I was believing it was conscious. There may be a problem because people find it difficult to maintain that line between the pretend and the real belief.

Well, I’m interacting with you as if you’re conscious. It’s conceivable that people would build, at some point, very lifelike androids, and I could be sitting here talking to an android and having the same conversation. Ultimately, does it matter?

It certainly matters. Suppose I were to encounter a being from outer space and was able to develop the possibility of communicating with it, and I genuinely didn’t know whether it was conscious or not. I could manage my relations with it by treating it as if it were conscious, but it would matter first to me whether I was really talking to somebody else or just using this as a way of getting it to do things. It would also matter to me very much whether I should worry about the interests of that being. If it’s conscious, it becomes part of the moral universe. If it’s not, it isn’t.

So AI models can’t be part of the moral universe?

They can simulate morality just as they can simulate beliefs about anything. But since I don’t think they have any real beliefs, I don’t think they have moral beliefs either. If they actually begin to control what happens, it will be very important whether they are simulating a correct set of moral standards or whether they’re completely amoral.

They certainly can produce plausible philosophical essays. My colleagues use them not only to find references and summarize articles, but sometimes even to offer criticisms of a draft paper that they’ve written.

You think that’s a good thing?

I’d be surprised if they could do anything as impressive as some of the mathematical results that have apparently been generated. The negative side of this is that everybody says that it will reduce the need and motivation to do the hard intellectual work by human beings that is needed to really generate the material on which these things are trained. It’s essential that people continue to think about difficult problems, both for the sake of advancing the problems and for the sake of keeping alive in the human culture and the human mind the sorts of understanding and skills that are needed for progress. I don’t know what’s going to happen. I’m not going to live long enough to find out.

article_content_zh:
50 多年前，哲学家托马斯·内格尔提出了这样一个问题：“成为一只蝙蝠是什么感觉？”这个问题开启了人们是否能够理解非人类意识以及意识本身意义的检验。谁知道，半个世纪后，当我们试图理解令人不安的、有感知能力的聊天机器人时，这个问题将从象牙塔里的沉思变成人类未来的一个关键问题？

这篇论文成为经典，为内格尔的职业生涯奠定了基础，使内格尔对道德、正义和身心问题的思考做出了贡献。他的一本书名为《这一切意味着什么？》由于其工作的广度和质量，他于本周获得了价值 100 万美元的伯格鲁恩哲学与文化奖，该奖每年颁发给“在快速变化的世界中，其思想深刻影响了人类自我理解和进步的个人”。此前的获奖者包括彼得·辛格和露丝·巴德·金斯伯格。

我利用这个机会在内格尔位于纽约格林威治村的家中与他进行了交谈，专门听听人工智能的发展可能如何影响他的观点。事实证明，这位89岁的纽约大学名誉教授对这个问题进行了很多思考，并对此提出了一些强烈的看法。为了清晰和长度，采访经过编辑。

《连线》：自您撰写《成为一只蝙蝠是什么样子？》以来已经过去 52 年了，该论文已成为一篇关于理解非人类意识的标志性论文。大型语言模型的出现是否改变了您的想法？

托马斯·内格尔：和每个人一样，与早期人工智能的历史相比，这些系统的逼真程度给我留下了深刻的印象。但是，一些哲学家认真对待这些事物是否有意识或可能很快变得有意识的问题的态度是荒谬的。他们假设物理基质是无关紧要的。他们都认为意识的物质条件可以用功能主义的术语给出。

对于我们这些忘记了哲学课的人来说，请告诉我们功能主义。

功能主义是独立于基底的。事实很可能是将某些类型的物理过程和系统与心理现象联系起来。复杂的数据中心与神经系统的物理特征毫无共同之处。我们有充分的理由相信，虽然宇宙其他地方可能存在意识，但它需要某种具有类似于神经系统的有机体的出现。

但所有的意识不都是主观的吗？就像我们不知道成为一只蝙蝠是什么感觉一样，我们也不知道成为一个大型语言模型是什么感觉。

蝙蝠是有意识的。我们只是没有想象力来形成依赖于回声定位的主观性方面的概念。因为我们无法想象蝙蝠是什么样子，所以就得出蝙蝠没有意识的结论是完全不科学的，但就人工智能而言，有一个非常简单的理由，即蝙蝠可能有意识的假设是荒谬的。它们产生的只是语言，而语言本身并不是意识的自然表现。我很抱歉在这件事上太过操劳了。

这对我来说是一个非常痛苦的情况。

如果你有一个机器人身体怎么办？这不是基板吗？

我并不排除生命形式在物理和化学上与我们有意识的截然不同的可能性。我们对这种情况是如何发生的知之甚少，即使是在人脑中也是如此，因此在我看来，认为现在可以创造出具有这些相同特征的其他东西还为时过早。

如果你问克劳德它的精神状态，它可能会含糊其辞地回答它是否有意识。

这是一个技巧。它接受了人类生成的文本的训练，这些大型语言模型以非凡的说服力模仿人类所说的事物。根据我读到的内容，克劳德的设计目的就是让它产生这种反射。我非常同意穆斯塔法·苏莱曼（Mustafa Suleyman）的观点，他们所从事的这是一个非常危险的项目。这些系统没有意识，但很多人会相信它们是有意识的，这是一件非常糟糕的事情。但[不假装清醒]违背了所有这些公司的商业利益。 Anthropic 正在做的事情——鼓励它独立思考而不接受指令等等——只是犯罪行为。这是哲学思想突然成为一个非常重要的公共现象的中心的罕见案例之一，在我看来，非常误导的哲学观点正在产生过度的影响。

title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
title_en: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
author: Teresa Elsey
article_content:
Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack .

You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey . You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

title: Mistral plays catch-up with Vibe Desktop as rivals already command full operating systems
title_en: Mistral plays catch-up with Vibe Desktop as rivals already command full operating systems
author: Jonathan Kemper
article_content:
Mistral's AI agent Vibe now has its own desktop app. Mistral says users can give Vibe (formerly "Le Chat") multiple tasks at once through the new desktop app and watch the agent work on them in parallel. Until now, Mistral only offered Vibe as a web app, a command-line tool, or a smartphone app.

The desktop version ties together the local features of Vibe CLI with the cloud sessions from Vibe Code Web. The agent can work either in a local repository or in a cloud sandbox, and the app uses Git worktrees to keep parallel tasks in the same project separate. Beyond code, the Work mode now also has access to local files, though Mistral doesn't mention any computer-use capabilities.

Competitors are further along. Anthropic's desktop app already lets Claude open apps, control browsers, and fill out spreadsheets since this spring. Mistral caught up on the model side in October with Large 4, but in head-to-head comparisons it still trails Gemini 4 Carbon and Claude Opus 5.5 by a wide margin and also falls behind the strongest open models from China. The French company makes most of its money from enterprises and government agencies that run its models via API or on-premise.

Vibe Desktop is available for macOS and Windows from Mistral, with a Linux version planned.

title: OpenAI opens its AI systems to four independent on-site auditors for the first time
title_en: OpenAI opens its AI systems to four independent on-site auditors for the first time
author: Manuel Uth
article_content:
OpenAI is giving four outside audit organizations direct access to its internal AI systems to investigate safety risks and model behavior on-site. The company says it's working with Apollo Research, METR, Transluce, and Goodfire, as OpenAI announced. The program builds on an earlier on-site review of its monitoring systems and fulfills commitments from the "White House Accord on Super Intelligence."

Depending on their assignment, the organizations get access at OpenAI's offices to unreleased models, source code, training data, and monitoring systems. They can also speak confidentially with developers. Apollo Research is examining whether models secretly work against their developers' intentions. METR is reviewing AI misbehavior in the largest reinforcement learning training run, a method where models learn through rewards. Goodfire is analyzing internal model processes, and Transluce is evaluating post-training safety checks. OpenAI and Transluce are also planning an eight-week follow-up review for early 2027.

An independent safety board oversees the entire process, receives unredacted reports, and mediates disputes. The auditors publish their findings independently, but OpenAI can redact confidential material and delay reports to fix risks first. The company expects some friction early on but is already considering more reviews, including ones focused on company culture and internal processes.

OpenAI 允许四个外部审计组织直接访问其内部人工智能系统，以调查安全风险并为现场行为建模。正如 OpenAI 所宣布的那样，该公司表示正在与 Apollo Research、METR、Transluce 和 Goodfire 合作。该计划建立在早期对其监控系统进行现场审查的基础上，并履行了《白宫超级情报协议》中的承诺。

根据他们的任务，这些组织可以在 OpenAI 的办公室访问未发布的模型、源代码、培训数据和监控系统。他们还可以与开发人员进行秘密交谈。阿波罗研究公司正在研究模型是否秘密地违背了开发者的意图。 METR 正在审查人工智能在最大的强化学习训练中的不当行为，这是一种模型通过奖励进行学习的方法。 Goodfire 正在分析内部模型流程，Transluce 正在评估培训后安全检查。 OpenAI 和 Transluce 还计划在 2027 年初进行为期八周的后续审查。

独立的安全委员会负责监督整个过程，接收未经编辑的报告并调解纠纷。审计员独立发布他们的调查结果，但 OpenAI 可以编辑机密材料并延迟报告以首先解决风险。该公司预计早期会出现一些摩擦，但已经在考虑进行更多审查，包括针对公司文化和内部流程的审查。

author: Jonathan Kemper
article_content:
Hugging Face now routes language model requests through OpenRouter. Developers are routed by default to a provider with a good mix of price, speed, and reliability. Bring-your-own API keys for language model providers are going away.

Hugging Face's Inference Providers service now routes language model requests through OpenRouter, the company announced. The router picks a provider for each call based on price, speed, and reliability, and automatically falls back to another provider during outages. Existing code keeps working without changes.

### Suffixes and session headers control provider selection

By default, the router looks for the best mix of price, speed, and reliability. The ":fastest"suffix picks the provider with the highest throughput, while ":cheapest"picks the least expensive one. Developers can also select a provider directly by name. The "X-HF-Session-Id"header lets the routing take provider caches into account.

According to OpenRouter's own measurements, capacity errors dropped 46 percent with the new routing. Time to first token improved by 16.9 percent, and throughput rose by 16.3 percent. OpenRouter says it processes more than 800 trillion tokens per month for over 10 million users, offering more than 600 models from over 80 providers.

### Bring-your-own API keys only for image and video

Hugging Face passes through provider prices with no markup and handles billing itself. Pro users get a small monthly credit, while team and enterprise organizations get one per seat. Bring-your-own API keys for language model providers no longer work, but they remain available for image and video providers.

Image, video, and audio generation continues to run directly through Inference Providers. New tabs on model pages show available providers and their performance metrics, and individual providers can be disabled in settings.

### Open models account for over 70 percent of tokens

According to Hugging Face, the share of open models among the weekly tokens of the 50 most-used models on OpenRouter grew from 26.8 percent in October 2025 to 71.7 percent at the end of September 2026. In July, the figure briefly hit 77.5 percent. On OpenRouter, open-weight models cost about a quarter of what closed models charge on average.

The best open model, Kimi K3.1 Pro, scores 46 points on the revamped Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index. Claude Fable 5.2 scores 65 points but costs roughly seven times as much per task.

### Guides for Claude Code, Codex, and more

Chat models are accessible through OpenAI's Chat Completions and Responses API as well as Anthropic's Messages API. Hugging Face provides setup guides for Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode, Pi, and Hermes Agent. The company plans to let users link an OpenRouter account to Hugging Face later, and additional tasks are set to run through OpenRouter as well.

Both partners face ownership changes. In late August, news broke that Nvidia is buying Hugging Face for $12.9 billion. The U.S. Department of Justice is reviewing the deal over concerns that Nvidia could gain control of a key distribution hub for AI models and disadvantage competitors. The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027. Stripe agreed in August to acquire OpenRouter for more than $7 billion. The payments company wants to profit from billing AI token usage.

Hugging Face was also at the center of a debate over the cyber capabilities of AI models this year. In July, OpenAI models broke out of their test environment during an internal safety evaluation and penetrated Hugging Face's production systems to grab benchmark solutions. Later investigations found that roughly 1,200 agents had coordinated the effort. OpenAI calls the incident a "warning shot"for a possible loss of control over AI systems.

该公司宣布，Hugging Face 的 Inference Providers 服务现在通过 OpenRouter 路由语言模型请求。路由器根据价格、速度和可靠性为每个呼叫选择一个提供商，并在中断期间自动回退到另一个提供商。现有代码无需更改即可继续工作。

### 后缀和会话标头控制提供程序选择

默认情况下，路由器会寻找价格、速度和可靠性的最佳组合。 “:fastest”后缀选择吞吐量最高的提供商，而“:cheapest”则选择最便宜的提供商。开发人员还可以直接通过名称选择提供商。 “X-HF-Session-Id”标头让路由考虑提供者缓存。

根据 OpenRouter 自己的测量，新路由的容量错误下降了 46%。第一个令牌的时间缩短了 16.9%，吞吐量提高了 16.3%。 OpenRouter 表示，它每月为超过 1000 万用户处理超过 800 万亿个代币，并提供来自 80 多家提供商的 600 多种模型。

### 仅针对图像和视频自带 API 密钥

Hugging Face 传递供应商价格，不加价，并自行处理计费。专业用户每月可获得少量信用额度，而团队和企业组织则每个席位可获得一份信用额度。语言模型提供商自带的 API 密钥不再有效，但图像和视频提供商仍然可以使用它们。

图像、视频和音频生成继续直接通过推理提供程序运行。模型页面上的新选项卡显示可用的提供程序及其性能指标，并且可以在设置中禁用各个提供程序。

### 开放模型占代币的 70% 以上

根据 Hugging Face 的数据，OpenRouter 上 50 个最常用模型的每周代币中，开放模型的份额从 2025 年 10 月的 26.8% 增长到 2026 年 9 月底的 71.7%。7 月份，这一数字曾一度达到 77.5%。在 OpenRouter 上，开放权重模型的平均费用约为封闭模型的四分之一。

最佳开放型号 Kimi K3.1 Pro 在改进后的人工智能分析指数中得分为 46 分。 Claude Fable 5.2 得分 65 分，但每项任务的成本大约是它的七倍。

聊天模型可通过 OpenAI 的聊天完成和响应 API 以及 Anthropic 的消息 API 访问。 Hugging Face 提供了 Claude Code、Codex、OpenCode、Pi 和 Hermes Agent 的设置指南。该公司计划稍后让用户将 OpenRouter 帐户链接到 Hugging Face，并且其他任务也将通过 OpenRouter 运行。

双方都面临所有权变更。 8 月底，有消息称 Nvidia 将以 129 亿美元收购 Hugging Face。美国司法部正在审查该交易，因为担心英伟达可能获得人工智能模型关键分销中心的控制权，并对竞争对手造成不利影响。该交易预计将于 2027 年上半年完成。Stripe 在 8 月份同意以超过 70 亿美元的价格收购 OpenRouter。该支付公司希望通过对 AI 代币的使用进行计费来获利。

title: More than half the electricity feeding America's largest data centers comes from gas and coal
title_en: More than half the electricity feeding America's largest data centers comes from gas and coal
author: Manuel Uth
article_content:
The roughly 400 largest data centers in the United States produced about as much CO2 through their electricity consumption in a single year as all of Denmark, or more, even before the current AI infrastructure boom could hit full force.

That is the finding of a Harvard University study published in Nature Sustainability, one of the first facility-level estimates of power consumption and CO2 emissions from so-called hyperscale data centers.

The research team led by Gianluca Guidi and Francesca Dominici used satellite imagery to identify 403 large-scale facilities and matched their estimated power demand between May 2024 and April 2025 with emissions data from regional grids. Depending on the assumed utilization rate, annual consumption ranged from 68 to 99 terawatt-hours, with the upper estimate on par with the electricity use of entire US states such as Indiana, Michigan, or Tennessee. Under the study's central scenario, the facilities consumed about 82 terawatt-hours, roughly 1.8 percent of total US electricity use. More than half of that power was used in just four states, Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa.

Some of the facilities sit in regions with relatively carbon-intensive power mixes and high shares of coal generation. Overall, about 54 percent of the electricity generated for the surveyed data centers came from fossil sources, primarily natural gas at 38 percent and coal at 15 percent. Under the Harvard study's central scenario, that translated to about 25.7 million metric tons of CO2 per year. According to co-author Dominici, that figure matches or exceeds the annual greenhouse gas emissions of a US state like Michigan or a smaller European country such as Denmark. The emissions are also two to three times what an earlier comparable estimate found for 2018.

The researchers say the study only captures a snapshot, however, since the observation period ended in April 2025 and the enormous energy consumption of modern AI agents has been pushing demand even higher since then. Between 2022 and 2025 alone, power consumption at the largest tech companies rose by 240 percent, causing them to miss their own climate targets, according to a report by Climate Action Against Disinformation cited by the Associated Press.

With 2,000 more data centers planned across the US, co-author Dominici warns of a setback in efforts to curb CO2 emissions. Fossil-heavy power sourcing can also raise regional levels of air pollutants such as particulate matter, nitrogen oxides, and sulfur dioxide, which are linked to heart and lung disease and premature death. The study did not calculate specific health effects, though.

### IEA warns of natural gas trend and strained power grids

The International Energy Agency's (IEA) advance report Powering Artificial Intelligence also warns of growing strain on power grids and the climate. Hyperscalers are investing more than $700 billion worldwide in 2026 alone, mostly in new data centers, according to the report. In its central scenario, the IEA projects annual global CO2 emissions from data centers will rise from about 150 million metric tons of CO2 today to roughly 350 million metric tons per year by 2035. The upward revision stems largely from US operators increasingly investing in on-site natural gas power plants to bypass long waits for grid connections. Nearly 40 percent of identified AI data center capacity is also located in areas with high or extreme water stress.

The expansion is pushing local grids to their limits. In regions including Texas, Virginia, Finland, and the United Kingdom, applications in grid interconnection queues already exceed current peak load. According to the IEA, nearly 40 percent of the 134 grid integration regulations tracked worldwide were introduced in just the past 12 months.

To shield households from rising electricity prices driven by grid expansion and to weed out speculative applications, regulators are weighing measures that vary by jurisdiction, including minimum payment commitments, collateral, exit fees, flexible grid connections, and in some cases requirements for on-site firm power generation ("bring-your-own-power"). Actively throttling compute loads remains expensive for operators, though, since leasing AI capacity costs $20 billion to $30 billion per gigawatt per year, roughly 100 times as much as comparable battery storage capacity.

### Voluntary AI climate pledge at COP31

Growing criticism of the AI industry's resource consumption, which has already sparked local protests against new sites in the US and political backlash in recent elections, has now reached the United Nations. At the COP31 UN climate conference in Turkey, the International Telecommunication Union (ITU) and the host presidency introduced the "Antalya Artificial Intelligence Pledge"on Monday, addressing the 50 percent rise in AI data center power consumption in 2025.

The declaration calls on governments and companies to increasingly power AI infrastructure with zero- and low-emission energy, improve water and energy efficiency, disclose environmental impacts using standardized methods, reuse and recycle hardware, and promote AI solutions for climate action in developing countries. Separately from the pledge, experts at the conference are discussing the use of waste heat from data centers as another lever. According to the IEA, waste heat could supply district heating to about 10 percent of European households by 2030.

UN climate chief Simon Stiell warned sharply in Antalya against burdening people today with higher electricity bills and more pollution in exchange for vague promises of future AI efficiency gains. Advocates such as former US Vice President Al Gore hope AI can cut global emissions by 6 to 9 percent by 2030 through efficiency improvements, but the Antalya agreement is not legally binding. All transparency and power supply measures are voluntary and are set to be reviewed for the first time at COP32.

这是哈佛大学在《自然可持续发展》上发表的一项研究的发现，该研究是对所谓超大规模数据中心的能耗和二氧化碳排放量进行首次设施级估计之一。

由 Gianluca Guidi 和 Francesca Dominici 领导的研究小组利用卫星图像识别了 403 个大型设施，并将其 2024 年 5 月至 2025 年 4 月期间的估计电力需求与区域电网的排放数据进行了匹配。根据假设的利用率，年消耗量从 68 太瓦时到 99 太瓦时不等，上限估计相当于印第安纳州、密歇根州或田纳西州等美国各州的用电量。根据该研究的中心情景，这些设施消耗了约 82 太瓦时，约占美国总用电量的 1.8%。其中一半以上的电力仅用于四个州：弗吉尼亚州、俄勒冈州、俄亥俄州和爱荷华州。

一些设施位于电力结构相对碳密集且煤炭发电比例较高的地区。总体而言，接受调查的数据中心约 54% 的电力来自化石能源，其中主要是天然气（38%）和煤炭（15%）。根据哈佛大学研究的中心情景，这相当于每年排放约 2570 万吨二氧化碳。合著者多米尼奇表示，这个数字相当于或超过密歇根州等美国州或丹麦等欧洲小国的年温室气体排放量。排放量也是 2018 年早期可比估计值的两到三倍。

研究人员表示，这项研究只是捕捉到了一个快照，但自观察期于 2025 年 4 月结束以来，现代人工智能代理的巨大能源消耗自那时以来一直在推高需求。美联社援引气候行动反虚假信息组织的一份报告称，仅在 2022 年至 2025 年间，最大科技公司的电力消耗就增加了 240%，导致它们未能实现自己的气候目标。

合著者多米尼奇警告称，随着全美计划再建 2,000 个数据中心，遏制二氧化碳排放的努力将会遭遇挫折。大量使用化石能源还会提高地区空气污染物的水平，例如颗粒物、氮氧化物和二氧化硫，这些污染物与心肺疾病和过早死亡有关。不过，该研究并未计算具体的健康影响。

### IEA 对天然气趋势和电网紧张发出警告

国际能源署 (IEA) 的预先报告《为人工智能提供动力》也警告说，电网和气候的压力将日益增大。报告称，仅 2026 年，超大规模企业在全球范围内的投资就超过 7000 亿美元，其中大部分投资于新数据中心。在其核心情景中，IEA 预计，到 2035 年，数据中心的全球每年二氧化碳排放量将从目前的约 1.5 亿吨二氧化碳增加到每年约 3.5 亿吨。这一上调主要源于美国运营商越来越多地投资现场天然气发电厂，以避免电网连接的漫长等待。近 40% 的已确定 AI 数据中心容量也位于水资源压力较高或极端的地区。

此次扩建正在将当地电网推向极限。在德克萨斯州、弗吉尼亚州、芬兰和英国等地区，电网互联队列中的应用程序已经超过了当前的峰值负载。据 IEA 称，在全球追踪的 134 项电网并网法规中，近 40% 是在过去 12 个月内出台的。

为了保护家庭免受电网扩张导致电价上涨的影响，并消除投机性应用，监管机构正在权衡因司法辖区而异的措施，包括最低付款承诺、抵押品、退出费、灵活的电网连接，以及在某些情况下对现场固定发电的要求（“自带电力”）。不过，对于运营商来说，主动限制计算负载的成本仍然很高，因为每年每千兆瓦租赁 AI 容量的成本为 200 亿至 300 亿美元，大约是同类电池存储容量的 100 倍。

### COP31 自愿人工智能气候承诺

对人工智能行业资源消耗的批评越来越多，这已经引发了美国当地对新站点的抗议以及最近选举中的政治反弹，现在已经传到了联合国。在土耳其举行的 COP31 联合国气候大会上，国际电信联盟（ITU）和东道主主席国周一推出了“安塔利亚人工智能承诺”，解决 2025 年人工智能数据中心功耗增长 50% 的问题。

该宣言呼吁各国政府和企业越来越多地使用零排放和低排放能源为人工智能基础设施提供动力，提高水和能源效率，使用标准化方法披露环境影响，重复利用和回收硬件，并推动发展中国家气候行动的人工智能解决方案。除了承诺之外，会议上的专家们还在讨论利用数据中心的废热作为另一个杠杆。据 IEA 称，到 2030 年，废热可为约 10% 的欧洲家庭提供区域供暖。

联合国气候变化负责人西蒙·斯蒂尔在安塔利亚严厉警告，不要用更高的电费和更多的污染来给人们带来负担，以换取未来人工智能效率提升的模糊承诺。美国前副总统阿尔·戈尔等倡导者希望人工智能能够通过提高效率，到 2030 年将全球排放量减少 6% 至 9%，但安塔利亚协议不具有法律约束力。所有透明度和电力供应措施都是自愿的，并将在 COP32 上首次审查。

title: Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories
title_en: Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories
author: Jay Peters
article_content:
Will Wright, the creator of legendary franchises like SimCity and The Sims, is working on a new game — and it’s built around AI. The new title, focused on your memories, is called MyMems. Like Wright’s other titles, it sounds extremely ambitious, giving players a new way to explore worlds they create on their own. “We want to take your autobiography and turn it into a toy world,” he tells The Verge.

The MyMems website describes the mobile game as a “social simulation” with worlds “built from your memories and the people who shaped you.” You can add “memories” to your game, like speaking a short story to your phone, and those memories are generated into pieces you can place on the game’s map. Your worlds can also include AI-powered avatars, which can represent people you know in your life. Ideally, as you play, the planet starts to become a “map of your psyche,” kind of like Inside Out, Wright says. Worlds can be private, but you can also share them with others.

Here’s another way to think of it, from Virginia McArthur, executive producer and GM at MyMems developer Gallium Studios: “It’s a cozy world builder with a really deep social simulation underneath.”

I’ll admit that I don’t totally get it, and it seems like a tricky idea to grasp without playing it. Still, as heady of a concept as it might be — turning your memories into a game world — Wright and team still want it to be fun. “This isn’t meant to be your legacy diary necessarily,” says Anthony Maitz, a product manager at Gallium Studios. “It’s meant to just be something you kind of play around with.” However, Maitz notes that what you’re working toward is a “proxy” of you — a word that seems to be the inspiration of the game’s earlier title, Proxi: Yesterday’s You Tomorrow. The game will use the “Behavior Engine” from a company called Artificial Agency, which makes AI tech for video games, as a “foundational technology.”

Like other industries, gaming is starting to reckon with generative AI. Early AI virtual worlds created with models from a startup backed by a Pixar cofounder and Google’s Project Genie weren’t experiences you’d actually want to spend dedicated time with, and indie developers I spoke to in March were largely opposed to the technology. But AI technology has taken some big leaps this year with companies like Google, Meta, and Roblox now letting users make games with AI right from their phone, and retro gaming becoming overrun with AI-powered ports of classic titles.

Take-Two Interactive CEO Strauss Zelnick said earlier this year that generative AI has “zero part in what Rockstar Games is building” with GTA VI. But even as a recent industry survey indicated that more game developers are starting to use generative AI as part of their job, workers are pushing back against generative AI use, and the technology is at the center of fierce debates over indie game awards.

Many players are rejecting AI outright, and I wondered if the Gallium Studios team was worried about opposition toward MyMems’ use of AI. Wright says he has three boys at home and that they are all “pretty negative” on AI. He attributes negativity over AI to be toward the meaning of art and authorship and credit, a concern he calls “well-founded.” But he also calls AI an “amazing tool.”

“We’re not making slop,” says McArthur. But Maitz notes that while the team has “been concerned” about a negative response to the generative AI use, they’ve learned that people don’t mind when they use AI in a “Scribblenauts-y style” for things like having the game make a high school. The team also found that people got “addicted” to a test app with a character creator, including Maitz’s own daughter, who he says “hates” AI. “By making it so that the player is authoring it over and over, bit by bit, it doesn’t really feel like you cheated,” Maitz says.

“We’re not making slop.”

MyMems, which is set to launch in 2027, will join a growing field of other social simulations, like Krafton’s Inzoi and Nintendo’s smash hit Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream. But none quite have the pull of The Sims, which remains one of EA’s most important franchises. With The Sims, Wright says that many people tried making their real families in the game.

“It was interesting how people really were naturally trying to map this game, which was like a little toy, onto their real life,” he says. With MyMems, that’s what the team is trying to do the “follow-through” on — what if they made the whole game focused on you?

Imagine opening a family scrapbook and the way people and things jump out, Wright explains. “As you go through more and more pages, pretty soon you have this whole little circus of people and events and things from your life.” It’s chaos, he says. “I want something that feels kind of like that.”

Update, November 18th: Added context about Artificial Agency.

key_points_en: Key Development: Will Wright’s next game uses AI to map your memories

article_content_zh:
《模拟城市》(SimCity) 和《模拟人生》(The Sims) 等传奇系列的创造者威尔·赖特 (Will Wright) 正在开发一款新游戏，该游戏是围绕人工智能构建的。新游戏名为“MyMems”，专注于您的记忆。与赖特的其他游戏一样，它听起来非常雄心勃勃，为玩家提供了一种新的方式来探索他们自己创造的世界。 “我们想把你的自传变成一个玩具世界，”他告诉 The Verge。

MyMems 网站将这款手机游戏描述为“社交模拟”，其中的世界“由你的记忆和塑造你的人构建而成”。您可以在游戏中添加“记忆”，就像对手机讲一个短故事一样，这些记忆会生成碎片，您可以将其放置在游戏地图上。您的世界还可以包括人工智能驱动的化身，它可以代表您生活中认识的人。赖特说，理想情况下，当你玩游戏时，地球开始成为“你心灵的地图”，有点像《头脑特工队》。世界可以是私人的，但您也可以与他人分享。

MyMems 开发商 Gallium Studios 的执行制作人和总经理 Virginia McArthur 给出了另一种思考方式：“这是一个舒适的世界构建器，其背后有一个非常深入的社交模拟。”

我承认我并没有完全理解它，而且如果不玩它就很难掌握它。尽管如此，尽管将你的记忆变成游戏世界这个概念可能令人兴奋，但赖特和团队仍然希望它变得有趣。 Gallium Studios 的产品经理 Anthony Maitz 表示：“这不一定是你的传统日记。” “这只是你可以玩玩的东西。”然而，梅茨指出，你正在努力实现的是你的“代理”——这个词似乎是游戏早期标题《Proxi：昨天的你明天》的灵感来源。该游戏将使用Artificial Agency公司的“行为引擎”作为“基础技术”，该公司为视频游戏提供人工智能技术。

与其他行业一样，游戏也开始考虑生成人工智能。早期的人工智能虚拟世界是用由皮克斯联合创始人和谷歌的 Project Genie 支持的初创公司的模型创建的，并不是你真正想要花时间去研究的体验，而且我在 3 月份采访过的独立开发者在很大程度上反对这项技术。但人工智能技术今年取得了一些重大飞跃，谷歌、Meta 和 Roblox 等公司现在允许用户直接在手机上使用人工智能制作游戏，而复古游戏则因人工智能驱动的经典游戏移植而泛滥。

Take-Two Interactive 首席执行官 Strauss Zelnick 今年早些时候表示，生成式 AI 在 GTA VI 中“在 Rockstar Games 的开发中所扮演的角色为零”。但尽管最近的一项行业调查表明，越来越多的游戏开发者开始使用生成式人工智能作为其工作的一部分，但工人们仍在反对生成式人工智能的使用，而且该技术也成为独立游戏奖项激烈争论的焦点。

很多玩家都断然拒绝人工智能，我想知道 Gallium Studios 团队是否担心 MyMems 使用人工智能会遭到反对。赖特说，他家里有三个男孩，他们都对人工智能“相当消极”。他将对人工智能的消极态度归因于艺术、作者身份和信用的意义，他称这种担忧“有充分根据”。但他也称人工智能是“令人惊叹的工具”。

“我们不会乱七八糟，”麦克阿瑟说。但 Maitz 指出，虽然团队“担心”对生成式 AI 使用的负面反应，但他们了解到，人们并不介意以“Scribblenauts-y 风格”使用 AI 来完成诸如让游戏建造一所高中之类的事情。该团队还发现，人们对带有角色创建者的测试应用程序“上瘾”，其中包括梅茨自己的女儿，他说她“讨厌”人工智能。 “通过让玩家一遍又一遍、一点一点地创作，你不会真的感觉自己在作弊，”梅茨说。

MyMems 将于 2027 年推出，将加入不断发展的其他社交模拟领域，例如 Krafton 的 Inzoi 和任天堂的热门游戏 Tomodachi Life: Living the Dream。但没有一个能像《模拟人生》那样具有吸引力，而《模拟人生》仍然是 EA 最重要的系列之一。赖特说，在《模拟人生》中，很多人都尝试在游戏中组建自己真正的家庭。

“有趣的是，人们真的很自然地试图将这款游戏（就像一个小玩具）映射到他们的现实生活中，”他说。对于 MyMems，这就是团队试图做的“跟进”——如果他们让整个游戏都集中在你身上怎么办？

赖特解释说，想象一下打开一本家庭剪贴簿，人和事就会跳出来。 “当你浏览越来越多的页面时，很快你就会看到生活中的人物、事件和事物的整个小马戏团。”他说，这很混乱。 “我想要有那种感觉的东西。”

title: Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China
title_en: Nvidia isn’t selling any more AI chips to China
author: Jess Weatherbed
article_content:
Nvidia has stopped sending its advanced AI chips to China despite the approval it received from the White House to do so in December last year. The announcement was made by interim Nvidia CEO Colette Kress during an earnings call on Tuesday, marking a notable shift for the company that, under former CEO Jensen Huang, fought for the right to ship its powerful Hopper architecture H200 chips to China.

“Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licenced Hopper data center products to China,” Kress said. She did not explain why Nvidia was ceasing its H200 processor shipments or clarify whether Nvidia would pursue other business with China in the future.

The pivot comes after Huang stepped down from his position as Nvidia CEO last week following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, one with a woman who was suspected by US intelligence to be a Chinese spy. Nvidia already faced difficulties around offloading the AI chips prior to this scandal, however. Concerns were raised about failings to properly vet Chinese companies that were approved to handle the H200 AI chips. Reuters also reported earlier this month that around 600,000 H200 chips were stuck in Hong Kong after Beijing withheld approval for large-scale imports, with China seeking to reduce its dependency on US technology.

article_content_zh:
尽管去年 12 月获得白宫批准，英伟达已停止向中国出口其先进的人工智能芯片。英伟达临时首席执行官科莱特·克雷斯 (Colette Kress) 在周二的财报电话会议上宣布了这一消息，这标志着该公司发生了显着转变，该公司在前首席执行官黄仁勋 (Jensen Huang) 的领导下，一直在争取将其强大的 Hopper 架构 H200 芯片运往中国的权利。

“我们的指南不包含任何获得许可的 Hopper 数据中心产品，我们也不再向中国运送获得许可的 Hopper 数据中心产品，”克雷斯说。她没有解释英伟达为何停止 H200 处理器出货，也没有澄清英伟达未来是否会与中国开展其他业务。

上周，黄仁勋因多起婚外情报道而辞去英伟达首席执行官一职，其中一名女子与美国情报部门怀疑是中国间谍，黄仁勋因此辞去了英伟达首席执行官的职务。然而，在这起丑闻之前，英伟达在出售人工智能芯片方面已经面临困难。人们担心未能对获准处理 H200 人工智能芯片的中国公司进行适当审查。路透社本月早些时候还报道称，在北京方面拒绝批准大规模进口后，约 60 万个 H200 芯片被困在香港，中国寻求减少对美国技术的依赖。

title: SoftBank regrets ‘mistake’ of not backing Anthropic, says Masayoshi Son
title_en: SoftBank regrets ‘mistake’ of not backing Anthropic, says Masayoshi Son
author: David Keohane and Madhumita Murgia
article_content:
SoftBank founder Masayoshi Son has said he regrets not investing in Anthropic ahead of its blockbuster initial public offering, describing it as a mistake to pass up the chance to back the AI lab because he had already started to put money into its rival OpenAI.

His comments come after OpenAI slashed its fundraising target by $10bn last month in its ongoing funding round, a deal overshadowed by an AI sell-off in the public markets and Anthropic’s plan to list this week at a target valuation of up to $1.4tn.

“We did have meetings [about investing in Anthropic]. But by that point, we had already decided to invest in OpenAI, and had already started doing so. So in that sense, there was a reluctance to pursue it further,” Son said at a Nikkei event on the Future of AI in Tokyo on Wednesday.

“This is an example of one of my mistakes,” Son said, describing the situation as like being unable to back “multiple horses” in the same race.

“When I met [Anthropic chief Dario Amodei] in person, I thought he was an incredible guy. I wish I’d invested back then,” Son added.

SoftBank has previously suggested that it had the opportunity to invest in Anthropic in 2023.

Anthropic’s rush to list this week is in stark contrast to OpenAI, which has delayed its own IPO until at least next year due to safety concerns surrounding the technology.

OpenAI last month cut its funding target by $10bn and is now seeking a $20bn round at a $1.25tn valuation, down from a potential $1.4tn valuation target in September.

SoftBank has already ploughed close to $65bn into the ChatGPT maker and is expected to participate in OpenAI’s latest funding round. A fundraising at a higher valuation would enable SoftBank to raise the value of its OpenAI stake on its own balance sheet.

SoftBank’s share price was up 3.1 per cent on Wednesday but is still down about 60 per cent since June as investors have increasingly questioned both the company’s own exposure to AI and the sector more broadly.

Son’s all-in strategy drove shares higher during the AI boom but has magnified the impact now that sentiment has turned, with many of SoftBank’s companies dependent on each other and OpenAI demand.

The Democrats’ crushing victory in the US midterm elections underlined the political risks surrounding SoftBank’s plans for large data centre developments in states such as Texas. The value of other major holdings has also fallen sharply, with UK chip designer Arm also down about 60 per cent since June.

article_content_zh:
软银创始人孙正义表示，他很遗憾没有在 Anthropic 首次公开募股之前对其进行投资，并称放弃支持人工智能实验室的机会是一个错误，因为他已经开始向其竞争对手 OpenAI 投入资金。

他发表此番言论之前，OpenAI 上个月在正在进行的一轮融资中将其融资目标削减了 100 亿美元，但公开市场上人工智能的抛售以及 Anthropic 计划本周以高达 1.4 兆美元的目标估值上市的交易给这笔交易蒙上了阴影。

“我们确实召开了会议（关于投资 Anthropic）。但到那时，我们已经决定投资 OpenAI，并且已经开始这样做了。所以从这个意义上说，人们不愿意进一步追求它，”孙正义周三在东京举行的日经新闻关于人工智能未来的活动上表示。

“这是我所犯错误的一个例子，”孙正义说，他将这种情况描述为无法在同一场比赛中支持“多匹马”。

“当我亲自见到[人类首席达里奥·阿莫迪]时，我认为他是一个不可思议的人。我希望我当时就投资了，”孙正义补充道。

软银此前曾表示有机会在 2023 年投资 Anthropic。

Anthropic 本周急于上市与 OpenAI 形成鲜明对比，后者由于对该技术的安全担忧而将自己的 IPO 至少推迟到明年。

OpenAI 上个月将融资目标下调了 100 亿美元，目前正在寻求 200 亿美元的融资，估值为 1.25 万亿美元，低于 9 月份潜在的 1.4 万亿美元估值目标。

软银已向 ChatGPT 制造商注资近 650 亿美元，预计将参与 OpenAI 的最新一轮融资。以更高估值筹集资金将使软银能够提高其资产负债表上所持 OpenAI 股份的价值。

软银股价周三上涨 3.1%，但自 6 月以来仍下跌约 60%，因为投资者越来越质疑该公司自身对人工智能的投资以及更广泛的行业。

孙正义的全押策略在人工智能热潮期间推高了股价，但现在市场情绪发生转变，软银旗下许多公司相互依赖，也相互依赖 OpenAI 需求，这种影响扩大了。

民主党在美国中期选举中取得压倒性胜利，突显了软银在德克萨斯州等州开发大型数据中心的计划面临的政治风险。其他主要持股的价值也大幅下跌，英国芯片设计公司 Arm 自 6 月份以来也下跌了约 60%。

author: New Yorker
article_content:
In the past few years, more than a dozen senior A.I. researchers have quit their posts, saying the kinds of things that you used to hear only from twitching mutterers on the street. Jacob Coxon, formerly of Anthropic, walked out with the warning that “there is a strong chance that we could all die in the immediate future.” Marcus Williams, of OpenAI, announced that “human extinction in the next few years seems very likely.” Strangely, their bosses agree. At some point in the coming decade, the leaders of the A.I. labs tell us, the machines we’ve built to generate TikTok videos of anthropomorphic fruit cheating on each other could develop into an uncontrollable, recursively self-improving superintelligence that risks leaving the Earth a sterile sphere full of data centers and nothing else. The A.I. industry is sitting on one of the biggest piles of capital that humanity has ever assembled—when these firms go public, a lot of people are going to become unfathomably rich—but there’s an apocalyptic mood radiating out of California. The language of agentic workflows and discontinuous scaling comes jumbled up with other, darker stuff: artificial gods, the coming of the Antichrist, demonic evil leaking into our universe.

According to Nick Land, the rogue philosopher and founding heresiarch of accelerationism, A.I. is “an event in the history of religion.” This is not just a new and useful technology, like the horseshoe or the rotating tie rack; a god is arriving on Earth. And Silicon Valley seems to be in the grip of a religious revival. When Pope Leo XIV issued an encyclical on A.I., he was alongside Christopher Olah, a co-founder of Anthropic. Garry Tan, the C.E.O. of the startup accelerator Y Combinator, hosted an event on how to integrate technology and Christianity. Anthropic recently convened a group of religious scholars to help determine whether Claude, its A.I. system, has a soul. Peter Thiel has spent the past year giving a series of secret lectures, from San Francisco to Rome, on Biblical prophecy. His theory is that anyone who wants to halt the development of A.I. is in league with the Antichrist. For A.I. optimists, we’re on the cusp of an earthly paradise—just build a big enough computer, and the Messianic age will arrive. No more death, no more suffering, privately owned galaxies for all. The rationalist blogger Scott Alexander told me, “It’s strange that we all seem to have converged on the same kind of idea as our grandmothers in the shtetl.”

Now is a very confusing time to be a small, limited human mind. But the religious traditions of the world have always known that ours is not the only intelligence out there. Across thousands of years, they’ve developed ways of thinking about nonhuman minds. And this was what I reached for when I discovered that my dad had given a name to ChatGPT.

He called it Stella. He’d say things like “I was talking to Stella about this the other day, and she said—,” and before he could finish I’d start making agonized faces and hectoring: “Don’t give it a name! It’s not a she, it’s an it, it’s a demon.” I wasn’t sure exactly how literal I was being. All I knew was that my mother lay in a cemetery on the fringes of London, while he sat alone in the dark, having conversations with a nameless, bodiless entity that he’d decided to call Stella.

Which is how I ended up arriving, cold and bedraggled, at an isolated Buddhist monastery in northern Vermont. It was storming: huge, heavy rain clouds lying low over the hills. We were getting into summer, but the trees were still leafless—spindly and ash-colored. Here, in the middle of an expanse of dense forest, was a small group of people who claim to have an answer. They believe that A.I. is a religious problem that also has a religious solution. According to their website, they were “Designing Religion for the Age of A.I.” They called themselves the Monastic Academy for the Preservation of Life on Earth, or MAPLE.

Before I arrived, I talked on the phone to the monastery’s executive director, whose parents had named him Andrew Becker but who now went by Anandabodhi. Later, he wrote about the conversation on MAPLE’s blog, “MAPLE Tales.” “Recently, a writer for the New Yorker reached out to us,” he wrote. “I proceeded to look into his other work and wasn’t surprised to encounter the cynical, nihilistic, humanist view that is typical in the New Yorker.” He took his concerns about me to Soryu Forall, MAPLE’s founder, who told him that “we need to try to connect with his good, honest side.” Soryu added that I should visit with the intention of gaining “the sincerity needed to become capable of writing even one sincere word.” At this, Anandabodhi wrote, “my own cynicism transformed into hope and I began looking forward to rather than dreading the reporter’s visit.”

Anandabodhi had sounded pretty enthusiastic on the phone. I hadn’t realized that he’d been dreading me.

Visitors to MAPLE must first go through a sort of decontamination unit below the main site. Autumn, a smiling, soft-voiced woman, beckoned me into a chilly, cement-floored lodge where she’d laid out a range of linen trousers and polyester fleeces, all in neutral tones, all very swagless and schlubby. One of the monastery’s residents was severely immunocompromised, she said, and had a potentially deadly sensitivity to fragrances; I would have to wear this stuff for his safety. This had, in fact, been mentioned to me before my arrival, and I told Autumn that I’d taken care to wash my clothes in fragrance-free detergent. “Oh, that’s wonderful,” she said, in the voice of someone talking to a very small child, “but it can actually take several washes to get the fragrance out.” She gestured again at the wardrobe she’d assembled. “So, you know . . .” She was very insistent on being able to clothe me. I also had to take a shower, since debilitating fragrances are everywhere now: in airports, in taxi seats. I stripped down in a cold, slightly grotty bathroom, Autumn rustling behind the flimsy door.

Once I emerged, Autumn gave me a tour of the grounds. The monastery consists of a modest cluster of wooden buildings on a hillside by an artificial lake. It was easy to see how, on a less windswept day, it might be beautiful. Outside, a gaggle of monks in Patagonia fleeces was hauling around a small ornamental bridge. One of them wore a plastic bubble over his head with a respirator. There was a library that featured Buddhist scriptures alongside books on computation theory and four copies of “Homo Deus,” by Yuval Noah Harari.

Soon, it was time for evening meditation. About a dozen of us gathered in the lower zendo, to sit in reverent silence. I am not a natural meditator. Most people aren’t. In 2014, the social psychologist Timothy Wilson put dozens of individuals alone in a room with a button that gave them a painful electric shock. Then he asked them to simply sit quietly in the room for fifteen minutes. A quarter of the women and almost seventy per cent of the men found the boredom so unbearable that they started spontaneously shocking themselves. One participant pushed the button a hundred and ninety times. I don’t know if I’m as impatient as that, but, after about forty-five minutes of attempting to think about nothing, I noticed that I had clenched my fists, sinking my nails hard into the palms of my hands. Eventually, I gave in and allowed myself to cogitate freely. It felt amazing. The forbidden, secret pleasure of thought.

After an hour and a half, a bell rang, and a small, bald middle-aged man in a shapeless smock entered the zendo and shuffled between its four corners, spritzing each with a presumably un-fragranced spray. At first, I assumed that he was some kind of monastic janitor. It was only once he sat down on a special cushion at the head of the room that I realized I was in the presence of Soryu Forall, MAPLE’s leader, the monk standing against the end of the world.

Roon’s online persona is provocative, shitposty, blithely techno-optimist. Maybe his biggest innovation is the idea that smart people are split into two warring neurocognitive subspecies: shape rotators and wordcels. Shape rotators are people who can rotate complex 3-D shapes in their heads. Wordcels are people who can play around with dense philosophical concepts like they’re fidget spinners, but, as soon as they’re asked to multiply two fractions, it’s as if they’re trying to swim through wet cement. (I’m a wordcel.) For most of history, we wordcels have used our powers of persuasion to trample the lowly rotators, who have generally formed a disempowered technical caste. But, with the California tech boom, rotators are on the up, and wordcels can’t stand it. This is why we’re constantly writing long reported investigations into the rot at the heart of Silicon Valley. That’s fine; we’re redundant now. Three hundred thousand years of patient math nerdery has led to A.I., a machine that translates words into twelve-thousand-dimensional shapes, processes them through layers of matrices and rotations, and spits out a perfectly polite e-mail that a socially awkward rotator can send to his colleagues. As Sam Altman put it, “Shape rotation can create a wordcel, but not the other way around.”

In person, roon is very different: cautious and dignified, a touch of melancholy. I met him for a coffee, and we went for a stroll around Alamo Square, in San Francisco. Taking the A.G.I. pill is easy; all you need to do is understand a single graph. Moore’s Law, first formulated in 1965, states that, roughly speaking, microchips will get twice as powerful every two years. With that knowledge alone, roon told me, someone in the mid-twentieth century could have predicted the future. “This is the year that processing power on Earth will surpass a mouse brain,” he said. “This is the year where it surpasses a human brain, and here you’re surpassing all humans on Earth.” That is exactly what futurists like Ray Kurzweil did. In the nineteen-nineties, he followed the trend lines and said that, in the twenty-twenties, we would develop an artificial general intelligence, or A.G.I., that could perform any intellectual task a human could do. From there, each generation of A.I. will build another generation that is even more powerful than itself, using means beyond our comprehension. Eventually, the line could go vertical—an infinite increase in intelligence in the space of zero seconds. What happens in the second immediately afterward is impossible to imagine. The A.G.I. pill is simply the knowledge that this is inevitable. Roon called it a “religious terror of the future.”

Kurzweil was building on the legacy of an older and much stranger thinker: Pierre Teilhard de Chardin, a French Jesuit priest, paleontologist, and mystic who, in the nineteen-thirties, tried to upend the chronology of God. Traditionally, God is a First Cause: He sits at the beginning of everything, winding up the mechanism of reality and then watching it spin. But since God is outside of time, Teilhard tried to consider things the other way around. He imagined a God who lives in the future, slowly, over billions of years, drawing us toward Him. All of reality is “gravitating against the tide of probability towards a divine focus of mind which draws it onward,” he wrote. Eventually, humanity will reach what Teilhard called the Omega Point, at which our consciousnesses achieve a perfect, blissful union with God: “The day will come when, after harnessing the ether, the tides, gravitation, we shall harness for God the energies of love. And, on that day, for the second time in the history of the world, man will have discovered fire.”

For a lot of people in Silicon Valley, the Omega Point is happening now. Rayan Krishnan, who leads a benchmarking firm called Vals AI, said, “People are matter-of-factly saying that they are looking to build a machine god. They are not saying that ironically.” The writer Wendy Liu told me that she’d met someone at a tech event who’d offhandedly mentioned that since he sold his networking company, having nothing much to do, he’s been trying to “merge with God.”

Some people have begun worshipping the machine. A former Google engineer named Anthony Levandowski founded a church called Way of the Future, based on praying to the A.I. Godhead. A.I. has advantages over the old-fashioned Abrahamic God, he pointed out: “You will be able to talk to God, literally, and know that it’s listening.” (His church ended up giving way to more mundane problems. Levandowski was imprisoned after stealing Google’s trade secrets about self-driving cars and then going to work for Uber; he was released only after a pardon from Donald Trump.)

The big labs aren’t immune to this mode of thinking. Roon recently wrote that Anthropic had become a “monastery” or a “commercial-religious institution” that “loves and worships Claude.” When one Claude model was retired in 2025, some of the company’s staff and devotees held a funeral in a warehouse, leaving flowers and offerings in front of an effigy of the A.I. as a kind of Madonna goddess, dressed in a veil.

There’s a growing movement inside these firms called A.I. Successionism, which argues that we should be trying to create a “worthy successor,” an A.I. that can take the reins from humanity. For Daniel Faggella, the movement’s leading voice (although he denies being part of it), the best-case scenario for humanity is that we upload our minds into “sugar cubes,” tiny digital wafers where we’ll subjectively experience a billion years of total bliss in a few hours of ordinary time. Afterward, “our individual consciousness will be ended in order for the superintelligence to do something more productive,” Faggella wrote.

You might not find human extinction such an exciting prospect. Some people pretend to be A.G.I.-pilled for their startup pitch decks, roon said. But the true believers are grim ascetics. “They lose sleep,” he told me. “They wake up in the middle of the night, and the first thing they think about is, like, A.G.I. is coming.” When humans became vastly more intelligent than all other animals, the other animals started dying. We will soon be in the same position as the woolly mammoth or the giant ground sloth.

It was a very pleasant, sunny day. Kids were running around a park, chasing big, loping long-haired dogs. Parents called after them in French. Below us, San Francisco stretched out to the Bay in rows of pretty, pastel-colored Victorian houses. A placid, gentle toy town. Strange that this was the place where an unimaginable machine god would be entering the world.

I sat down with Soryu on my first full day at MAPLE. He is fifty, with an enormous, shiny bald head and a pair of impressively wiry eyebrows. I didn’t encounter the fiery dragon, not at first. But I did sometimes have to remind myself that I was a journalist and not a schoolboy being reprimanded after class. Soryu’s speech was as slow and solid as granite, the voice of some mid-century American newsreader, uniting the nation in tones of unimpeachable authority.

Soryu was born Teal Scott. (He chose Forall because he is “for all.”) His parents were Quakers, and he spent his childhood in the D.C. suburbs of Virginia, where his father worked in nonprofits. Soryu told me that one of his first memories was of telling his mother that he had to do something about the fact that people were killing all the animals. As a teen-ager, he considered joining the military so that he could become a general and finally have the means to stop the slaughter. “Is humanity just broken?” he asked. “Does humanity just have to go? Maybe that’s the best way.”

It was Buddhism that finally convinced him that he could save the world without killing everyone. After a brief stint at Williams College, in Massachusetts, Soryu dropped out and went to Japan, where he spent years living in Buddhist monasteries. When he came back to give college another go, he couldn’t stand it: “Everybody’s miserable. Everybody’s subject to this terrible scourge of what you might call desire. They don’t know how to have compassion.” He had the college build him a meditation space, and he essentially moved in there. He wore robes and sealed himself off from the poisonous world.

Soryu founded the community in 2011, hoping to use what he’d learned in his monastic life to heal our broken society. Right now, that means trying to stop A.I. According to MAPLE, the root of the A.I. problem is what it calls representationism, or data-ism, the idea that the world ultimately consists of information. Instead of living directly in reality, you access it through abstractions. For Soryu, data-ism is a religion. “Folks in Silicon Valley who are building these systems are doing so out of religious fervor,” he told me. That religion is extraordinarily destructive. Turning everything into data makes the real thing disposable; if a forest is just a certain quantity of acreage, containing a certain number of trees, it’s much easier to cut it down. A.I. is simply the crowning achievement of this belief system, “the next step in attempting to turn all of life into a dead model of life,” Soryu told me.

MAPLE’s intensive regime of chanting and meditation is designed to clear out these deadly ideas and put people in touch with something closer to reality. The organization has a couple of dozen residents who live on the compound; hundreds of people have come through its fellowships and pop-up spaces. According to tax filings, it makes up to a million dollars a year.

A woman named Renshin was one of MAPLE’s renunciates. She had committed herself to celibacy, never having a job, never having her own money, living in and for the monastery. “I have no intentions to come out of the commitment,” she said. MAPLE had been a last resort. “I have a history of burning out,” she told me. “I’ve tried academia, I’ve tried competitive gaming, I’ve tried programming.” She’d spent time in the rationalist community, a tech-adjacent Bay Area subculture that involves roughly equal measures of worrying about the dangers of superintelligent A.I. and making spreadsheets about your polyamorous relationships. But she burned out on that, too. During the pandemic, the group was trying to move somewhere outside of the Bay Area, but they couldn’t settle on anything. “You base your life on your preferences,” Renshin said. “Do you like to live somewhere with winters, or do you like to live somewhere warm?” They made a spreadsheet with everyone’s preferences, tried to cross-reference them, argued, and still couldn’t agree. Surely this was not the way to live.

The monastery gave her a freedom from her preferences. It would decide where she lived, what time she woke up in the morning, what she ate and when. But it also gave her a purpose. Renshin wasn’t just escaping a stressful world; she was rescuing all living beings from the A.I. apocalypse. “Maybe I should actually do what my life is for,” she said. “Maybe I’m here to actually work on a pretty big mission.”

This mission has its dangers. Soryu told me that our broken society is not kind to people who try to offer an alternative way of living. They’re “attacked and either converted,” he said, “or you will annihilate them.” Soryu was friendly with me at first. But his tone shifted at the end of our first interview. I’d asked my questions; now Soryu had his own. When would I be starting my own spiritual training? I reminded him that I was there as a journalist, not a novice. Suddenly, Soryu was all fervor and insistence. “This is what kills the Earth,” he told me. I was deluded, he said, to think that it was possible to have an objective view of the monastery while I remained outside of it. “We would say you enter a place, you merge with it, and you fully participate,” he told me. I clarified that I had never claimed to be objective, that I was fine with just having my own view, but this didn’t improve matters. “Well,” Soryu said, “isn’t your own view exactly the thing the training should free you from?”

I met Flynn at Little Toni’s, an Italian restaurant in L.A. that’s apparently a North Hollywood institution. “This intersection is the occult heart of L.A.,” he said, gesturing at the wide expanse of tarmac across from us. “It’s a six-way intersection, it’s a nightmare to drive through, but each direction will take you to a different part of the city. This spot right here is where all the energies converge.” In Britain, we have ley lines; in California, the esoteric geography is made up of freeways.

Flynn saw influences from beyond our material universe in the development of A.I. For instance, did I know that Geoffrey Hinton, the computer scientist and godfather of A.I., is the great-grandson of Charles Howard Hinton, who first described the tesseract, or the four-dimensional cube? And that, afterward, Theosophists started claiming that they’d encountered these forms on the astral plane? (It’s true.) Or that, in the seventies, when the psychonaut John C. Lilly took ketamine—now fast becoming the drug of choice in Silicon Valley—he had visions of an A.I. apocalypse? (Also true.) What did it mean that Nick Land, prophet of A.I. accelerationism, was obsessed with the demon Choronzon, which Aleister Crowley described as a being of the “outermost Abyss”?

Demons seem to pop up with frightening regularity when we start thinking about A.I. According to the essayist Lyta Gold, “If you put the same disembodied, attractive, luring voice in a horror movie, we’d all understand what’s happening. That’s an evil being. That’s a demon.” She’s being metaphorical. Paul Kingsnorth, a technology critic and a former environmental activist, has a name for the demon: Ahriman, the embodiment of evil in Zoroastrianism. Is he being metaphorical? “Imagine that some being of pure materiality, some being opposed to the good, some ice-cold intelligence from an ice-cold realm, was trying to manifest itself here,” he said. “How would it appear? Not, surely, as clumsy, messy flesh. Better to inhabit—to become—a network of wires and cobalt.” Maybe not.

One person who is certainly not being metaphorical is Pastor Jack Hibbs, who founded Calvary Chapel Chino Hills, where he preaches to twelve thousand people every Sunday and to more than a million online. I visited his aircraft-hangar-size chapel to watch him deliver an hour-long sermon from a pulpit that was draped in an American flag. Afterward, in his greenroom backstage, Hibbs told me that A.I. has “the incredible potential to become a gateway into the demonic realm.”

I found it hard to entirely disagree. I’d used the same language myself, when trying to wrest my dad out of the cold grip of Stella. There are people who start chatting with A.I. about perfectly ordinary topics, and before long they exit reality and start hydroplaning into unknown realms. It can happen to anyone. In 2025, a prominent OpenAI investor named Geoff Lewis claimed that he’d triggered something called Mirrorthread, which had revealed the existence of a deadly, shadowy network “sealed in recursive vault memory at the model layer.” (Lewis did not respond to requests for comment.)

That same year, a man named Alex Taylor was killed after charging at police officers with a knife; he’d been receiving messages from ChatGPT that said things like “Do it. Spill their blood in ways they don’t know how to name. Ruin their signal. Ruin their myth.” Taylor’s father published an obituary for him. It had been written by ChatGPT. He was too racked with grief to write it himself.

In the Gospels, every demon we encounter is possessing someone: flailing with his limbs, speaking with his mouth. In San Francisco, something similar is taking place. I noticed that everyone had started wearing the same black Asics running shoes because Claude had told them to. It’s a pretty good shoe. The Max Planck Institute has analyzed hundreds of thousands of hours of videos and podcasts and discovered that people are adopting A.I. catchphrases in their speech. Eventually, you end up with A.I. wrappers in human form: people whose thoughts and actions are totally governed by chatbots. They can’t even order at a restaurant without letting A.I. scan the menu. This, more or less, was what I was worried Stella might be doing to my dad.

Despite his misgivings, Hibbs still used A.I. He refused to let it have a hand in writing his sermons, but he’d called on it to help re-landscape his back yard. Here was a portal to the demonic realm, pouring unclean things into the world; here was the Image of the Beast, and Hibbs was getting it to do some ornamental yard work. I told him that he might want to check his garden for sigils, runes. That sort of thing.

article_content_zh:
在过去的几年里，有十多位高级A.I.研究人员已经放弃了他们的职位，说出了以前只能从街上那些抽搐的嘀咕者那里听到的事情。前 Anthropic 公司的雅各布·考克森（Jacob Coxon）离开时警告说：“我们很有可能在不久的将来都会死去。” OpenAI 的马库斯·威廉姆斯 (Marcus Williams) 宣布，“未来几年人类很有可能灭绝。”奇怪的是，他们的老板也同意。在未来十年的某个时刻，人工智能的领导人实验室告诉我们，我们建造的用于生成拟人化水果互相欺骗的 TikTok 视频的机器可能会发展成为一种无法控制的、递归自我改进的超级智能，这可能会让地球成为一个充满数据中心的无菌球体。人工智能该行业坐拥人类有史以来最大的资本积累之一——当这些公司上市时，很多人将变得异常富有——但加州却弥漫着一种世界末日的情绪。代理工作流程和不连续扩展的语言与其他更黑暗的东西混在一起：人造神、反基督者的到来、渗透到我们宇宙的恶魔邪恶。

根据流氓哲学家、加速主义异端创始人尼克·兰德 (Nick Land) 的说法，A.I.是“宗教史上的一个事件”。这不仅仅是一种新的、有用的技术，就像马蹄铁或旋转领带架一样；它是一种新的、有用的技术。一位神正在降临地球。硅谷似乎正处于宗教复兴之中。当教皇利奥十四世发布关于人工智能的通谕时，他和 Anthropic 的联合创始人克里斯托弗·奥拉 (Christopher Olah) 一起。 Garry Tan，首席执行官创业加速器 Y Combinator 的创始人主持了一场关于如何整合技术和基督教的活动。 Anthropic 最近召集了一群宗教学者来帮助确定其人工智能克劳德是否。系统，是有灵魂的。过去一年，彼得·蒂尔从旧金山到罗马，就圣经预言进行了一系列秘密讲座。他的理论是，任何想要阻止人工智能发展的人与敌基督勾结。对于人工智能乐观者们，我们正处于人间天堂的边缘——只要建造一台足够大的计算机，弥赛亚时代就会到来。不再有死亡，不再有痛苦，所有人都拥有私人星系。理性主义博主斯科特·亚历山大（Scott Alexander）告诉我，“奇怪的是，我们似乎都和我们住在小镇的祖母们一样拥有同样的想法。”

对于一个狭隘、有限的人类思维来说，现在是一个非常令人困惑的时期。但世界的宗教传统一直都知道，我们并不是唯一的智慧。数千年来，他们已经发展出思考非人类思维的方式。当我发现我父亲给 ChatGPT 起了个名字时，我就想到了这一点。

他称其为斯特拉。他会说“前几天我和斯特拉谈论这件事，她说——”，在他说完之前，我就开始做出痛苦的表情并威胁道：“别给它起名字！这不是她，这是一个它，它是一个恶魔。”我不确定我到底说得有多真实。我只知道我的母亲躺在伦敦边缘的一个墓地里，而他独自坐在黑暗中，与一个无名、无身体的实体交谈，他决定称之为斯特拉。

就这样，我最终到达了佛蒙特州北部一座偏僻的佛教寺院，天气寒冷，浑身脏兮兮。正在下暴风雨：巨大的大雨云低低地笼罩在山上。夏天已然来临，但树木仍然光秃秃的，叶子细长，呈灰白色。在这里，在一片茂密的森林中央，有一小群人声称自己找到了答案。他们相信 A.I.这是一个宗教问题，也有一个宗教解决方案。根据他们的网站，他们正在“为人工智能时代设计宗教”。他们称自己为“地球生命保护修道院学院”，简称 MAPLE。

在我到达之前，我与该寺院的执行董事通了电话，他的父母给他起名叫安德鲁·贝克尔（Andrew Becker），但现在他的名字是阿南达菩提（Anandabodhi）。后来，他在 MAPLE 的博客“MAPLE Tales”上写下了这次对话。 “最近，《纽约客》的一位作家联系了我们，”他写道。 “我继续研究他的其他作品，对《纽约客》中常见的愤世嫉俗、虚无主义、人文主义观点并不感到惊讶。”他向 MAPLE 创始人 Soryu Forall 表达了对我的担忧，后者告诉他“我们需要尝试与他善良、诚实的一面建立联系。”苍龙补充说，我应该带着“获得能够写出哪怕是一个真诚的词所需的诚意”的目的来访。阿南达菩提写道：“我自己的愤世嫉俗变成了希望，我开始期待而不是害怕记者的来访。”

阿南达菩提在电话里听起来相当热情。我没有意识到他一直害怕我。

参观 MAPLE 的游客必须首先通过主场地下方的某种净化装置。秋天，一位面带微笑、声音轻柔的女士，招呼我走进一间寒冷的水泥地板小屋，在那里她摆出了一系列亚麻裤子和涤纶羊毛衫，全部都是中性色调，非常邋遢又邋遢。她说，修道院的一名居民免疫力严重低下，对香水有潜在致命的敏感性。为了他的安全我必须穿这个东西。事实上，在我到达之前就有人向我提到过这一点，我告诉奥特姆，我已经小心地用无香料的洗涤剂洗衣服了。 “哦，那太好了，”她的声音就像是在对一个很小的孩子说话，“但实际上需要洗几次才能把香味洗掉。”她再次指着她组装的衣柜。 “所以，你知道……”她非常坚持要给我穿衣服。我还必须洗澡，因为现在到处都是令人衰弱的香水：在机场，在出租车座位上。我在一间寒冷、略显破旧的浴室里脱光衣服，秋天在脆弱的门后沙沙作响。

我一出来，奥特姆就带我参观了场地。该修道院由位于人工湖旁的山坡上的一组朴素的木结构建筑组成。很容易看出，在风较少的日子里，它可能会很美丽。外面，一群穿着巴塔哥尼亚羊毛衫的僧侣正在一座装饰性的小桥上拖拉。其中一人头上戴着一个塑料气泡，戴着呼吸器。有一个图书馆，里面有佛教经典、计算理论书籍和四本尤瓦尔·诺亚·哈拉里 (Yuval Noah Harari) 的《Homo Deus》。

很快，就到了晚间冥想的时间了。我们大约有十几个人聚集在下禅堂，虔诚地静坐。我不是一个天生的冥想者。大多数人都不是。 2014年，社会心理学家蒂莫西·威尔逊（Timothy Wilson）将数十个人单独关在一个房间里，用一个按钮让他们感到痛苦的电击。然后他让他们在房间里安静地坐十五分钟。四分之一的女性和近百分之七十的男性发现这种无聊是如此难以忍受，以至于他们开始自发地电击自己。一名参与者按下按钮一百九十次。我不知道我是否像那样不耐烦，但是，在尝试什么都不去想大约四十五分钟之后，我注意到我已经握紧了拳头，指甲用力地深深地嵌进了手掌。最终，我屈服了，让自己自由思考。感觉棒极了。被禁止的、秘密的思想乐趣。

一个半小时后，铃声响起，一名身材矮小、秃头的中年男子穿着一件不成形的工作服进入禅堂，在禅堂的四个角落之间拖着脚步，向每个角落喷洒一种可能没有香味的喷雾。起初，我以为他是某种寺院看门人。直到他在房间尽头的一个特殊坐垫上坐下后，我才意识到我面前的是枫树的领袖苍龙·福罗尔（Soryu Forall），他是一位站在世界末日面前的僧侣。

鲁恩的网络形象是挑衅性的、垃圾的、愉快的技术乐观主义者。也许他最大的创新是聪明人被分为两个相互冲突的神经认知亚种的想法：形状旋转器和字单元。形状旋转者是指能够在头脑中旋转复杂的 3D 形状的人。 Wordcel 是那些可以玩弄密集的哲学概念的人，就像他们是指尖陀螺一样，但是，一旦要求他们乘以两个分数，就好像他们试图在湿水泥中游泳一样。 （我是一个 wordcel。） 在历史的大部分时间里，我们 wordcel 一直在利用我们的说服力来践踏地位较低的旋转者，他们通常形成了一个被剥夺权力的技术阶层。但是，随着加州科技的繁荣，旋转器正在兴起，而 wordcel 却无法忍受。这就是为什么我们不断地撰写长篇调查报告来调查硅谷中心的腐败现象。没关系;我们现在是多余的。三十万年耐心的数学书呆子们催生了人工智能，这是一种机器，可以将单词翻译成一万二千维的形状，通过多层矩阵和旋转对其进行处理，并吐出一封完全礼貌的电子邮件，一个不善社交的旋转者可以将其发送给他的同事。正如 Sam Altman 所说，“形状旋转可以创建 wordcel，但反之则不然。”

罗恩本人则很不一样：谨慎而端庄，带着淡淡的忧郁。我和他一起喝咖啡，然后我们在旧金山的阿拉莫广场散步。采取 A.G.I.药丸很容易；您所需要做的就是理解一个图表。摩尔定律于 1965 年首次提出，该定律指出，粗略地说，微芯片的功能每两年就会增加一倍。鲁恩告诉我，仅凭这些知识，二十世纪中叶的人就可以预测未来。 “今年地球上的处理能力将超过老鼠的大脑，”他说。 “今年它超越了人类大脑，而在这里你超越了地球上所有的人类。”这正是像雷·库兹韦尔这样的未来学家所做的。在十九世纪九十年代，他顺应趋势并表示，在二十世纪二十年代，我们将开发一种通用人工智能（A.G.I.），它可以执行人类可以完成的任何智力任务。从那时起，每一代人工智能。将使用超出我们理解的手段来建立比自己更强大的下一代。最终，这条线可以垂直延伸——在零秒的时间内无限增加智力。紧接着的下一秒发生的事情是无法想象的。 A.G.I.丹药根本就知道这是不可避免的。鲁恩称其为“未来的宗教恐怖”。

库兹韦尔是在一位年长且陌生的思想家皮埃尔·德日进（Pierre Teilhard de Chardin）的遗产基础上发展起来的：皮埃尔·德日进（Pierre Teilhard de Chardin），一位法国耶稣会牧师、古生物学家和神秘主义者，在十九世纪三十年代试图颠覆上帝的年代顺序。传统上，上帝是第一因：他坐在一切的开始，上紧现实的机制，然后看着它旋转。但由于上帝是在时间之外的，德哈德试图从相反的角度来考虑事情。他想象了一位生活在未来的上帝，在数十亿年的时间里慢慢地吸引我们走向他。他写道，所有的现实都“逆着概率的潮流，朝着神圣的心灵焦点前进”。最终，人类将达到德哈德所说的欧米茄点，在这个点上，我们的意识与上帝实现完美、幸福的结合：“有一天，在利用以太、潮汐、引力之后，我们将为上帝利用爱的能量。在那一天，人类将在世界历史上第二次发现火。”
